title: Paris Perdikaris: When And Why PINNs Fail To Train
speaker: Paris Perdikaris
one_sentence: This lecture explains that physics-informed neural networks fail not because adding physics to training is wrong, but because the resulting math problem for the optimizer can become stiff, spectrally biased, and badly balanced—where one loss term overpowers others.
core_problem: PINNs turn a PDE problem into a composite neural-network training problem: fit data, boundary conditions, initial conditions, and PDE residuals at the same time. That sounds elegant, but the optimizer may not send each constraint enough gradient signal—the mathematical direction and strength telling the network which way to update. High-frequency components, multiple scales, and boundaries especially suffer because the gradients pointing toward satisfying each constraint can be weak or cancel out.
first_principles_model: A PINN represents the unknown field with a differentiable neural network—one whose output can be taken apart mathematically to compute derivatives. Automatic differentiation evaluates these derivatives, the PDE residual becomes a loss term to minimize, and gradient descent updates the network. The real object being solved is therefore not just the PDE; it is a constrained optimization dynamics—a system where changes to the network weights chase down multiple simultaneous goals. If that dynamics is stiff (requiring tiny steps) or biased (favoring certain frequencies), the PDE can be simple while training still fails.
key_claims: Physics can be inserted through network design choices (architecture-level inductive bias) or through loss terms (loss-level regularization); PINNs mostly use the second route.
PINNs are unusual regularizers because they penalize the function output and its derivatives, not just the network weights themselves.
Even simple linear elliptic problems can fail if the training dynamics cannot satisfy boundary conditions or high-frequency structure.
PINN gradient flow can become stiff, forcing impractically small learning rates if trained without special techniques.
Different loss terms can produce imbalanced gradients, so one constraint can dominate while another receives almost no update.
Neural tangent kernel analysis helps diagnose spectral bias: low-frequency components are learned faster than high-frequency components.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to represent a solution to a differential equation while also penalizing violations of that equation and its boundary or initial conditions.
A training goal made from several terms added together, such as data mismatch, boundary loss, initial-condition loss, and PDE residual loss.
A training problem where the continuous-time optimization system contains widely separated time scales, forcing stable gradient descent to take tiny steps.
A failure where different loss terms produce very different gradient sizes, so some constraints are effectively ignored while others move the network.
The tendency of standard neural networks trained by gradient descent to learn smooth, low-frequency patterns before sharp, high-frequency patterns.

stanford_connections: This is the natural starting point for the playlist because it separates the PINN idea from whether PINNs can actually train well.
It connects to later talks on weak forms, adaptive weighting, operator learning, and architectures that preserve physical structure.
It builds a diagnostic habit: do not ask only whether the physics loss is correct; ask whether the optimizer can actually use it to improve the network.
practical_caution: Do not treat a small PDE residual loss as proof that the learned field is physically reliable. The loss weights, collocation points (where the PDE is checked), network architecture, optimizer choice, and the frequencies present in the true solution can all change whether the method is actually solving the intended problem.
selected_evidence: Failure can happen at any time even for the simplest problems.
This gradient flow problem becomes very stiff.
Stiffness leads to imbalance gradients during back propagation.
The network cannot really change the parameters in order to fit the boundary condition.
Neural networks are known to suffer from spectral bias.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that PINNs are optimization systems, not magic PDE solvers. Their success depends on whether the training dynamics can send the right physical constraints into the right parts of the network function.

title: Donsub Rim: Distilling Nonlinear Shock Waves
speaker: Donsub Rim
one_sentence: This lecture explains why classical linear reduced-order models fail on transport-dominated problems and how nonlinear representations can capture moving shocks and interfaces more efficiently.
core_problem: Classical reduced-order models assume a solution manifold (the smooth surface where all solutions live) can be well represented by a low-dimensional linear space. Transport-dominated problems break that assumption: a pulse or shock moving across a domain generates many nearly orthogonal snapshots, so linear rank grows even when the underlying motion is simple. Moving things look complicated when you write them as combinations of fixed basis vectors.
first_principles_model: For transport, the low-dimensional object is often not the field values themselves but the map that moves information through space. If a feature shifts from one place to another, the set of snapshots may be high-rank, while the characteristic flow (how the medium carries the wave forward) or deformation map may be low-dimensional. Nonlinear model reduction tries to represent that moving geometry directly instead of collecting snapshots in a linear space.
key_claims: Transport-dominated and moving-interface problems are hard for traditional reduced models because motion spreads snapshots across many dimensions.
Kolmogorov n-width (a measure of how well a solution set fits into an n-dimensional subspace) explains why a linear basis can need many modes even for simple moving discontinuities.
The solution manifold may be high-rank while the characteristic map that transports the solution is low-dimensional.
Nonlinear reduced representations can be built by composing reduced bases with learned or constructed maps.
Shock formation creates additional difficulty because the characteristic representation can break or become non-smooth.
Deep networks can be interpreted as a way to compress a large solution representation into a smaller nonlinear reduced network.

important_terms.meaning: A PDE problem where motion, advection (waves carried by flow), shocks, or interfaces dominate the dynamics.
A number measuring how well a solution manifold can be approximated by an n-dimensional linear subspace.
A map showing how points or features move through the domain under transport dynamics.
A reduced model that approximates a solution manifold using nonlinear coordinates or transformations instead of only a linear basis.
A compact neural representation built to approximate a solution family more efficiently than a large generic network.

stanford_connections: This connects directly to the reduced-order modeling concept page and gives the first major exception to linear ROM intuition.
It prepares later lectures on nonlinear manifolds, registration-based reduction, and latent-space simulation.
It also explains why data-driven simulation cannot ignore geometry: a simple translation can look high-dimensional in raw coordinates.
practical_caution: If a reduced model fails on shocks or advection, the problem may not be lack of data. The coordinate system may be wrong: the low-dimensional structure may live in transport maps, not in linear combinations of snapshots. Choosing how to represent the solution matters more than gathering more snapshots.
selected_evidence: Transport dominated problems are hard to handle with traditional reduced models.
Low-dimensional reduced spaces cannot exist.
The solution manifold itself is not low rank.
There is still a low dimensional structure available.
When there's shock formation.
takeaway: The lecture's key move is to distinguish low-dimensional physics from low-rank snapshots. Moving waves can be simple in the right coordinates and expensive in the wrong ones.

title: Jan Hesthaven: Non-Intrusive ROMs Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
speaker: Jan Hesthaven
one_sentence: This lecture shows how neural networks can replace mathematical projections in reduced-order modeling when you cannot look inside the full simulator and must learn from its input-output data alone.
core_problem: Projection-based ROMs work well if you can access the governing equations, but many real solvers are old, proprietary, classified, or commercial and only available as closed programs. For nonlinear problems, even ROMs built with full access can slow down because evaluating the projected nonlinear equations still requires returning to the full state dimension.
first_principles_model: A ROM trades generality for speed by learning a compact map from parameters to solution coefficients. If the full operator is open, projection-based math gives you equations for those coefficients directly. If the operator is closed, a neural network can learn the parameter-to-coefficient map from repeated runs of the simulator, and adding physics-informed loss terms can improve how closely the predictions obey the underlying physics.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling speeds up repeated parameterized PDE solves by representing solutions using a small set of basis vectors.
Nonlinear problems create a bottleneck because the projected nonlinear equations still depend on the full-dimensional state.
Non-intrusive ROMs are necessary when you have only the input and output of the solver, not its internal structure.
A neural network can map parameters directly to the expansion coefficients in the reduced basis.
If a good reduced basis exists, the parameter-to-coefficient map should usually be smooth enough for a small neural network to learn.
Physics-informed neural networks can supplement classical ROM construction, solving specific bottlenecks rather than replacing numerical solvers entirely.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that needs access to the solver's equations or internal structure.
A reduced-order model built from input-output data without modifying or examining the full solver.
The low-dimensional numbers multiplying each reduced basis vector to rebuild an approximate solution.
The cost or access barrier that arises when reduced equations still require full-dimensional operator calculations.
A failure where the neural parameter-to-coefficient map is too complex for the number of simulator runs used to train it.

stanford_connections: This lecture lays out the practical ROM workflow that later talks build on: collecting snapshots from the full simulator offline, constructing a reduced basis from them, then using a fast predictor online.
It places PINNs in a concrete engineering role: fixing specific bottlenecks in ROM construction rather than replacing full numerical solvers.
It connects to design workflows because ROMs become most valuable when you must run many parameterized simulations in sequence.
practical_caution: A neural ROM only works if the reduced basis captures the essential shape of solutions and if the learned coefficient map works on new parameter values outside the training set. Making the neural network deeper or wider without proportionally more simulator data can cause overfitting, making predictions worse on untested parameters.
selected_evidence: Creating the reduced model becomes intrusive.
All you have is a piece of code that can provide you input output.
The key problem becomes how to go from choosing a parameter.
Let's use a neural net for this exercise.
When you don't have enough data... you're overfitting.
takeaway: The lecture's central lesson is practical: use neural networks where classical ROM methods hit a wall, particularly when the solver is only available as a closed program or when nonlinear coefficient maps are expensive.

title: Nils Thuerey: Differentiable Physics Simulations For Deep Learning
speaker: Nils Thuerey
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to connect simulators and deep learning by making the simulator compute gradients, so that signals from physical laws can guide learning, answer inverse problems, and improve control.
core_problem: Using simulators only to generate training data misses a chance. Many real applications need to know: if I change an input, a parameter, or a control signal, how would the physical outcome change? To answer that question, you need gradients that flow back through the simulator.
first_principles_model: A simulator takes initial conditions, parameters, or control actions and predicts future physical states. If the simulator computes gradients, you can turn the problem around: start from a desired outcome and work backward to find what causes would produce it. This lets you reduce numerical error, infer what controls produced an observation, improve designs, and train neural networks inside the physics simulation loop. The simulator stops being just a data generator and becomes part of the optimization path itself.
key_claims: Physical models and numerical methods have real value and should be preserved when possible, with learning handling measurement noise, observation gaps, and unknown effects.
Forward simulation shows you what will happen; inverse problems ask what initial conditions or actions would lead to a desired outcome.
Learning from simulator-generated data is helpful but loosely connected to the physics.
Adding physics only to the loss function creates a tighter connection, but differentiable simulation creates the tightest coupling between simulator and learning.
What matters most is the gradient of the simulation result with respect to the starting conditions or the action taken.
Solvers that compute gradients can be used inside the training loop for learning, control, and fixing errors in approximate numerical methods.

important_terms.meaning: A simulator that computes and returns gradients showing how its outputs would change if inputs, states, control signals, or parameters changed.
A learning system where a numerical solver runs as part of training and provides gradient information to guide the learning.
A method for efficiently calculating how a small change at the end of a simulation would have needed to change earlier steps to produce that outcome.
A problem where you start with observed or desired outcomes and work backward to find the hidden causes, parameters, or actions that led to them.
Learning a small adjustment that cancels out errors introduced by using coarse computational grids, simple mathematical methods, or approximate solvers.

stanford_connections: This is the differentiable-simulation foundation for the playlist and extends PINNs by moving the solver into the learning process rather than only adding penalty terms.
It connects to control, inverse design, fluid simulation, and upcoming talks on machine learning for science.
It also bridges classical adjoint methods from scientific computing to modern automatic differentiation tools.
practical_caution: Gradients are useful only if they accurately reflect what really happens and if computing them stays fast enough. Large codes that combine many physics domains, long prediction horizons, sudden discontinuities, and unstable math can still make this approach impractical despite the theory.
selected_evidence: Ideally there shouldn't be much of a boundary between learning and simulation.
We have a gradient of this simulation.
This actually lets us combine simulation very neatly with the deep learning process.
The first example... is this solver in the loop project.
Differentiable solvers is a very useful tool.
takeaway: The core insight is that gradients turn simulation from an opaque data source into something you can optimize through. That is why differentiable physics matters for inverse problems, control, and machine learning applied to science.

title: Pawan Goyal: Physics-Informed Learning For Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
speaker: Pawan Goyal
organization: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems
one_sentence: Operator inference learns reduced dynamical models from data while keeping the known physics structure built in.
core_problem: Engineering design, control, optimization, and uncertainty studies need dynamical models you can simulate many times over. High-fidelity detailed models can take too long to run, and older or commercial simulators may not give you the internal equations needed for classical projection-based model reduction.
first_principles_model: A dynamical system can often be captured by a small set of key directions (dominant modes—the low-dimensional patterns that describe the main behavior). Operator inference tries to learn the small reduced operators directly from trajectory data, using the known structure of the governing equations so the learned model looks like what classical reduction would have produced if you had access to all the equations.
key_claims: Dynamical models are needed to analyze how systems change over time under new operating conditions.
Two major obstacles are turning complex processes into equations and the huge size of detailed high-fidelity models.
The goal is to jump from differential equation data straight to small reduced models without needing the full discretized model.
Operator inference learns the reduced equations from data while keeping the known structure of the physics.
If the data excite enough different behaviors, the learned equations can match the reduced models that classical methods would have found.
The approach is especially useful when data come from older codes, commercial solvers, or specialized simulation tools.

important_terms.meaning: A method that learns the equations of a reduced dynamical system by studying state trajectory data.
A detailed mathematical model with many degrees of freedom, often so expensive to run that you cannot simulate it repeatedly.
Low-dimensional patterns that capture the main behavior of a large dynamical system.
A simulator that produces output data but does not easily give you the internal equations or matrices that make it work.
Learning that follows known equation structure instead of fitting an unconstrained general-purpose predictor.

stanford_connections: This continues the non-intrusive ROM theme but focuses on learning the reduced dynamics themselves.
It connects to differentiable simulation and inverse problems because a learned reduced model can become the fast inner loop for control.
It also reinforces the series-wide pattern: use data to infer missing equations, but keep physical structure whenever possible.
practical_caution: Operator inference is not just fitting a curve. If the assumed operator structure is wrong or the training trajectories do not exercise important modes, the reduced model may predict accurately on short runs and then fail in longer predictions or control.
selected_evidence: We have focused on operator inference approach to learn dynamical systems.
We need dynamical models to analyze transient behavior.
There are two main bottleneck.
Can we go out of these two steps?
Compute reduced order model directly from the data.
takeaway: Learn the small dynamical system that classical reduction would have produced, but infer it directly from data when the full detailed model is unavailable or too costly to use.

title: Youngsoo Choi: Efficient Nonlinear Manifold Reduced Order Model
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This short lecture explains how nonlinear manifold ROMs (a way to turn a huge simulation into a small one using a curved space instead of a straight one) can stay accurate on flows where material moves fast, and how hyper-reduction makes the curved-space decoder cheap enough to use.
core_problem: Linear-subspace ROMs are fast when solution snapshots cluster near a flat low-dimensional space. But advection-dominated flows (where fluid or material gets pushed around), shocks, and moving structures often do not. A curved manifold (a nonlinear space) can show these solution families more faithfully, but a simple curved-manifold ROM can run slower than the full simulation because the decoder and residual terms still need full-dimensional work.
first_principles_model: A full simulation tracks a very large state (all the numbers). A ROM swaps that for a small latent coordinate (a handful of numbers that stand in). In a linear ROM, you rebuild the big state by multiplying a basis by coefficients. In a curved-manifold ROM, you rebuild it using a learned nonlinear map, often built as an autoencoder (two neural networks—one that compresses, one that expands). The remaining slowdown is that evaluating the nonlinear residual (the mismatch between the model and the actual behavior) still touches every entry, so hyper-reduction picks only the entries you actually need to approximate the residual.
key_claims: Surrogate models (quick stand-ins for expensive simulations) matter for multi-query tasks like design optimization because full simulations can take too long.
More invasive surrogate models (ones that dig into the physics equations) can be more accurate but usually demand more access to the equations and are harder to speed up.
Curved-manifold ROMs use nonlinear maps, like autoencoder decoders, instead of linear basis times coefficients.
Without hyper-reduction, curved-manifold ROMs stay impractical because nonlinear terms still scale with the full simulation size.
Gappy POD (a sampling method where you pick a few key spots instead of using the whole field) can shrink how many decoder outputs you have to compute.
On a flow with both pushing (advection) and smoothing (viscosity) like Burgers equation, the curved-manifold ROM matches the full simulation better than a flat-subspace ROM.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that rebuilds full states from a few latent numbers using a curved map instead of a straight one (linear basis).
The part of a neural network that takes a handful of latent numbers and expands them back into a full state.
A speed-up trick that cuts the cost of nonlinear term evaluation by only calculating a sampled subset of entries instead of the whole vector.
A method that reconstructs a full field by taking samples at chosen spots and combining them in a reduced basis.
A flow where material gets pushed around and traveling fast, which tends to break the flat low-rank structure that linear methods assume.

stanford_connections: This continues the shock-wave lecture: if pushing (advection) breaks flat low-rank structure, switch to curved coordinates.
It ties to later latent-space and autoencoder ROM talks by making the decoder cost visible and real.
It also reinforces a recurring DDPS theme: getting the shape right (representation) is only half the job; the actual running speed also matters.
practical_caution: A curved latent code can look accurate but still run slower than the original solver if you don't also cut the cost of residual evaluation. Real ROM design must measure both how close the approximation is to the truth and how fast it actually runs.
selected_evidence: One full simulation takes 7.4 days.
More intrusiveness means more accuracy.
NM ROM uses a non-linear manifold representation using non-linear map G.
These non-linear terms still scale with the full order model size.
NM ROM achieves less than 1% maximum relative error.
takeaway: The lecture's core lesson is that curved manifolds solve a shape problem (how to represent the solutions), while hyper-reduction solves a speed problem (how to make it run fast). A useful ROM needs both.

title: Jesse Chan: Entropy Stable Schemes For Nonlinear Conservation Laws
speaker: Jesse Chan
one_sentence: This lecture explains entropy stability as a way to build high-order discretizations of nonlinear conservation laws that stay reliable near shocks, turbulence, and features too small to resolve.
core_problem: High-order numerical methods can be accurate on smooth PDE solutions but unreliable on nonlinear conservation laws. Shocks, turbulence, and under-resolved gradients can cause the solution to blow up unless the method adds filtering, limiting, or artificial viscosity. Those fixes can work, but they create a tuning tradeoff between reliability and accuracy.
first_principles_model: A nonlinear conservation law transports conserved variables through fluxes. For many physical systems there is an entropy or energy-like quantity that should satisfy an inequality. An entropy-stable discretization is built so the semi-discrete numerical scheme respects the same entropy inequality, making stability a built-in property rather than a repair added when the scheme starts to fail.
key_claims: Burgers, shallow water, Euler, Navier-Stokes, and MHD systems can be viewed through nonlinear conservation laws with entropy structure.
High-order DG methods are attractive because they combine geometric flexibility with high-order accuracy.
Under-resolved shocks and turbulence make naive high-order schemes unreliable.
Traditional stabilization through artificial viscosity, filtering, or slope limiting can reduce accuracy and require tuning.
Entropy-stable schemes use entropy variables, numerical fluxes, and discrete entropy inequalities to build reliability into the scheme.
The method can be extended beyond collocation-style methods toward modal DG and reduced-order modeling.

important_terms.meaning: A PDE expressing that conserved quantities change through fluxes (flow) across boundaries.
A mathematical inequality for an energy-like quantity (one that increases with disorder, never decreases) that physically valid solutions must satisfy.
Variables obtained by taking the derivative (rate of change) of the entropy with respect to the conservative quantities.
A high-order finite-element-style discretization that represents solutions separately in each region and connects regions through numerical fluxes.
Added numerical diffusion used to stabilize features too small to resolve, often at the cost of accuracy.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds the numerical-analysis side of reliability to the ML-heavy talks: physical validity depends on discretization structure too.
It connects to fluid simulation and reduced-order modeling because learned or reduced models inherit stability issues from the equations they approximate.
It is a useful counterweight to learned surrogates without validation: before learning the solution, understand what the numerical scheme must preserve.
practical_caution: Do not evaluate a learned fluid surrogate only by short-horizon error. If the underlying conservation-law structure or entropy behavior is wrong, under-resolved shocks and turbulence can create unstable or incorrect rollouts that violate conservation.
selected_evidence: They generally blow up whenever they encounter under-resolved solutions.
Shocks and turbulence... are highly under-resolved solutions most of the time.
I wanted to avoid the common metrics used for higher schemes... artificial viscosity filtering... slope limiting.
They can tend to reduce the amount of the accuracy.
A class of nonlinear conservation laws which all admit an entropy inequality.
takeaway: Entropy stability is the idea that reliability should be built from the physics of the PDE, not added after the scheme starts failing.

title: Irina Tezaur: Schwarz Alternating Method For Concurrent Multiscale Coupling In Solid Mechanics
speaker: Irina Tezaur
one_sentence: This lecture presents Schwarz alternating domain decomposition as a way to couple different solid-mechanics models across scales without forcing the whole domain to use one resolution or solver.
core_problem: Engineering solids often contain localized small-scale physics that determines global behavior. Simulating the entire structure at the finest scale is too expensive, but coupling coarse and fine models can introduce errors at the interface, require incompatible solvers, and create unstable information flow between regions.
first_principles_model: Domain decomposition splits a difficult PDE domain into subdomains. Schwarz iteration solves each subproblem while exchanging boundary or overlap information with neighboring subdomains, repeatedly updating until the coupled solution is consistent. For multiscale mechanics, this allows different discretizations (ways of converting the continuous problem into discrete pieces), material models, or time integrators to coexist in different regions.
key_claims: Concurrent multiscale coupling is needed when a local small-scale event controls system-level performance.
The coupling method should allow different solvers and time integrators in different regions.
The interface should not introduce errors that don't exist in the actual physics.
Schwarz alternating methods split a large domain into smaller, simpler subdomains and iteratively assemble the global solution.
The approach has convergence theory for finite-deformation quasistatic nonlinear PDEs.
Small overlap regions can be sufficient in practical examples, but non-overlapping and contact cases require additional care.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation approach where different scales are solved at the same time in different parts of the domain.
An iterative domain-decomposition method that solves subdomain problems and exchanges boundary or overlap information.
A shared region between subdomains used to pass solution information and accelerate convergence (the process of reaching a stable, correct answer).
A mechanics regime where deformations are large enough that nonlinear geometry and material response matter.
An unphysical behavior introduced by coupling models or meshes incorrectly across a subdomain boundary.

stanford_connections: This lecture broadens DDPS from learned surrogates to hybrid numerical coupling: not every data-driven physical simulation problem is solved by replacing the solver.
It connects to hybrid twins because real systems often need local high-fidelity patches inside larger coarse models.
It also reinforces the importance of interface conditions, a recurring issue in multiphysics and differentiable-simulation workflows.
practical_caution: A multiscale simulation can fail at the coupling interface even if each submodel is correct in isolation. The handoff of boundary, overlap, or contact information is part of the model and determines whether the global prediction stays true to physics.
selected_evidence: A small-scale event will eventually determine the performance of the entire system.
Allow us to use different solvers and time integrators in different regions.
We don't want the coupling to introduce any non-physical artifacts.
The earliest known domain decomposition method.
You decompose that domain into simpler subdomains.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that multiscale modeling is an interface problem: the global prediction is only as trustworthy as the exchange rule between local and coarse physics.

title: Steven Brunton: Interpretable And Generalizable Machine Learning For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Steven Brunton
one_sentence: This lecture argues that fluid ML should prefer simple, interpretable, physically meaningful models that work well on new problems not seen during training.
core_problem: Fluid mechanics produces high-dimensional data and expensive simulations, but just predicting outputs is not enough. A model can match the flow it has seen before while failing when conditions change—new controls, different shapes, changed parameters—if it has not captured the sparse (few important) physical structure hiding inside the flow.
first_principles_model: Many fluid systems show a lot of data in how we measure them but simplify into just a few key directions, and their governing dynamics often use only a sparse subset of possible terms. Interpretable ML tries to find those directions, identify which terms matter, find correction terms for missing physics, or spot where approximate models need adjustment rather than building a hidden system that just maps inputs to outputs.
key_claims: Machine learning for engineering can be viewed as optimization and regression over rich data.
Generalization requires more than fitting trajectories; models should capture simple structure where it exists.
The principle of simplicity motivates sparse models: as simple as possible, but no simpler.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) learns governing equations from measured states and how they change over time.
Choosing the right coordinates (ways to measure and describe the flow) can turn a high-dimensional fluid problem into a low-dimensional model.
ML can also focus on discrepancy modeling: learning the mismatch between an imperfect physical model and observed dynamics.

important_terms.meaning: The modeling principle that a useful explanation should use the simplest structure sufficient to describe the phenomenon.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics, a method that selects a small number of active terms from a library of candidate dynamics.
Regression that encourages most candidate coefficients to be zero, leaving only the important terms.
Finding variables in which complicated high-dimensional dynamics become simpler.
Learning the mismatch term between an approximate physical model and the true observed system.

stanford_connections: This is the conceptual link between reduced-order models (simpler versions that keep key behavior), operator inference (learning how operations change the system), and scientific ML: learn structure, not just outputs.
It connects to later surrogate and closure talks because closures are often discrepancy models for physics that happens below our measurement resolution.
It also gives a benchmark for interpretability: can the learned object be inspected as equations, modes (directions of motion), balances (how forces relate), or correction terms?
practical_caution: A neural model that forecasts fluid snapshots may still be scientifically weak if it does not show what variables, balances (how different forces add up), or missing-physics terms are driving the flow. Generalization should be tested by trying new regimes, not just checking whether it works on data in between the training examples.
selected_evidence: It would not generalize beyond fall.
Things should be as simple as possible and no simpler.
Mathematically today in my opinion is sparsity.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics or SINDy.
If we pull out the right coordinate system you can get a very very simple model.
takeaway: The lecture's first-principles message is that interpretability is not decoration. In fluids, when you can actually see and write down the structure, that is often exactly what lets the model work on new problems.

title: Alfio Quarteroni: The Mathematical Heart
speaker: Alfio Quarteroni
one_sentence: This lecture treats the heart as a coupled multiphysics, multiscale simulation problem spanning electrophysiology, mechanics, blood flow, valves, circulation, and coronary perfusion.
core_problem: Heart function is not a single PDE or a single simulator. Electrical activation drives contraction; contraction deforms tissue; deformation moves blood; valves open and close; coronary flow perfuses the myocardium; and the whole organ couples to external circulation. Each subsystem has different scales, meshes, equations, and numerical requirements.
first_principles_model: A computational heart model starts from geometry, meshes, and core cardiac physics modules. Electrophysiology models electrical propagation through the myocardium. Active and passive mechanics model contraction and tissue deformation. Fluid dynamics models blood in chambers and vessels. Circulation and perfusion models provide boundary and network coupling. The system-level model combines all these modules.
key_claims: First-principles mathematical models can describe the electrical, mechanical, and fluid-dynamical processes of the heart.
The heart is a multiphysics problem (many interacting physical systems) with multiscale behavior in space and time.
Patient-specific geometry can come from CT, MRI, atlas models, or CAD-like solid models.
Different meshes may be needed for myocardium electrophysiology/mechanics and chamber blood flow.
Core cardiac models include electrophysiology, active mechanics, passive mechanics, fluid dynamics, valve motion, and coronary perfusion.
Comprehensive finite-element and reduced-order libraries are needed because full models are computationally expensive and uncertainty matters.

important_terms.meaning: The modeling of electrical activation and propagation through heart tissue.
Cell-level contractile mechanics that generate force in response to electrical activation.
Organ-level tissue deformation due to material elasticity and loading.
Coupling between blood flow and deforming cardiac walls or valves.
Modeling blood supply through large coronary vessels and many smaller intramyocardial vessels using separate descriptions for each scale.

stanford_connections: This is the playlist's clean example of a hybrid multiphysics simulator where data-driven methods must respect several coupled physical modules.
It connects to ROMs because patient-specific studies and uncertainty quantification need faster surrogates of expensive heart simulations.
It connects to differentiable simulation and inverse problems because clinical use often asks for parameter estimation from patient data.
practical_caution: A model of one cardiac subsystem can be mathematically correct but fail clinically if the interactions between systems are wrong. The hard part is not solving electrophysiology, mechanics, or flow separately—it is keeping their time scales, boundary conditions, and feedback loops in sync.
selected_evidence: Electrical, mechanical and fluid-dynamical processes occurring in the heart.
A classical multi-physics problem featuring multi-scale solutions in space and time.
They include the electrophysiology, the active mechanics... the passive mechanics... the fluid dynamics.
We need however a second grid... for simulating the fluid dynamical processes.
You have to account for variability and uncertainty.
takeaway: The heart lecture shows what first-principles scientific ML must eventually handle: not a single learned model, but a coupled computational physiology stack.

title: Byungsoo Kim: Data-Driven Methods For Fluid Simulations In Computer Graphics
speaker: Byungsoo Kim
one_sentence: This lecture explains how computer graphics simulates fluids using data-driven methods to speed up calculation while keeping the look convincing, giving artists control, and letting animators direct the result.
core_problem: Computer graphics needs fluid simulations that look convincing, run fast enough to use in production, and respond to artist control. Real-world accuracy matters, but the main goal is usually how the motion looks and whether artists can shape it, not whether every number exactly matches physics equations.
first_principles_model: A physics-based graphics simulator creates motion for water, smoke, splashes, or similar materials. Data-driven methods—trained models learned from example data—can replace slow parts of the solver, add visual detail to coarse simulations, work in compressed space, stylize flow patterns, or optimize control settings through differentiable simulation (where you can take gradients of the simulator to guide optimization). The key constraint is not only matching physics; it is creating visually convincing, controllable output for production.
key_claims: Physics-based animation has developed, but production work still needs fast and controllable simulation tools.
Graphics can accept some loss of exact accuracy in exchange for speed, control, and visual quality.
Neural networks can speed up particle or grid solvers and the pressure calculation step.
Latent-space fluid solvers use autoencoders and sequence models to evolve smaller, compressed representations instead of full-resolution fields.
Data-driven methods can enhance visual detail through turbulence synthesis, splash generation, and super-resolution upscaling.
Differentiable physics provides a way to optimize controls or starting states by taking gradients through the simulator toward a target result.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation that lets artists control what the motion looks like while still staying physically plausible.
Applying artistic style ideas to fluid volumes, such as artistic smoke patterns or color changes.
Training a neural network to add sharp, smooth high-resolution detail to low-resolution fluid simulations.
A solver that evolves compressed representations of the flow instead of the full-size field.
Using gradients computed through a simulator to optimize motion controllers or initial starting states.

stanford_connections: This talk shows that data-driven simulation goals differ by field: graphics values control and appearance in ways engineering verification does not.
It connects to differentiable physics by showing a concrete use case where simulator gradients enable creative control.
It also links to compressed-space approximations and super-resolution as practical examples of trained simulation speedup.
practical_caution: A graphics shortcut should not be measured by engineering or scientific accuracy standards alone, but the opposite is also true: a visually convincing flow model may fail for scientific prediction or safety-critical design.
selected_evidence: For visual effect artists it is necessary to have a physically plausible but computational efficient and also art-directable simulation tool.
It's allowed to sacrifice accuracy to some extent for performance and controllability.
Deep learning methods can provide faster realistic and more controllable simulations.
Latent space fluid solvers with auto encoders and LSTM architectures.
Differentiability... optimize its motion controller or initial parameter settings to achieve a target state.
takeaway: The lecture's first-principles lesson is that what you measure determines the simulator: graphics data-driven simulators optimize for convincing controllable appearance, while engineering data-driven simulators optimize for accurate prediction.

title: Karthik Duraisamy: Towards Robust, Accurate And Tractable Reduced-Order Models
speaker: Karthik Duraisamy
one_sentence: This lecture organizes practical reduced-order modeling around three competing needs: building models that stay accurate even when conditions change, match the real physics with low error, and run fast enough to be useful for design and prediction.
core_problem: Reduced-order models are appealing because they replace a huge full-order system with a much smaller one that runs in seconds instead of hours. But flows like combustion combine many hard things at once: equations that evolve on different timescales, transport and acoustic waves, heat from chemical reaction, shapes that change topology, and residuals with strong nonlinearities. A model that works perfectly under one operating condition may become unstable, violate conservation laws, or stay expensive when the physics or parameters shift.
first_principles_model: A reduced-order model represents the governing equations on a lower-dimensional manifold, a simplified geometric space. For nonlinear systems, working in fewer dimensions does not automatically make the residual (leftover error from approximate equations) cheap to evaluate, stable during evolution, or conservative (preserving mass or energy). Robust model design therefore needs structure-preserving variables that respect physical laws, discrete consistency in how residuals are minimized for stability, adaptivity that adjusts the model when parameters change, and hyper-reduction that evaluates nonlinear terms at only a small subset of locations instead of everywhere.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling means solving the same governing equations on a lower-dimensional manifold.
Complex flows with multiple physics create reduced-order modeling challenges through equations at different timescales, multiscale structure, wave transport, and topology changes.
Standard Galerkin reduced-order models can be stable in theory but may become unstable when flows are difficult or parameters move far from training conditions.
Least-squares Petrov-Galerkin formulations improve discrete consistency by minimizing actual residuals rather than just enforcing orthogonality.
Hyper-reduction is required because nonlinear residual evaluation can still scale with the full-order model size if every degree of freedom must be evaluated.
Tractability matters most when full-order simulations are so expensive that even generating training data becomes a bottleneck.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced model that stays stable and respects physical laws through challenging dynamics or when parameters move away from the training data.
A projection method that minimizes the residual (leftover error) measured at selected points rather than enforcing the standard orthogonality condition of Galerkin projection.
A change of variables designed to preserve conservation laws, symmetries, numerical stability, or other important mathematical properties.
Cutting cost by evaluating nonlinear residuals at a small number of selected sample points instead of at every full-order grid point.
A reduced model built for one part of a system that can be connected with other reduced or full-order subsystems.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together earlier ROM talks into a practical checklist: speed and low dimension are not enough without stability.
It connects to hybrid digital twins because a digital twin that works in the field needs stable reduced components, not just fast approximations.
It also links to entropy-stable schemes and differentiable simulation by showing that reduced models must match the numerical structure and conservation laws of the full system.
practical_caution: A model can fail even with an excellent basis if the residual is inconsistent with physical laws, the nonlinear terms are not hyper-reduced, or operating conditions shift the flow in ways the training data did not see (changing whether vortices form, for example). Always check stability, computational cost, and how well the model handles parameter changes together rather than separately.
selected_evidence: The first part is on robustness and accuracy.
The third part of the talk is on tractability.
How to handle things like chaotic flows and big parameter changes.
For many problems stability is a major issue.
Hyper reduction... ensuring that the residual is only evaluated at a few points.
takeaway: The core lesson is that having fewer dimensions does not mean the problem is simpler. Practical models must preserve physical structure, adapt when physics changes, and cut down the cost of evaluating nonlinear pieces.

title: Mario Ohlberger: Model Reduction With Adaptive Enrichment For Large Scale PDE-Constrained Optimization
speaker: Mario Ohlberger
one_sentence: This lecture explains adaptive enrichment as a way to use reduced models in large-scale PDE-constrained optimization without paying the full offline cost upfront.
core_problem: Traditional reduced-basis methods rely on an expensive offline stage that builds a rich reduced space before online queries become cheap. In large-scale PDE-constrained optimization, uncertainty quantification, battery degradation, and multiscale settings, the offline solves themselves can be too expensive to afford, and a fixed reduced space may not be accurate where the optimizer actually travels.
first_principles_model: A PDE-constrained optimization problem repeatedly solves a PDE while changing design or control variables. A reduced basis can accelerate those solves, but the optimizer must know when the reduced model is trustworthy. Adaptive enrichment starts with a smaller model and enriches it during the optimization process, often inside a trust-region method that limits reduced-model use to regions where error is controlled.
key_claims: Adaptive enrichment goes beyond the traditional offline-online split of reduced-basis methods.
The target setting is large-scale PDE-constrained optimization and related uncertainty quantification problems.
Traditional offline construction can require very large-scale solves and become too expensive.
Reduced-basis methods need efficient a posteriori error estimators to identify where the current basis is weak.
Trust-region ideas can control when an approximate reduced model is reliable enough for optimization steps.
For hyperbolic, shock-forming, or slow Kolmogorov-width problems, linear reduced spaces may need nonlinear extensions.

important_terms.meaning: An optimization problem whose feasible states are governed by a partial differential equation (a mathematical rule describing how a quantity changes in space and time).
Growing the reduced basis during the solve or optimization process when the current reduced model is not accurate enough.
A low-dimensional space built from representative full-order solutions to speed up later PDE solves.
A calculable estimate of how far off the reduced model is after a solution has been computed.
An optimization area where the approximate model is judged reliable enough to guide a step.

stanford_connections: This extends the ROM discussion from prediction to optimization loops, where repeated solves and reliability guarantees matter.
It connects to inverse problems and control because optimization requires deciding when a cheap model can stand in for an expensive PDE solve.
It also foreshadows nonlinear ROM talks by noting that linear reduced spaces cannot keep up with slow Kolmogorov-width decay.
practical_caution: Do not build a giant offline reduced basis without checking if it is needed. If the optimizer only visits a small portion of parameter space, adaptive enrichment can spend expensive full-order solves where they are actually needed.
selected_evidence: A new paradigm that goes beyond the classical offline online splitting.
Large scale PDE constraint optimization.
The classical approach has limitations because in the offline stage we usually need to solve very large scale problems.
Reduced basis trust region approach.
You will never beat the Kolmogorov... with a linear method.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that reduced-order models in optimization must be managed dynamically: use the cheap model when it is accurate, enrich it when needed, and let error control govern the loop.

title: Tommaso Taddei: Registration-Based Model Reduction Of Parameterized Advection-Dominated PDEs
speaker: Tommaso Taddei
one_sentence: This lecture presents registration—a technique to align moving features in advection-dominated PDEs (partial differential equations where material flows and carries features)—so that a linear reduced model works well in the aligned coordinates.
core_problem: Advection-dominated problems contain moving discontinuities, fronts, or shocks that shift as parameters change. In raw coordinates, these moving features mean the solution set cannot be well approximated by a small fixed low-dimensional space. Standard projection ROMs (reduced-order models: approximate solutions using a small number of basis vectors) then require too many basis vectors or lose sharp features.
first_principles_model: Registration introduces a coordinate transformation from the physical domain to a reference domain that aligns local solution features across different parameter values. Once moving features line up, the transformed solution snapshots become easier to compress linearly. A reduced model can then combine registration, projection (expressing solutions as linear combinations of basis vectors), and hyper-reduction (selectively evaluating only some points to save computation) to produce faster approximations.
key_claims: Advection-dominated PDEs with parameter-dependent features are difficult for model reduction because moving features cannot be well represented by a single fixed low-dimensional linear space.
Registration aligns local features in a reference configuration to make the solution set more compressible and easier to represent with fewer dimensions.
The method is designed to work across different equations, focusing on geometric alignment before applying reduced modeling.
Registration can be combined with projection-based reduction and multifidelity approaches (mixing models of different accuracy and cost).
The method includes hyper-reduced least-squares Petrov-Galerkin steps (using sparse sampling and optimization to speed computation).
The transcript quality is poor, so the strongest evidence comes from the talk abstract and only broad fragments of the recorded words.

important_terms.meaning: A procedure that finds coordinate transformations to align solution features so they appear in similar positions across different parameter values or samples.
A common coordinate system where transported or moving features are aligned before applying dimension reduction.
A partial differential equation where the transport and flow of material dominates and often creates moving fronts or sharp discontinuities.
How well a collection of solutions can be represented by a small number of fixed linear combinations.
A reduced modeling approach that mixes data and models of different accuracy levels and computational costs to improve speed or precision.

stanford_connections: This is the geometric counterpart to nonlinear manifold ROM lectures: transform the data into better coordinates before reducing dimensions.
It connects directly to shock-wave and transport-dominated discussions because moving discontinuities appear to have high rank (need many dimensions to describe).
It also shows a useful pattern for scientific machine learning: sometimes the best model improvement comes from a preprocessing transformation that respects physical meaning.
practical_caution: The local transcript for this talk is heavily corrupted by speech recognition errors. The deep dive should be treated as a preliminary interpretation using the abstract as the main source until a cleaner transcript or paper notes become available.
selected_evidence: Parameterized advection-dominated problems.
Parameter-dependent discontinuities that cannot be adequately represented through linear approximation spaces.
Registration procedure to align local features in a fixed reference domain.
Improve the linear compressibility of the solution manifold.
Registration based projection based multi fidelity model.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that transport problems may only become reducible after aligning moving features. Registration tries to reduce the motion itself before reducing the number of dimensions needed to describe the state.

title: Francisco Chinesta: Empowering Hybrid Twins From Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence
speaker: Francisco Chinesta
organization: ENSAM Institute of Technology / ESI Group
one_sentence: A hybrid twin combines physics-based models with learned models that predict what the physics model misses, correcting the gap between simulation and reality.
core_problem: A physics model is only an approximation of reality. Real systems behave under real loading histories that a pure physics model cannot capture fully. Industrial users increasingly need twins that represent both the known physics and the unmodeled deviation between what the simulation predicts and what actual measurements show. Pure physics may be incomplete; pure data without physical constraints may be unstructured and unreliable.
first_principles_model: The core idea is this equation: reality equals known physics plus the unknown gap. A hybrid twin keeps the physics-based model for the known part and learns a data-driven model that predicts the gap between predictions and measurements. When you combine the physics model and the gap model, the virtual twin gets closer to the real system and can support both diagnosis (figuring out what is wrong now) and prognosis (predicting future behavior).
key_claims: Industrial modeling is shifting from selling products to guaranteeing performance under real usage.
A physics model is an approximation, so mismatch between prediction and measurement should be modeled directly.
Hybrid twins combine physics-based simulation with a learned model that predicts the gap.
The learned gap model should respect physical rules, including conservation laws when relevant.
Once the twin matches reality better, it can support diagnosis from data and prediction of future system behavior.
Model reduction, regression, and machine learning are related tools for building accurate approximations in this hybrid approach.

important_terms.meaning: A digital twin that combines mechanistic simulation with learned models that correct or fill gaps in the physics.
The difference between what a physics model predicts and what measurements show the real system actually does.
Using current observations to infer the present state or discover a defect in a system.
Predicting future system behavior or failure based on the updated and corrected twin.
A rule that learned material or process models must obey the basic laws of thermodynamics and not violate them.

stanford_connections: This is the clearest DDPS direction for hybrid physics-ML systems: learn the missing part instead of learning the whole system from raw data alone.
It connects to fast reduced-order models because these lean physics models often become the core of a real-time twin.
It also connects to uncertainty and control because diagnosis and prognosis require the twin to stay aligned with actual observations.
practical_caution: A digital twin is not just a dashboard or a trained surrogate model. If it does not separate known physics from learned corrections, you cannot tell when the model is predicting outside the range of its evidence, which breaks trust in the results.
selected_evidence: Reality... is equal to the things that you know... plus the things that you ignore.
The physics-based model... can be enriched with a data-driven model of the gap between predictions and measurements.
When you put both together... you obtain the physical reality.
Digital twin of the deviation.
Data serves in order to make diagnosis... and... prognosis.
takeaway: The core lesson is that hybrid twins are gap models wrapped around physics: keep what you already know, learn what you do not, and update the twin to match reality.

title: Priya Donti: Incorporating Power System Physics Into Deep Learning Via Implicit Layers
speaker: Priya Donti
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to build neural networks where internal layers solve optimization problems and satisfy power-system rules, so the network itself enforces what a real power grid must do.
core_problem: Deep learning models can predict numbers accurately but still violate hard rules that power grids must follow. Electricity grids require supply and demand to match, power lines to handle their loads, equipment to stay stable, and physical limits to be respected. So a prediction only matters if it fits into the optimization and control problems that grid operators actually solve.
first_principles_model: A neural network layer does not have to be a direct computation. Instead, it can be defined as the answer to a hidden problem: an optimization task, a differential equation (one that describes how things change over time), an equilibrium point (a balanced state), or a control rule. If that hidden problem can be differentiated through its optimal answer or its KKT conditions (mathematical rules that define when a solution is best), the entire network can learn end-to-end while keeping the domain structure intact.
key_claims: Implicit layers can encode rich computations such as optimization problems, differential equations, and other structured tasks.
Power-system physics and hard rules can be built into deep networks rather than handled only as a step after prediction.
AC optimal power flow can be embedded inside a network by differentiating through a sequence of optimization steps or through KKT conditions.
Models trained around downstream system outcomes can optimize for what actually matters to operators, not just prediction error.
Implicit layers provide prior structure by reflecting the physical relationships of the domain.
They also enforce hard requirements and support stable control in physical systems.

important_terms.meaning: A part of a neural network defined by solving an equation, optimization problem, or system of rules for change, rather than by direct computation.
An optimization problem that chooses how much power to generate and how it flows through lines while satisfying all physical and network limits.
Mathematical rules that state when a solution to a constrained optimization problem is best, and how to compute gradients through that solution.
Training a prediction model by measuring how good the decision is that results from its predictions, not just the prediction error alone.
A requirement that must be satisfied exactly or provably, not just encouraged by a penalty added to the loss.

stanford_connections: This talk extends physics-informed learning beyond PDE (partial differential equation) residuals to optimization layers and operational constraints that must be met in real time.
It connects to inverse problems and control because the model is trained around the decision or control problem it serves, not around prediction alone.
It also complements differentiable simulation: both make a structured physical computation part of the learning graph.
practical_caution: Low prediction error is not sufficient for grids. The learned model must be tested by whether it produces decisions that are feasible (possible to carry out), stable (safe to operate), and useful under the actual physical rules and constraints of the power system.
selected_evidence: Incorporate physics and hard constraints from the electric power system into deep learning methods using... implicit layers.
Layers that encode... optimization problems.
Incorporate ACOPF into a neural network.
Differentiate through it... KKT conditions.
Implicit layers can be a really powerful tool for physical applications like energy systems.
takeaway: The core lesson is that a neural model for real infrastructure should include the decision physics—what the system must do—not just predict numbers that sit upstream of the actual problem.

title: Traian Iliescu: Large Eddy Simulation Reduced Order Models
speaker: Traian Iliescu
one_sentence: This lecture explains LES-ROMs as reduced-order models for turbulent flows that directly handle unresolved scales by applying ROM filtering and adding models for the effects of missing scales.
core_problem: Turbulent flows contain many scales of motion that interact with each other. A reduced-order model (a simplified version that captures only the biggest structures) can represent only the largest patterns, so the small-scale motion that was ignored can feed back and change how the large scales evolve, making predictions unstable or wrong. Standard reduced-order models do not automatically solve this problem of accounting for the missing scales.
first_principles_model: Large eddy simulation divides the flow into two parts using a mathematical filter: the large scales you can track, and the small scales you skip. You then add an extra term that models how the small scales affect the large ones. LES-ROM applies the same idea to reduced-order models: use filters to divide which patterns the model tracks, evolve only the tracked patterns, and add models for how the untracked patterns influence the motion.
key_claims: Reduced-order modeling for turbulence is still an open problem with no single agreed approach.
Galerkin reduced-order models express the solution as a sum of basis functions (computed from data) and project the governing equations onto those functions.
When you filter nonlinear equations, the small scales you filtered out create an extra term that must be estimated or modeled.
Models for the missing effects can be either functional (adding a dissipation-like term) or structural (altering the equations themselves).
Practical tricks like pressure stabilization may lack theoretical elegance but are needed to make real calculations work.
Scaling laws for models of missing effects may be specific to each problem rather than working across all Reynolds numbers and flow types.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation method that tracks large flow patterns directly and adds a model for how untracked small-scale motion affects the tracked patterns.
A mathematical tool in a reduced-order model that defines which flow scales the model can represent.
The challenge of estimating how the small-scale motion you cannot track affects the large-scale motion you can track.
A model that adds damping to represent the mixing effect of small-scale turbulent motion on large-scale flow.
A method that combines multiscale mathematical theory with information learned from simulated or measured flow data to model the effects of small scales.

stanford_connections: This connects to entropy-stable fluid schemes, interpretable machine learning for fluids, and reduced-order models around the shared problem of accounting for motion at scales you cannot resolve.
It is a central warning for neural surrogates of turbulent flow: the untracked small scales still have real effects on the tracked large scales, even if the model ignores them.
It also explains why testing a turbulent surrogate model over long prediction windows matters — the missing small scales accumulate errors over time.
practical_caution: Do not expect one set of numbers or a simple scaling rule to work when the Reynolds number (a measure of flow speed), geometry, or flow conditions change. Turbulent reduced-order models must be tuned and tested for the specific type of flow you care about.
selected_evidence: Reduced modeling is not... for turbulence... a settled field.
When you filter nonlinear equations you're gonna get the closure term.
The non-linear term... you have to model.
Functional means physical eddy viscosity type of thing and structural... mathematical.
Our models should not be expected to be valid over a range of Reynolds numbers.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that turbulence reduced-order models are inherently filtered models. If you ignore the small scales, the simplified model is not just smaller in size; it is missing real physics that affects what happens.

title: George Karniadakis: Approximating Functions, Functionals, And Operators Using Deep Neural Networks
speaker: George Karniadakis
one_sentence: This lecture connects PINNs and DeepONets by showing how neural networks can approximate not only functions, but functionals and operators—maps that take functions as input and produce functions as output.
core_problem: Many physical systems are not one fixed input-output map between finite vectors. They are families of PDE solves, inverse problems, or system responses where the input may itself be a function, such as an initial condition, forcing, geometry, coefficient field, or sensor history. Standard neural networks can approximate functions, but simulation requires learning solution operators and doing so with limited data.
first_principles_model: A function maps points to values. A functional maps a function to a scalar. An operator maps a function to another function. DeepONet represents an operator by combining a branch network that encodes the input function, often through measurements at specific points, with a trunk network that encodes the output location. Physics-informed losses and conservation laws can regularize these models when data are sparse or noisy.
key_claims: Scientific machine learning often needs to learn from small data by using physics as priors or regularization.
PINNs are especially suited to inverse problems because measurements help guide the optimization.
Operator learning is broader than learning a single solution; it approximates mappings between function spaces.
DeepONet uses branch and trunk networks to learn operators with continuous inputs and outputs.
The representation of the input function through measurements or basis choices matters.
Neural operator ideas can support digital-twin-like models of large physical systems.

important_terms.meaning: A map whose input is a function and whose output is usually a scalar value.
A map from one function to another function, such as a PDE solution map.
A neural operator design with a branch network that encodes the input function and a trunk network that encodes output coordinates.
A finite set of sampled measurements used to represent an input function for training or inference.
Using governing equations or conservation laws to constrain a learned model when data are limited.

stanford_connections: This is the main operator-learning anchor for the early DDPS sequence and extends the PINN lectures from solving one PDE to learning a whole solution map.
It connects to graph simulation and ROM-net because all three ask how to represent physical states and maps compactly.
It also connects to hybrid twins because an operator model can serve as a fast learned component inside a larger twin.
practical_caution: Operator learning still depends on the distribution of input functions and how they are represented. A DeepONet trained on one function family may not generalize to very different forcings, geometries, or measurement layouts.
selected_evidence: Approximating functions functionals and operators using deep neural networks.
Unlike other approaches that rely on big data, here we learn from small data.
A branch associated with this... and then there's a trunk.
We map from an infinite dimensional space to an infinite... space.
How you represent the input space is important.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific machine learning often needs to learn maps between spaces of functions, not just labels. Neural operators are built for that level of abstraction.

title: Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez And Tobias Pfaff: Learning Physical Simulation With Graph Networks
speaker: Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez and Tobias Pfaff
one_sentence: This lecture explains graph networks as learned simulators that represent particles, meshes, and deformable systems as graphs and advance them through message passing.
core_problem: Learned simulators can be fast, but many neural architectures generalize poorly outside the training distribution. Physical simulations also come in many forms: particles, triangular meshes, tetrahedral meshes, and adaptive cloth meshes. A useful architecture should handle variable structure and generalize to larger or different systems.
first_principles_model: A physical state can be encoded as a graph: nodes represent particles or mesh vertices, edges represent neighborhood interactions, and features store physical quantities. A graph network performs message passing—exchanging information across connected neighbors—so local interactions update edge and node representations. An encode-process-decode model then predicts the next simulation state, and repeated next-step prediction creates a rollout.
key_claims: Graph networks can model particle, mesh, and deformable simulations with the same broad architecture.
The model learns next-step prediction and then rolls out over time.
Message passing mirrors the local pairwise or neighborhood interactions common in physics.
Permutation equivariance makes predictions independent of arbitrary node and edge ordering.
Using relative local structure helps extrapolate to larger domains and different positions.
Graph structure can generalize better than fixed-grid CNN-style representations for irregular simulation domains.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network that operates on nodes (points), edges (connections), and graph-level properties.
A computation where edge and node values are updated by exchanging information across graph neighborhoods.
A pipeline that converts a physical state into a graph, repeatedly updates it via message passing, and converts the result back to the next state.
Repeatedly applying a one-step simulator to predict a trajectory over many time steps.
The property that reordering graph nodes or edges does not change the physical prediction.

stanford_connections: This talk adds a representation alternative to grids and bases: graph structure can track physical adjacency directly.
It connects to operator learning because both learn reusable physical maps, but graph networks emphasize local interaction structure.
It also connects to long-rollout robustness concerns in fluid and turbulence talks because one-step errors compound over rollout.
practical_caution: A graph simulator must be evaluated on rollout stability and out-of-distribution geometries, not just one-step error. Local message passing helps generalization, but it does not guarantee physical conservation or stability on its own.
selected_evidence: We learn a next step prediction model.
The model is an encode process decode graph network.
They are learned using the same model with the same architecture.
Graph networks were based on something called message passing.
This property allows the model... to be used on systems that are much larger.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that physical simulation is often local and relational. Graph networks exploit that by learning interactions on the structure the simulator already uses.

title: Romit Maulik: Neural Architecture Search For Surrogate Modeling
speaker: Romit Maulik
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to automate surrogate-model design by searching over neural-network architectures, and how to use collections of different architectures to measure uncertainty.
core_problem: Surrogate modeling usually requires hand-designed architectures (the overall shapes and sizes of neural networks), hyperparameters (settings that control how networks train), bottlenecks (narrow layers that compress information), symmetry assumptions (the idea that encoder and decoder halves must mirror each other), and sequence-model choices. That manual work can take up most of the project time, and it can hide better architectures that humans would not naturally try, especially for weather forecasts or autoencoders (networks that compress data down and then rebuild it) trained to find low-dimensional patterns.
first_principles_model: A neural architecture can be drawn as a directed acyclic graph: a flowchart where each box is an operation (matrix multiply, add, skip connection, dropout, etc.) and arrows point forward with no loops. Neural architecture search defines the space of all possible graphs—varying the number of layers, widths, skip connections (shortcuts that feed information forward to later layers), dropout rates (which nodes randomly turn off during training), tensor operations, and hyperparameters. An optimizer like aging evolution treats each candidate architecture as if it were a genome, evaluates performance on validation data, and breeds better candidates over generations. Sampling many different points in this space also produces an ensemble (a collection of diverse trained networks) that can be used for uncertainty quantification (measuring how confident predictions are).
key_claims: DeepHyper automates the search over neural-network architectures and hyperparameters across many different network types.
Architecture search can discover surrogate models that work well without being physically encoded into the network structure.
The search space can be drawn as a directed acyclic graph showing all possible operations the search can choose.
Aging evolution interprets each candidate architecture as a genome and optimizes how well it performs on held-out validation data.
Neural architecture search can question default assumptions, such as the idea that encoder and decoder halves of autoencoders must have matching structures.
Collections of different architectures can support uncertainty quantification by sampling different model designs.

important_terms.meaning: Automated search over the structure and hyperparameters of neural networks, instead of designing them by hand.
All possible architectures, operations, and hyperparameter settings that the algorithm is allowed to try.
An evolutionary algorithm that treats candidate architectures like living organisms: it keeps the best ones, mutates them slightly, and removes the weakest ones over many generations.
A group of different trained networks, each with its own architecture, combined together to improve predictions and measure how much the choice of architecture affects the answer.
A network that compresses data in an encoder half and reconstructs it in a decoder half, where the decoder structure is not forced to match the encoder structure.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on ROM-net and nonlinear manifold ROM work: the choice of architecture is something the scientific workflow should optimize over, not assume.
It relates to uncertainty and robustness because using many different architectures shows how much prediction changes when the model structure changes.
It also relates to hyper-reduction (using only the most important dimensions) because efficient, smaller architectures can reduce the cost of running predictions in real applications.
practical_caution: Neural architecture search does not eliminate the need to check against physics and domain knowledge. If the search objective rewards only validation error (how well the model fits held-out test data), the search can find models that appear accurate on that test data but behave erratically, grow too large, or produce physically implausible predictions when deployed in the real world.
selected_evidence: Automate the construction of neural networks and the optimization of its hyper parameters.
Represent the neural network as a directed acyclic graph.
The aging evolution algorithm actually interprets... neural networks as a genetic algorithm.
Uncertainty quantification and deep learning is a big issue.
By losing the restriction of symmetry our auto encoders were actually able to get far better performance.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that model architecture is itself a design choice. Neural architecture search searches over that choice instead of relying only on default designs that humans picked.

title: Harbir Antil: Applications Of Fractional Operators From Optimal Control To Machine Learning
speaker: Harbir Antil
one_sentence: This lecture introduces fractional operators (mathematical tools that work with non-integer orders of derivatives) as nonlocal models for imaging, geophysics, optimal control, data science, and deep neural networks.
core_problem: Many physical and data systems show nonlocal behavior—long-range correlations, memory effects, or anomalous diffusion (spreading that doesn't follow standard random-walk rules)—that classical integer-order differential operators cannot capture naturally. Using only local derivatives can miss how heterogeneous materials, images, or reacting flows influence each other across distances.
first_principles_model: A fractional operator extends the standard idea of differentiation to non-integer orders.
