Instead of measuring change only at one point, the operator can encode interactions reaching across distance or back through time. The fractional Laplacian is one example: it spreads or diffuses information in a way that reflects how systems interact over distance. Fractional exponents can also become parameters you estimate from data or random variables that capture uncertainty.
key_claims: Fractional calculus handles anomalous diffusion and systems where effects reach back in time or across distance.
In some cases, fractional operators can replace complicated nonlinear image-smoothing models with simpler linear fractional differential equations.
Controlling systems with fractional differential equations raises new mathematical and computational questions.
Unknown fractional exponents can be treated as tunable parameters or as random variables when uncertainty matters.
Fractional operators can be built into deep neural network layers.
Chemical reacting flows show abrupt time-scale changes where fractional neural models may help.

important_terms.meaning: A mathematical operation with a non-integer order, typically encoding how influence spreads across distance or persists over time.
A nonlocal (affects things far away) generalization of the Laplace operator; used to model diffusion and change in ways that reflect real-world spreading or long-range interaction.
Spreading of particles or information that deviates from standard diffusion; particles wander farther or slower than expected from classical theory.
Dependence on prior states or history; the system's current behavior carries imprints of its past.
A neural network layer or module designed using ideas from fractional operators to capture nonlocal or time-dependent patterns.

stanford_connections: This talk expands the conversation about operator learning by focusing on operators that capture nonlocal physics.
It ties to optimal control and uncertainty quantification because fractional exponents and nonlocal dynamics can become uncertain parameters that affect control decisions.
It also relates to graph networks: both are ways to represent how things influence each other beyond a fixed small neighborhood on a grid.
practical_caution: Fractional models can fit data well but introduce choices: which fractional order to use, how to handle boundaries, and how to compute the operator all shape the results. Use fractional operators when the physics genuinely shows nonlocal behavior, not as a generic dial to turn up complexity.
selected_evidence: Applications of fractional operators from optimal control to machine learning.
Long-range correlations or hereditary material properties.
Modeled by fractional-order differential operators.
You have to solve a more challenging problem with the fractional Laplacian.
I started with several applications of fractional operators in imaging in geophysics... and machine learning.
takeaway: The core insight is that not all dynamics happen only locally. Fractional operators give machine learning and science a way to describe nonlocality, memory, and anomalous transport.

title: David Ryckelynck: Model Order Reduction Assisted By Deep Neural Networks
speaker: David Ryckelynck
one_sentence: This lecture presents ROM-net, which uses neural networks to pick or adapt local simplified models from a dictionary for high-dimensional inputs like images.
core_problem: Many real simulations take random or image-like inputs, and how these inputs vary strongly shapes the answer you care about. A single global simplified basis may work poorly or be hard to understand across that variability, while using a neural network as a complete replacement loses the structure and speed benefits of projection-based reduced-order models (ROMs—versions of a simulation that run much faster by solving in fewer dimensions).
first_principles_model: ROM-net combines deep learning with projection-based ROM. A dictionary of local simplified models is built by grouping similar simulation data and computing a reduced basis (a small set of directions that capture the main variation) for each group. A feedforward neural network takes an input tensor, such as an image showing where a material is damaged, and routes it to the right local ROM or subspace (a lower-dimensional space that captures the key behavior). This gives a piecewise-linear reduced version—made from pieces of different linear spaces—that still works with hyper-reduction (a speedup method that reduces not just dimensions but also the number of calculations needed).
key_claims: ROM-net extends model order reduction to settings where inputs are high-dimensional and image-like.
Sparse dictionary learning can be read as a piecewise-linear latent space (a lower-dimensional representation built from separate linear pieces).
Grouping data allows each group to get its own local reduced basis.
Local ROM dictionaries are easier to understand and work with compared to autoencoders (neural networks that compress data to a dense code and uncompress it).
Hyper-reduction becomes straightforward when the latent structure is made of separate linear pieces.
The method works with simulation data you already have while keeping the understanding that comes from classical mathematical models.

important_terms.meaning: A neural-network-assisted approach that connects input data to projection-based reduced-order models (simplified versions that run much faster).
A collection of local simplified models from which the right one is selected or combined for a given input.
Learning representations that use only a small number of dictionary elements or local lower-dimensional components.
A lower-dimensional representation built from multiple local linear subspaces (separate flat regions) rather than one global flat region.
A high-dimensional input, such as medical scan data, used as a simulation parameter.

stanford_connections: This talk sits between non-intrusive ROM (reduced-order models that work from data without needing to change the original simulator), neural architecture search (NAS—automatically finding network designs), and nonlinear manifold ROMs (advanced simplifications that handle curved spaces): it uses neural networks to route among structured simplified models.
It connects to hybrid twins because image or sensor inputs can choose the right local digital twin behavior.
It reinforces a recurring DDPS theme: neural networks are often most useful when they assist classical reduction methods rather than replace them.
practical_caution: The number and quality of groups matter. Too few local models may not capture the range of different inputs, while too many demand more memory and training time. The neural routing model must also be tested to make sure it works well when the input changes in new ways.
selected_evidence: Model order reduction assisted by deep neural network so-called ROM-net.
Images are input parameter for numerical models.
Sparse dictionary learning can be understood as a piecewise linear latent space.
For each cluster we can use... SVD... to get... a proper reduced basis.
A ROMnet is a feed forward artificial neural network that ends with a reduced order model.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that neural networks can select the right simplified model for each input, while keeping the structure and efficiency that come from projection and hyper-reduction.

title: Matthew Zahr: Model Reduction Of PDEs Via Optimization-Based Feature Tracking
speaker: Matthew Zahr
one_sentence: This lecture explains how optimization-based feature tracking warps the computational mesh so shocks and discontinuities align before compressing the model.
core_problem: Convection-dominated PDEs with shocks and discontinuities are difficult for standard ROMs (reduced-order models—mathematical approximations that capture the most important behavior) because moving features force the snapshot set (the collection of solution states at different times) to have high rank. When the basis stays fixed while shocks move, many modes are needed and reduced solutions may blur or oscillate instead of staying sharp.
first_principles_model: Instead of approximating moving discontinuities in fixed coordinates, feature tracking warps the mesh or domain so discontinuities line up in a reference configuration. The method writes shock tracking as an optimization problem over both the DG (discontinuous Galerkin, a high-order numerical method) solution and mesh coordinates. In the reduced setting, it optimizes reduced state coordinates and reduced mesh deformation coordinates at the same time.
key_claims: Shock tracking can be written as an optimization problem over solution and mesh coordinates.
High-order DG properties like consistency, conservation, and accuracy are kept when DG equations appear as constraints.
Domain warping lines up discontinuities across snapshots to improve compression.
The reduced problem optimizes both the ROM state and the mesh deformation.
Boundary-preserving maps are needed so mesh motion does not harm the physical domain.
Feature tracking lets simple linear-subspace tools like SVD stay useful for convection-dominated problems.

important_terms.meaning: Warping the mesh or coordinate system so important solution features like shocks line up across time steps.
An optimization-based method that finds shocks through the solution and mesh solve rather than building the shock front by hand.
A change to the computational domain shape used to line up moving features.
Low-dimensional variables that control mesh deformation in a reduced model.
A transformation that moves interior mesh points while keeping the domain edges valid.

stanford_connections: This talk is the optimization-based version of registration-based ROMs: both reduce transport by lining up features.
It ties to entropy-stable schemes because shock handling is not just a learning problem but also a discretization and geometry problem.
It also connects to nonlinear manifold ROMs because domain deformation creates a nonlinear representation while keeping simple linear tools useful.
practical_caution: Tracking features adds its own optimization cost and mesh-validity challenges. A poor deformation map can keep rank small while harming boundaries, conservation of physical quantities, or solver stability.
selected_evidence: Optimization based implicit feature tracking.
Formulated as an optimization problem over the DG solution and mesh coordinates.
We want to deform the domain... to align... the shock.
Minimizing over the ROM state... and the mesh.
Introduce this mapping... to guarantee that the boundaries are preserved.
takeaway: The core lesson is that for shocks, model reduction can start by letting the coordinate system move with the physics before compressing the state.

title: Tan Bui-Thanh: Model-Constrained Deep Learning For Inference, Control And UQ
speaker: Tan Bui-Thanh
one_sentence: This lecture explains how to embed scientific forward models (mathematical rules that predict observations from parameters) into learning systems for inference, control, and uncertainty quantification.
core_problem: Inverse problems and control tasks cannot rely on unconstrained prediction alone. Measurements may be sparse, noisy, high-dimensional, and indirect—meaning you get few readings, they contain errors, and each reading depends on many hidden causes. The unknown parameter space can also be high-dimensional. Bayesian or optimization-based inference may need to solve the forward model thousands of times, making computation prohibitively expensive.
first_principles_model: A forward model takes parameters or shapes and predicts observations by solving a PDE (partial differential equation—an equation describing how something changes in space and time). An inverse problem tries to recover the hidden parameters from observations. In Bayesian inversion, the solution is a posterior distribution (a probability distribution over possible parameter values, updated after seeing the data). Model-constrained deep learning places the mathematical model inside the neural network or variational approximation so learning respects the physics while reducing the cost of exploring the posterior or control space.
key_claims: Scientific machine learning combines scientific computing, which uses laws and equations from physics, with learning, which finds patterns in data.
Forward problems solve equations from known parameters; inverse problems work backward to find hidden causes from limited measurements.
High-dimensional parameters and high-dimensional data create severe computational challenges because there are too many possibilities to explore.
Bayesian inverse problems are expensive because finding the posterior distribution repeatedly calls the forward model.
Variational approaches can approximate the posterior by replacing it with a simpler, fast-to-compute distribution.
The key idea is to put the underlying mathematical model inside the variational or deep-learning architecture so the learning respects the physics.

important_terms.meaning: A learning approach where predictions or latent variables are forced to obey a governing scientific model.
Computing observations or states from known parameters by solving the physical model.
Inferring hidden parameters, shapes, or sources from observations.
A probability distribution over unknowns after combining prior assumptions with observed data.
Approximating a difficult posterior distribution with a simpler, parameterized distribution that is fast to compute.

stanford_connections: This talk bridges differentiable simulation (running physics models backward through neural networks), implicit layers (neural networks that embed equations), and uncertainty-aware scientific machine learning.
It connects to digital twins because real twins need inference and uncertainty quantification, not only forward prediction.
It also connects to control because decision quality depends on model-constrained inference of the current state and its uncertainty.
practical_caution: A model-constrained neural method is only as reliable as both pieces: the forward model must represent the relevant physics accurately, and the variational or neural approximation must capture the posterior uncertainty well enough for the downstream decision to be sound.
selected_evidence: Model constrained deep learning approaches for inference control and uncertainty quantification.

The inverse problem is more difficult.
The posterior is the solution... probability density.
Put the underlying mathematical model inside the variational encoder.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that inference and control need learning systems that respect the forward physics while making uncertainty computation fast enough to use.

title: Rui Wang: Physics-Guided Deep Learning For Dynamics Forecasting
speaker: Rui Wang
one_sentence: This lecture shows how adding physics knowledge directly into deep learning models improves spatiotemporal dynamics forecasting by building in numerical methods, constraints, and symmetry.
core_problem: Dynamics forecasting is hard because physical fields evolve across different scales, conditions change between systems, and tiny errors compound over time. A purely data-driven model might fit large patterns while missing small eddies, incompressibility, or quantities that should stay constant.
first_principles_model: A forecasting model maps recent states of a dynamical system to future states. Physics-guided learning modifies that map by adding physics bias into the neural network: numerical-method-inspired components, symmetry that stays correct under transformations, divergence or conservation losses, and multiscale decompositions that force the model to represent both large and small features.
key_claims: Dynamics forecasting benefits from combining deep learning with prior physics knowledge.
TF-Net marries numerical techniques with custom neural-network design for physical fields.
For incompressible flow, divergence should be small and can be used as a physical measure or loss.
Symmetry and equivariance can improve generalization across transformations such as rotation, translation, uniform motion, or scaling.
Mean-squared-error training can overemphasize large scales and ignore small eddies.
Robust forecasting still needs better theory for nonstationary and chaotic dynamics when conditions differ from training data.

important_terms.meaning: Predicting future states of a time-evolving physical system from current or past states.
Deep learning that incorporates known physical constraints, symmetries, or numerical methods.
A property where transforming the input transforms the output in the corresponding physically meaningful way.
A penalty that encourages incompressible flow predictions to have near-zero divergence.
A mismatch between training and test conditions that often degrades forecasting performance.

stanford_connections: This talk connects graph simulators, differentiable physics, and fluid reduced-order models around the issue of long-rollout physical consistency.
It complements PINNs by using physics to guide both the architecture and the losses for forecasting, rather than only fitting PDE equations.
It also reinforces the series-wide warning that generalization across different regimes is harder than interpolation within one regime.
practical_caution: Do not judge a dynamics model only by pixelwise or fieldwise short-horizon error. Check physical diagnostics such as divergence, spectra, conserved quantities, and how well it performs when conditions differ from training.

The divergence is supposed to be zero.
The model may... with the MSE loss... only focus on the large scale component and overlook these small eddies.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that forecasting is not just extrapolating frames. The model must preserve the physical structure that makes future states plausible.

title: Yeonjong Shin: A Mathematical Understanding Of Modern Machine Learning
speaker: Yeonjong Shin
one_sentence: This lecture studies machine learning mathematically by separating approximation, estimation, generalization, and optimization errors, with special attention to PINNs.
core_problem: Modern ML often works through empirical tricks, but scientific ML needs robustness and reliability. PINNs and neural solvers may look promising, yet without mathematical analysis it is unclear when they actually solve the equations correctly, when they work on new data, or when gradient-based training will find a useful solution.
first_principles_model: A learning method has several errors. Approximation error comes from the expressiveness of the model class—how much can the model shape itself to match reality. Estimation error comes from finite data, not infinite samples. Generalization error combines these statistical effects—the gap between what you learned on your data and what happens on the world. Optimization error comes from the training algorithm returning a model that is not the ideal minimizer. Scientific ML theory asks how these errors behave when physics constraints and neural networks are combined.
key_claims: The success of ML depends on modeling, gradient-based optimization, data, and computing power.
Scientific ML adds physical laws to the standard learning setup.
PINNs have strong promise but need consistency and optimization theory.
Generalization error and optimization error are distinct and should not be conflated.
The talk presents convergence theory for PINNs based on Holder regularization and classical PDE analysis.
Mathematical understanding can motivate improved algorithms for training neural networks.

important_terms.meaning: Error caused by the best available model in the chosen function class still not matching the target.
Error caused by learning from a finite sample rather than infinite data.
The gap between learned model behavior and true target behavior outside the training sample.
Error caused by the training algorithm failing to find the best model in the class.
A theoretical property that PINN solutions converge to the correct PDE solution under appropriate limits and assumptions.

stanford_connections: This is the theory counterpart to the Perdikaris PINN failure lecture: it asks when the method should work in principle.
It connects to robustness and UQ because dependable scientific ML needs error decomposition, not just benchmark accuracy.
It also helps interpret later operator-learning and neural-solver talks by separating expressiveness from trainability.
practical_caution: A theorem about the ideal minimizer does not guarantee that a practical optimizer will find it. PINN reliability needs both consistency theory and optimization diagnostics.
selected_evidence: Lacks theoretical understanding and also it has some potential issues in optimization procedure.
Combining these two errors together we call it generalization error.
The difference between these two is called optimization error.
First convergence theory of the physics informed neural network.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific ML needs an error budget. Approximation, data, generalization, and optimization failures are different failure modes.

title: Marta D'Elia: Data-Driven Learning Of Nonlocal Models
speaker: Marta D'Elia
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to use data to find the right nonlocal kernels—mathematical descriptions of how far-away particles influence each other—so that a coarse model can capture the effects of tiny details it doesn't explicitly track.
core_problem: Normal differential equations work locally: they say a change at one point depends only on what's happening right there. But many materials and systems that involve multiple scales don't follow this rule—tiny interactions far away matter. You can build models using integrals over a region instead of just local derivatives, but you need to know what weights those distant interactions. Those weights must be learned from real, high-resolution data.
first_principles_model: A nonlocal operator computes how a state changes by adding up influences from all points within a certain distance, using a weighted sum. The kernel is the weighting function—it determines which distant neighbors matter most. When you train this on pairs of high-resolution data (what you observe) and what forces caused it, you get a coarse model that reproduces the large-scale results without having to simulate every tiny detail.
key_claims: Nonlocal models build length scales directly into integral operators.
They work well when tiny-scale behavior drives global results but is too expensive to compute directly.
The real problem to solve is finding the kernel function that defines the nonlocal operator.
Peridynamic operators extend nonlocal ideas to solid mechanics by including material properties.
Neural networks designed to learn operators can help speed up molecular-dynamics simulations and coarse-graining.
Nonlocal kernel ideas suggest new ways to design neural-network layers that respect physical structure.

important_terms.meaning: A mathematical model where the state at any point depends on values spread across a region, not just on a single point's properties.
A function that assigns weights to how much each distance contributes to an interaction in a nonlocal operator.
A simplified model that reproduces large-scale behavior accurately without tracking every small-scale detail.
A mechanics theory that describes materials by how forces travel over finite distances, instead of using only pointwise stresses.
A neural-network design inspired by learnable nonlocal kernels, treating layers as learnable weighted-average operations across neighborhoods.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together fractional calculus, graph neural networks, and operator learning through the common idea of nonlocal interaction.
It builds on the multiscale-coupling theme by replacing the need to resolve fine details with learned operators that mimic their effects.
It also touches on mechanistic interpretability because inspecting learned kernels can reveal the underlying physical interaction rules.
practical_caution: A learned kernel only tells you something real if your training data actually exercises all the important interactions and your choice of kernel shape can actually match the true physics. Otherwise you get a model that matches your data but doesn't reliably transfer to new problems.
selected_evidence: Data-driven learning techniques for nonlocal equations.
Complex systems where the small scale dynamics...
The real goal is to find the optimal kernel k.
We collect measurements... high fidelity pairs of solution and forcing function.
Linear peridynamic solid operator.
takeaway: The big idea is that nonlocal learning tries to discover the interaction law—the rule for how distant parts influence each other—not just fit a curve to outputs. The kernel is the bridge connecting small scales to large scales.

title: Dmitriy Anistratov: ROMs For Thermal Radiative Transfer Based On Moment Equations And POD
speaker: Dmitriy Anistratov
one_sentence: This talk builds smaller, faster models for radiation heat transfer by simplifying the transport equation into moment equations and using data to capture the missing pieces.
core_problem: Thermal radiation heat transfer is high-dimensional (depends on position, time, direction, and photon energy), nonlinear, changes across many scales, and couples tightly to material temperature. Solving the full transport equation directly is expensive. Simple old models like diffusion or P1 approximation run fast but can miss important effects.
first_principles_model: The method uses nonlinear projection to break down the complex Boltzmann transport equation into a simpler hierarchy of moment equations. The hard part is closure: when you project out details, you lose information that you have to recover. The low-order equations need extra quantities like the Eddington tensor (a measure of how radiation travels in different directions) to stay accurate. POD (proper orthogonal decomposition, a data-compression method) or DMD (dynamic mode decomposition, which finds repeating patterns in time series) compresses these closure terms using examples from expensive full simulations.
key_claims: Thermal radiation heat transfer is a useful testing ground for extreme-energy and radiation-coupled gas dynamics problems.
The main cost comes from solving the high-dimensional transport equation.
Nonlinear projection can derive low-order moment equations for radiation intensity.
The Eddington tensor supplies the closure that moment systems need.
POD and DMD can approximate closure information across different conditions and time.
Removing the expensive transport equation from online calculations can bring cost down to match simple models while keeping predictive quality under control.

important_terms.meaning: Predicting how radiation energy moves through a material while the material heats up or cools down by absorbing or emitting that energy.
An equation describing how radiation intensity (amount and direction of light energy) changes across space, direction, energy, and time.
A simpler equation created by integrating the transport equation over some of its variables (like direction), reducing the number of unknowns.
A closure term that captures how radiation travels in different directions; needed when you simplify a transport equation into moment form.
Using data-compression methods (proper orthogonal decomposition or dynamic mode decomposition) to approximate the closure terms from training simulations.

stanford_connections: This talk extends reduced-model ideas beyond fluids and structures to a transport-heavy application.
It parallels large-eddy simulation (LES) reduction: both take a high-dimensional physics model and replace removed details with a learned or data-fitted closure.
It also demonstrates hybrid physics-data modeling, where the equations set the low-order structure and data fills in the missing closure.
practical_caution: A simplified radiation model is only as good as its closure—the extra terms that stand in for what was thrown away. To compress the Eddington tensor with POD or DMD, you need training data that covers all the conditions where you'll actually use the model.
selected_evidence: Reduced models for thermal radiative transfer problems based on moment equations and POD DMD of Eddington tensor.
High dimensionality non-linearity different scales in time and space and energy strong coupling.
The main burden here is actually the transport equation.
Data compression techniques for approximative closures... Eddington tensor.
The transport equation is removed from calculations.
takeaway: The central insight is that moment-based reduced models work by keeping the low-order structure of the physics and using data to learn or compress the closure terms that the projection step creates.

title: Christopher Earls: Gaining Mechanistic Insight Through Learning Green's Functions
speaker: Christopher Earls
one_sentence: This lecture shows how learning Green's functions can turn observed system responses into interpretable solution operators (maps that convert inputs to outputs) for hidden PDEs.
core_problem: Deep networks can predict what a system does, but science requires understanding why. When the equation that governs the system is unknown, you can learn the solution operator, or Green's function, that maps sources to fields, then examine that operator to find physical structure hiding in the data.
first_principles_model: For a linear PDE, a Green's function is the response to an impulse source. Once you have it, it acts as an integral kernel: you integrate the Green's function against a source to produce the solution. Learning this kernel from data gives a compact, interpretable operator that can suggest what PDE structure is hidden and which predictions you can test.
key_claims: Observed system responses hold patterns that reveal hidden mechanistic structure.
The goal is not only to learn the PDE directly but to learn linear solution operators and compact integral kernels.
Green's functions provide a classical bridge between impulse response and PDE solution.
Deep learning can extend empirical Green's function ideas to new settings.
Extracted operators can be inspected for features suggesting hidden mechanisms.
The method is related to but distinct from broader neural operator approaches.

important_terms.meaning: The response of a linear differential operator to an impulse, used as a kernel inside an integral to construct solutions.
A map that takes forcing, sources, or inputs and produces the corresponding system response.
A function used inside an integral to convert input functions into output functions.
An unknown governing equation inferred indirectly from data, not written down in advance.
Understanding the physical or mathematical mechanism behind observed behavior, not just predicting it.

stanford_connections: This talk links operator learning with interpretability: the learned operator should teach us something about the hidden physics.
It connects to nonlocal kernels because both learn integral kernels from response data.
It also complements SINDy-style equation discovery by learning the solution operator rather than directly selecting PDE terms.
practical_caution: A learned Green's function is most natural for linear or linearized systems. For strongly nonlinear regimes, the operator interpretation must be checked carefully or applied only near the conditions where you trained it.
selected_evidence: Gaining mechanistic insight through learning Green's functions.
Uncovering the solutions to hidden PDEs.
This kind of reminds me of a Green's function.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that an interpretable learned operator can be more scientifically useful than a pure predictor, because it points back toward the mechanism.

title: Jesse Capecelatro: Turbulent Disperse Two-Phase Flows
speaker: Jesse Capecelatro
one_sentence: This lecture studies turbulent gas-particle flows where particles strongly change the carrier turbulence, and the math model must account for how the two phases change each other.
core_problem: Dispersed two-phase flows happen everywhere: smokestacks, spray engines, ocean sediment. But modeling them is hard because particles interact with turbulence, create wakes behind them, bump into each other, pile up locally, and hit walls. The physics of a single fluid alone does not capture what happens when you add many particles that are not moving with the fluid.
first_principles_model: A gas-particle flow has two parts: a carrier fluid (the gas) and a dispersed particle phase (the small drops or solids). Each particle feels drag and other forces from the fluid, but each particle also pushes back on the fluid through wakes and momentum transfer. When you write the math for the average flow and average turbulence, you end up with terms you cannot close because the small-scale details matter. Data-driven methods can learn those missing pieces while keeping the known physics intact.
key_claims: Particles can change background turbulence by a factor of two or more.
Most multiphase average-flow models have been simple additions to single-fluid turbulence models.
These additions do not work when particle concentration swings from very low to very high, where the two-way effects become large.
Data-driven modeling now appears in more applications: learning closures, guessing model errors, and fixing models when physics is incomplete.
The talk shows approaches beyond just using neural networks to guess closure terms directly.
Adding chance into particle-force models can help the math keep the right particle speed variations and how far particles spread.

important_terms.meaning: A flow where droplets or solid particles are suspended and spread throughout a liquid or gas.
When the fluid pushes on particles AND particles push back hard on the fluid, changing how the fluid itself moves.
Math that averages out the small wiggles in a two-phase flow to find the mean gas and mean particle motion.
A method to approximate terms that show up in the averaged equations because you averaged out the small-scale details.
A model where particle forces include randomness to match what you measure in real or simulated flows.

stanford_connections: This talk continues the theme from earlier lectures: when you average or filter the equations, you lose information, and you have to model what you lost. Here it is two-phase flows; before it was turbulence alone.
It touches data-driven model repair because the learned part targets just the missing pieces, not the whole solution.
It shows a real case where forgetting that particles and fluid change each other leads to big prediction errors.
practical_caution: A math model trained on single-fluid turbulence or on one particle density regime will often fail when the particle concentration changes or when particles reshape the flow noticeably. Always test across both particle-sparse and particle-dense conditions and check whether the model predicts the way particles spread and move, not just the average gas velocity.
selected_evidence: Particles have an order one effect on the background turbulence.
Data-driven modeling has exploded... closure modeling uncertainty quantification model augmentation.
Multiphase turbulence modeling has really... lags the development.
Extensions of single-phase turbulence.
Treating the force stochastically is showing promise to guarantee certain statistics.
takeaway: The core idea is that multiphase turbulence modeling is really about getting statistics of particle and fluid interaction right: particles are not just tiny objects drifting along; they actively reshape how the turbulence behaves.

title: Ionut-Gabriel Farcas: Learning Hierarchies Of Reduced-Dimension And Context-Aware Models For Monte Carlo Sampling
speaker: Ionut-Gabriel Farcas
one_sentence: This lecture presents multi-fidelity Monte Carlo methods (where you combine cheap approximate models with expensive accurate ones) where low-fidelity models reduce the cost of high-fidelity uncertainty propagation by providing information about where expensive runs matter most.
core_problem: Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation using high-fidelity simulations is expensive. Adding a low-fidelity model (a cheap approximation) can reduce total cost, but only if three things line up: the low-fidelity model agrees with the high-fidelity one, the low-fidelity model is cheap enough to run many times, and the low-fidelity model makes sense for the input region you are sampling.
first_principles_model: A multi-fidelity estimator mixes samples from high-fidelity and low-fidelity models. The low-fidelity model may be biased (systematically off), but if it follows the high-fidelity output closely and costs far less to run, it cuts down the spread (variance) of your estimate for a fixed computational budget. Context-aware methods build or switch low-fidelity models on the fly, tailoring them to the specific region or sample being evaluated.
key_claims: In multi-fidelity methods, low- and high-fidelity models work as a team rather than one taking over from the other.
The purpose of a low-fidelity model is to reduce the total cost of high-fidelity computation.
How well your estimate performs depends on how closely the models agree and what they cost to run.
Reduced-basis surrogates (simplified models built from high-fidelity data) can be accurate but may still cost a fair amount to run.
Regression-based models are cheaper but need many samples before they become reliable.
Building models that adapt to the current context gives more options than using one fixed model for everything.

important_terms.meaning: A statistical sampling method that mixes cheap approximate models with expensive accurate ones to reduce total computation cost.
A cheap approximation that runs fast but may not be perfectly accurate; used to inform where to spend expensive simulations.
A model that is chosen or built based on the current input values, task, or the specific sample being evaluated.
A single number measuring both how far off an estimate is on average (bias) and how much it wobbles (variance).
A number from zero to one showing how closely the low-fidelity model output tracks the high-fidelity output; the stronger this is, the more the low-fidelity model helps.

stanford_connections: This talk links reduced models (simplified models built from full simulations) and uncertainty to show that simplified models work as information sources, not just cheaper replacements.
It builds on adaptive enrichment: focus expensive high-fidelity runs where the results change the most.
It also supports the hybrid-twin theme because digital twins need uncertainty estimates but often have limited computation available.
practical_caution: A biased low-fidelity model can still be useful, but you must check: Does the correlation with the high-fidelity model and the cost ratio actually improve your final estimate? Never assume a cheap surrogate helps Monte Carlo just because it is cheaper.
selected_evidence: Low- and high-fidelity models are used together.
The primary purpose of low-fidelity models is supporting computations with the high-fidelity models.
The mean squared error... depends on the correlation coefficients and the evaluation costs.
Low fidelity models are contextual.
If you need to invest only 10 high-fidelity runs and 1 million... runs then you can do it.
takeaway: The core idea is that uncertainty estimation is a budget allocation puzzle. A useful low-fidelity model cuts uncertainty per unit of computation cost, even if it is not accurate enough by itself to replace the simulator.

title: Peter Benner: Identification Of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems From Noisy Measurements
speaker: Peter Benner
organization: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems
one_sentence: This lecture studies how to identify nonlinear differential equations from noisy and sparse measurements by combining sparse identification (which picks the most active terms from a list of candidate equations) with numerical time-integration methods that step through time in steps rather than differentiating the data directly.
core_problem: System identification tries to recover dynamical equations from observed trajectories. For nonlinear systems, sparse observations and measurement noise create hard challenges: computing derivatives from noisy data gives unreliable results, the choice of candidate terms in the dictionary matters greatly, and spurious terms can be selected when noise is high.
first_principles_model: A dynamical system defines time derivatives as a function of the current state. Sparse identification assumes that this function can be represented by only a few active terms selected from a candidate library. Instead of differentiating noisy data directly, numerical integration methods such as Runge-Kutta—which evolves the state through small time steps using weighted combinations of derivatives—can connect states across time and make the identification problem more stable.
key_claims: Discovering dynamical models from measurements is essential for analysis, optimization, and control.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics popularized the idea of selecting only active terms from a large library of candidates.
Noise and sparse sampling remain central obstacles when identifying nonlinear systems.
Integrating the equations through time rather than differentiating the data directly can make identification more stable.
Choosing the candidate dictionary automatically remains an open problem.
For wave or transport equations, the time-stepping method should match the dynamics being identified.

important_terms.meaning: Inferring a mathematical dynamical model by fitting equations to observed input-output or trajectory data.
Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics: a method that selects only the most important terms from a library of candidate nonlinear functions.
A candidate library of functions—such as powers, products, or sines—from which the actual terms of the dynamical system are selected.
A time-integration method that evolves the state forward by computing weighted averages of derivatives at intermediate time points within each time step.
Observed data corrupted by measurement error, which distorts derivative estimates and can mislead term selection.

stanford_connections: This talk extends the Brunton interpretability lecture by focusing on the numerical-analysis details of equation discovery.
It connects to Koopman and Green's function talks because all three seek dynamical structure from data.
It also connects to control because an identified model is often needed before designing optimal or feedback-based strategies.
practical_caution: Sparse discovery can return elegant equations that actually reflect noise patterns or limitations of the candidate dictionary rather than true underlying physics. The dictionary, integration method, and noise model are all assumptions built into the identification approach and must be chosen carefully.
selected_evidence: Identification of nonlinear dynamical systems from noisy measurements.
Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics approach.
We will focus on one issue with this approach and suggest a new variant.
We will add a higher level of noise.
Optimizing the choice of the dictionary automatically... is an important question.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that equation discovery requires more than just fitting numbers to data. It requires combining regression with time-evolution rules, noise treatment, and a good choice of candidate physics.

title: Youngsoo Choi: libROM For Physics-Constrained Data-Driven Physical Simulations
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This lecture introduces libROM as a practical software library for physics-constrained data-driven reduced-order modeling across LLNL physical simulation workflows.
core_problem: Data-driven physical simulation needs working software, not just published papers. Models trained only on data can be easy to build but may ignore the underlying physics laws, while models built from first principles and constrained by data can be accurate and reliable but need infrastructure to handle bases, hyper-reduction, linking components together, and checking sensitivity.
first_principles_model: A projection ROM squeezes full-order state data into reduced bases, evolves low-dimensional coordinates, and rebuilds the full state. For nonlinear systems, hyper-reduction samples residual or nonlinear terms so the cost to run online does not grow with the full model size. libROM bundles these ingredients so users can build physics-constrained reduced models and repeat examples.
key_claims: Physical simulations have always relied on data, from measurements to calibrated laws.
Models trained only on data ignore first principles, while models constrained by physics combine both data and the governing equations.
libROM supports POD (principal orthogonal decomposition, a method to find the most important patterns in data) through static, incremental, randomized, and space-time SVD methods.
Hyper-reduction is required to make nonlinear ROM fast enough to run.
The library includes working examples such as Poisson, nonlinear diffusion, and Lagrangian hydrodynamics.
Time-windowing and nonlinear manifold ROMs handle long-time simulations where flow pushes material around strongly.

important_terms.meaning: An LLNL software library for reduced-order modeling that builds smaller, faster versions of physics simulations by combining data and first-principles constraints.
A reduced model that uses both data and the governing equations or first-principles residuals to stay accurate.
An algorithm that updates the most important patterns as new data arrive without rebuilding the entire basis from scratch.
Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method, a hyper-reduction technique that samples only the most important nonlinear terms instead of computing all of them.
A reduced model built from smaller reduced pieces that are linked together into a coupled system.

stanford_connections: This talk turns many earlier ROM concepts into a working software stack.
It connects to nonlinear manifold ROM, hyper-reduction, and component ROM talks by showing them as reusable software capabilities you can actually use.
It also supports the full study-system goal because libROM is where concepts become workflows you can redo and validate.
practical_caution: A library makes ROM workflows simpler, but it does not remove the need for modeling judgment. Users still need to choose suitable bases, sampling points, physics constraints, and testing strategies for the target simulation.
selected_evidence: libROM has greedy algorithm capability.
A library for reduced models.
Efficient proper orthonormal decomposition using various singular value decomposition techniques.
In order to achieve the efficiency we have to apply the hyper reduction.
Black box approach... and physics constraints approaches.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scalable scientific machine learning needs software tools. libROM is the engineering layer that turns ROM theory into workflows you can repeat and trust.

title: Masayuki Yano: Reliable, Efficient, And Automated Model Reduction Of Parametrized Nonlinear PDEs
speaker: Masayuki Yano
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to automatically build reduced models for nonlinear PDEs by controlling errors from discretization, basis selection, and numerical integration together.
core_problem: Engineering simulations need fast PDE solutions across many configurations, but reduced models can fail if the full-size discretization, basis, or quadrature rule isn't trained well enough. Building ROMs by hand is also costly and error-prone for complex flows with nonlinear aerodynamics.
first_principles_model: A goal-oriented ROM targets a specific outcome such as lift or drag. Adaptive DG methods (a high-order element-based approach) control how finely the mesh is divided; basis selection compresses the solution shape space across parameter changes; empirical quadrature speeds up residual (leftover error term) computation by evaluating it on just a few elements; and error weights from adjoint equations guide where to add training samples. A greedy algorithm picks the next training point whenever error predictions fall below the target tolerance.
key_claims: Reliable ROM construction must track errors from finite-element approximation, basis selection, and numerical integration together.
Adaptive high-order element methods can make the offline phase—where you compute training snapshots—much faster.
Error weighting by adjoint equations can estimate mistakes in the quantities you actually care about.
Empirical quadrature speeds up residual computation by evaluating it on a sparse subset of elements.
Greedy iteration can build finite-element meshes, bases, and quadrature rules automatically.
Many parameters and shock-dominated flows still pose open challenges.

important_terms.meaning: Building a reduced model while keeping error small for one specific predicted quantity (such as lift).
High-order discretization where the mesh is refined and polynomial degree adjusted based on error estimates.
Error estimation that weights solution mistakes using sensitivity information from solving the problem backwards.
Speed-up method that computes sums and residuals on a chosen subset of elements instead of the full grid.
Iterative selection that adds the next training sample or basis element where error prediction is largest.

stanford_connections: This automated approach mirrors earlier ROM talks but shifts focus: not how to tune ROM by hand, but how the algorithm should tune itself.
It ties to trust-region ROMs and error-controlled basis building through principled error tracking and sample selection.
It also connects to aerodynamics and shock studies because convection-heavy PDEs push both discretization refinement and basis reduction to their limits.
practical_caution: The talk uses the word 'certified' carefully: some error bounds are estimates rather than hard guarantees. Automated workflows still need sanity checks by hand, especially when parameters are numerous or shocks appear.
selected_evidence: Reliable efficient and automated model reduction of parameterized nonlinear PDEs.
Control all three sources of the error... finite mesh... reduced basis... reduced quadrature.
Adaptive high order method enables efficient offline training.
Evaluate it in a very small subset of elements.
Certified here in quotes because we don't have error bounds these are simply estimates.
takeaway: The main lesson is that automation needs an error model. Anyone building a ROM must know what is being compressed, what error is controlled, and which new samples to try next.

title: Misha Khodak: Automatic Architecture Design For Emerging Machine Learning Tasks
speaker: Misha Khodak
one_sentence: This lecture explores how to automate the process of adapting neural network designs so they work on new scientific tasks, beyond the hand-tuned convolutions built for images.
core_problem: We have successful neural network designs that were carefully tuned for images, but real scientific problems involve sequences, graphs, differential equations, and other distinct structures. Inventing new building blocks by hand for each new domain is slow and needs expert knowledge; standard neural architecture search might only try different network connection patterns, missing the chance to discover the right operations needed for a specific task.
first_principles_model: An architecture encodes what kinds of patterns a network can learn: convolution limits how weights are shared across space. XD-operations expand this by creating flexible neural operations that can capture the same useful constraints while still being searchable for different domains. This turns architecture design into a transfer problem: find or search for operations that match the structure of a new task.
key_claims: Hand-tuned neural networks sped up traditional machine learning but don't move easily to new domains without task-specific operations.
New tasks like learning on graphs, processing sequences, and solving differential equations need matching neural operations.
XD-operations generalize the useful constraints of convolutions while letting you express more.
You can treat architecture design as an automated search over operations.
The best architecture depends on how much data you have and the problem structure.
Searching over both the connection pattern and the specific operations at once is possible but computationally hard.

important_terms.meaning: Taking successful design patterns from one task and adapting them for a different task.
A type of neural operation that generalizes the core useful constraints of image convolutions to work on many different problem types.
A structural limit on model parameters that builds in sharing, locality, symmetry, or other built-in learning preference.
Searching for the best way to connect neural operations together in a network.
Choosing the neural operations and how to connect them in a way that defines what the model can do.

stanford_connections: This talk adds to the neural architecture search lecture by focusing on the operations themselves, not just how they are wired together.
It ties to graph networks, Fourier neural operators, and differential equation solvers because the architecture must match the shape of your data.
It reinforces the series theme that learning preferences built into a model often decide whether it can generalize or just memorize.
practical_caution: Automating architecture search can make finding good designs faster, but it has no way to know what matters scientifically unless you put that directly in how you measure success. Accuracy, computational cost, training stability, and whether predictions make physical sense should all guide the design process.
selected_evidence: Towards automatic architecture design for emerging machine learning tasks.
Manual design of task-specific neural operations.
XD-Operations that mimic the useful degree-of-freedom constraints of convolutions.
If you don't have a lot of data... you can use XD.
Discrete continuous optimization simultaneously... difficulty there.
takeaway: The core insight is that architecture is a language for encoding learning biases. Automatic design searches for the right biases that fit a new scientific problem.

title: Steve Sun: Data-Driven Constitutive Updates From Model-Free Poroelasticity To Level Set Plasticity
speaker: Steve WaiChing Sun
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to build material models from data, starting with fluids flowing through solids, and moving to interpreting how materials yield and deform.
core_problem: Simulations of materials need equations that connect stretching and squeezing (strains), internal forces (stresses), fluid pressure, and flow speed. For complex materials, these equations may be unknown, cost too much to measure, or have only sparse experimental data to back them up. Using data directly, without a prebuilt equation, can work, but you need the result to be understandable and to respect the physics.
first_principles_model: A constitutive update (the local rule for how a piece of material responds) sits inside a larger mechanics solver. In poroelasticity (the mix of solid deformation and fluid flow through rock or soil), data can tell you how strain connects to effective stress, and how pressure gradient connects to Darcy flow velocity. A model-free approach searches through the data points to find a physically sensible response; neural networks or level-set functions (defined surfaces that track transitions) can approximate yield surfaces or plastic deformation when data are scarce.
key_claims: Data-driven material modeling using neural networks goes back decades.
The goal is to make material laws readable and to work with the limited data you actually have.
Simulations of fluids in solids need both solid-deformation and flow equations.
You can switch between data-driven and equation-based updates depending on how much data exists.
Fast search methods (like KD-trees, which divide space to speed up lookups) can make data-driven updates efficient.
Level-set plasticity (surfaces that track yield boundaries) can learn simplified plasticity models by learning from higher-resolution simulations.

important_terms.meaning: An equation or model connecting local mechanical variables: stress (internal force), strain (deformation), pressure, and flow.
Simulation that uses measured material data directly, instead of writing down an explicit equation ahead of time.
The simultaneous deformation of solid material and flow of fluid through its pores (as in water moving through soil or oil through rock).
The set of all physically allowed local material states, either measured in experiments or represented by a learned model.
A way to describe yielding (when material starts to permanently deform) using a learned or designed surface that marks the boundary between elastic and plastic behavior.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds material modeling to the data-driven physics stack: the learned object is often the material law, not the entire PDE.
It connects to hybrid twins because combining data and physics equations is most natural at the material-response level.
It also connects to model-constrained learning because the full PDE solver limits which learned local responses are actually admissible.
practical_caution: A material model learned from data can break the global solver if it violates admissibility (physics-allowed states), consistency (the math stays sound step-to-step), or energy conservation. The learned local material model must be tested inside the full coupled simulation, not just on isolated plots of stress versus strain.
selected_evidence: Data-driven constitutive updates from model-free poroelasticity to level set plasticity.
Relationship between the strain and the effective stress.
Relationship between the pressure gradient and the Darcy velocity.
Identifying the constitutive manifold.
We want something very easy to interpret but... work well with limited data.
takeaway: The deeper lesson is that data-driven mechanics often does its work at the constitutive update—the local material response. Learn the material behavior from data, but keep it compatible with the overall physics.

title: Igor Mezic: Koopman Operator Theory For Dynamical Systems, Control And Data Analytics
speaker: Igor Mezic
one_sentence: Koopman operator theory describes nonlinear dynamics through a linear operator that acts on functions of the state.
core_problem: Nonlinear dynamical systems are hard to analyze, reduce, and control because the state changes in a nonlinear way. Koopman theory shifts the view: instead of tracking how the state itself changes, track how functions of the state change. The operator becomes linear, but infinite-dimensional, so the real challenge is finding useful functions and understanding the operator's spectral structure.
first_principles_model: An observable is a function of the system state. The Koopman operator moves observables forward in time by composing them with the nonlinear flow. Its eigenfunctions evolve by multiplying with simple exponential factors, so if you find useful eigenfunctions, nonlinear dynamics can be written in linear form. Numerical methods like DMD approximate parts of this operator from data.
key_claims: Koopman theory reformulates dynamical systems by evolving functions of the state instead of the state itself.
The Koopman operator is linear even when the original system is nonlinear.
Eigenfunctions give coordinates whose evolution is governed by linear equations.
Koopman decompositions are orthogonal in time rather than necessarily in space.
DMD is one numerical method for approximating Koopman spectra and modes.
POD can miss important dynamics when coherent Koopman structure has not been extracted.

important_terms.meaning: A linear operator that moves observables forward in time by composing them with the system flow.
A function of the state whose evolution can be studied instead of the state itself.
An observable that evolves by multiplying with an exponential factor under the Koopman operator.
Dynamic Mode Decomposition, a data-driven method for approximating Koopman modes and eigenvalues.
Persistent dynamical structures whose time behavior can be captured by spectral components.

stanford_connections: This talk links equation discovery, Green's functions, and reduced-order models through the structure of the Koopman operator.
It connects to control because linear representations of nonlinear dynamics simplify feedback and prediction.
It offers a different approach to reduction than POD: choose coordinates based on dynamics, not only on variance.
practical_caution: Koopman methods depend heavily on which functions you choose or discover. A finite-dimensional approximation can look linear but still miss important dynamics if the observable space is not right.
selected_evidence: Koopman operator theory... for dynamical systems control and data analytics.
A reformulation... in terms of evolutionary observables.
The operator is linear.
Eigenfunctions are special functions... governed by linear equations.
DMD is... ways of approximating the Koopman operator.
takeaway: The lesson is that nonlinear dynamics may become linear in the right space of functions. Koopman theory is a search for that space.

title: Miles Cranmer: The Problem With Deep Learning For Physics And How To Fix It
speaker: Miles Cranmer
one_sentence: This lecture argues that deep neural networks that hide their inner workings can create scientific debt in physics and proposes interpretable alternatives such as inductive biases and symbolic regression.
core_problem: Deep learning can solve high-dimensional prediction problems, but if the learned solution is opaque, science may gain performance without understanding. That creates scientific debt: future researchers must explain what the model learned and whether it reflects real physical mechanism.
first_principles_model: Physics already has a language for explaining things: mathematics. Instead of using neural networks only as hidden-solution predictors, you can build physical structure into the network itself, such as Lagrangian neural networks (where the network learns an energy-like quantity and applies physics equations to compute motion), or distill trained networks into symbolic equations using symbolic regression (a method that searches for formulas fitting data). The goal is to turn learned patterns into testable scientific statements you can inspect.
key_claims: Using deep learning without guidance can delay the need to understand the physical problem.
Standard interpretation methods from computer vision do not work well for physics because physics has symbolic mathematical structure.
Inductive bias restricts the space of functions a model can learn toward physically realistic forms.
Lagrangian neural networks learn a physical quantity (like energy) inside an existing mechanics framework.
Graph networks match particle-like physical systems well because natural systems are relational rather than only gridded.
Symbolic regression can approximate internal neural-network components with analytic equations.

important_terms.meaning: The accumulated explanatory burden created when a model predicts well without producing scientific understanding.
A prior restriction on what functions a model can learn, often used to encode physical structure.
A search method for finding analytic equations that fit data or approximate a learned model.
A neural model that learns an energy-like function and derives dynamics through mechanics equations.
Extracting simpler symbolic formulas from a trained neural network or its learned components.

stanford_connections: This talk stands in opposition to hidden-solution surrogate modeling throughout the series.
It connects to SINDy, Green's functions, and nonlocal kernels because all emphasize learning inspectable mechanisms.
It also ties back to physics-guided forecasting: inductive bias is not optional decoration, it is what makes models scientifically usable.
practical_caution: A physically inspired neural network can still fail if the prior is too weak or the variables cannot be determined from the data. Interpretability methods should produce testable equations or mechanisms, not just prettier graphs.
selected_evidence: The problem with deep learning in physics and how to fix it.
We are postponing our need to understand that problem.
Physics has a good symbolic model... math.
An inductive bias is some kind of prior on what possible functions your model can learn.
Symbolic regression... searching for equations.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific machine learning should pay back its explanatory debt. Use neural networks to discover mechanisms, not merely to hide them.

title: Greg Beroza: Towards Complete Machine-Learning-Based Earthquake Monitoring Workflows
speaker: Greg Beroza
one_sentence: This lecture shows earthquake monitoring as an end-to-end workflow where machine learning can improve how we detect waves, group them into earthquakes, locate where they happened, and measure their size—but only when we treat training data, data variants, model design, and catalog checking as interconnected pieces of the system.
core_problem: Earthquake monitoring is not one single prediction task. A seismic network constantly records ground motion, and a real monitoring system must clean up the signals, spot wave arrivals, group arrivals into events, pinpoint earthquake locations, estimate sizes, and keep records accurate over time. Swapping out one step with a neural network helps, but errors in one stage can still contaminate the whole catalog.
first_principles_model: A monitoring workflow turns raw seismic recordings into a structured earthquake catalog. At each step, the information changes shape: raw signals become phase picks (identified wave arrivals), phase picks become events, events become locations and source details. Machine learning shines when it learns these transformations from labeled seismic data and artificially varied examples, but the final product is the catalog, so the right way to measure success is how good the entire workflow is, not just how well the neural network performs on one isolated piece.
key_claims: Standard earthquake monitoring is a pipeline of signal cleaning, wave-phase detection, grouping phases into events, location calculation, and size estimation.
Deep learning can replace individual steps and sometimes creates much more complete earthquake records than methods used before machine learning.
High-quality training labels, model architecture choices, and creating realistic data variants are not minor details; they decide whether the model works on real seismic networks it has never seen.
Replacing one workflow piece at a time is easiest to put into practice because each step can be upgraded separately.
Combining several monitoring tasks in a single model that learns them together can work better because different seismic tasks share information.
Better earthquake catalogs matter because they reveal small and previously missed earthquakes that show earthquake patterns and where hazards are located.

important_terms.meaning: A complete list of detected seismic events, recording when and where each happened, how big it was, and other properties of the earthquake.
Identifying the exact times when different seismic wave types (such as P and S waves) arrive at recording stations in continuous ground-motion data.
Grouping wave arrivals recorded at many sensors so they are recognized as coming from one earthquake.
Creating varied training examples from known seismic signals so a model learns what stays the same across different network conditions instead of memorizing one specific setup.
A model design where several related monitoring tasks are learned together instead of as separate independent modules.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on earlier lectures on physics-informed models and surrogate models: a learned system must fit into a scientific workflow, not stand alone.
It connects to methods for active learning and smart data collection because training labels and realistic data variants are essential to good scientific machine learning.
It also connects to uncertainty and inverse problems: how good the earthquake catalog is determines what downstream geophysical conclusions can be trusted.
practical_caution: Do not judge a monitoring model only by how well it picks wave phases. A model can score well at spotting phases but still produce a bad catalog if it fails at grouping arrivals into events, locating them, estimating magnitudes, or working on a new seismic network.
selected_evidence: Standard earthquake monitoring workflows can be described with... pre-processing, phase detection, event-phase association, location, and characterization.
Machine learning methods, particularly deep neural networks, have been shown capable of replacing these steps.
Generate earthquake catalogs that are far more comprehensive than those developed using standard approaches.
Appropriate architecture, accurate data labels, and data augmentation all play an important role.
The simplest approach... is modular.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that machine learning for earthquake monitoring should be judged as a complete measurement system. What comes out is not a classification score; it is a catalog that geophysicists and hazard models will actually use.

title: Pat Langley: Computational Scientific Discovery
speaker: Pat Langley
organization: Institute for the Study of Learning and Expertise / Stanford Center for Design Research
one_sentence: This lecture treats scientific discovery as a guided search through possible laws and models, directed by observations, mathematical forms scientists use, and what we already know.
core_problem: Most machine learning chases accuracy in prediction but ignores whether the result is a real scientific theory—something researchers can state, examine, and use elsewhere. True scientific discovery needs more than fitting numbers to curves: it needs to explore a structured space of possible laws or models that explain what we observe in a language scientists recognize and trust.
first_principles_model: A discovery system rests on three things: observations to explain, a space of possible laws or models you can search through, and heuristics (decision rules) that guide the search. The core requirement is that the result must be communicable—a law, equation, a description of how something works, or a model stated in forms that science already accepts. Background knowledge about the domain narrows the search and ensures the candidate models make sense.
key_claims: Scientific discovery can be framed as guided search across candidate laws, hypotheses, or models—not random exploration.
What sets discovery systems apart from simple data-mining algorithms is that they output something like a scientific theory: a communicable object in an established form.
Equation discovery searches for mathematical relationships, but model discovery must also capture how things work qualitatively—the mechanisms and structure.
Qualitative explanatory models often matter more than exact numbers because they show cause-and-effect or how a process unfolds.
Inductive process modeling learns dynamic models (ones that change over time) from sequences of measurements, using existing knowledge to infer differential equations that describe the process.
Domain knowledge is not a problem to ignore; it is what makes the search manageable and ensures the result is actually useful to science.

important_terms.meaning: A way of exploring a huge set of possibilities by using rules or scores to prefer candidates that seem most promising, rather than checking every option.
A discovered relationship written in a compact scientific form—an equation, a process description, or another form scientists accept—rather than a hidden prediction machine.
The process of finding mathematical equations that match observed data and capture an underlying law or pattern.
A model that explains how or why something happens—the mechanisms and structure—even when the precise numeric values are less important.
Learning models of systems that change over time by analyzing sequences of measurements and using existing knowledge to build differential equations that describe the dynamics.

stanford_connections: This lecture relates directly to SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics), symbolic regression, Koopman analysis methods, and Miles Cranmer's work on why we still owe science better tools for discovery.
It bridges the gap between data-driven modeling and how science has traditionally explained nature.
It also explains why surrogate models that humans can read matter: a good prediction tool is not automatically a scientific discovery.
practical_caution: A symbolic equation does not automatically count as a discovered law. If the space of possibilities, the background knowledge, or the search rules are chosen poorly, the system can produce short equations that happen to fit the data but are meaningless in science.
selected_evidence: Discovery involves heuristic search through a space of candidate laws or models.
Those are stated in some established scientific formalism.
That distinguishes work in this area from pretty much everything else in machine learning.
The interesting thing here is not the parameters... the qualitative structure of these laws.
Inductive process modeling... multivariate time series... background knowledge.
takeaway: The main lesson is that scientific machine learning should search in science's own language. Observations constrain what's possible, but mathematical forms and domain knowledge make the result something a scientist can use.

title: Ashesh Chattopadhyay: Deep Learning Meets Data Assimilation
speaker: Ashesh Chattopadhyay
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to combine deep learning with data assimilation to forecast chaotic weather and climate, where you must blend sparse noisy measurements with imperfect forecast models.
core_problem: Weather and climate systems are high-dimensional, multiscale, and chaotic—small errors grow rapidly. A forecast cannot simply start from perfect truth because observations are noisy, sparse, and unevenly sampled, while numerical or learned forecast models are imperfect. The immediate problem is estimating a usable starting state before you forecast.
first_principles_model: Data assimilation is Bayesian state estimation (combining prior knowledge with new evidence) for dynamical systems. A background forecast provides a prior state; observations provide partial noisy evidence; the assimilation algorithm weighs both to produce an analysis state. Deep learning can help by learning unresolved small-scale effects, forecast operators, observation corrections, or hybrid ensemble Kalman filters, but it must respect dynamical consistency because small state errors can amplify rapidly in chaotic systems.
key_claims: Weather and climate forecasting is hard because the system spans many spatial and temporal scales and is chaotic.
Forecasting requires an initial condition, but observations are sparse and noisy.
Data assimilation merges background forecasts and observations to estimate the state used to start prediction.
Deep models can learn how small-scale unresolved processes affect the system by training on high-resolution simulations or observations.
Hybrid approaches combine learning-based parts with numerical models rather than replacing the entire forecasting pipeline.
Physically consistent network designs and ensemble Kalman filtering are central tools for making learned forecasts work reliably in operations.

important_terms.meaning: A method that merges model predictions with noisy measurements to estimate the current state of a system that changes over time.
The corrected state estimate produced after you incorporate observations into a background prediction.
The model prediction before you apply corrections based on observations.
A data assimilation method that represents forecast uncertainty using many parallel predictions and updates them with observations.
A forecasting method that combines numerical physics models with learned data-driven parts.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to physics-guided learning because the structure of the model matters when small errors grow through the dynamics.
It also links to neural operators and reduced-order models: learned parts must work together with state estimation, not just free-running prediction.
The lecture is a practical partner to uncertainty talks because the uncertainty in the starting state is a major source of forecast error.
practical_caution: A neural forecast model that performs well from clean starting states can fail in real-world settings if it cannot handle noisy sparse observations or if its errors grow unchecked over time.
selected_evidence: Weather and climate system... is a multi-scale chaotic dynamical system.
Observations... could be noisy, it could be sparse.
Data assimilation... ensure that information from both the background forecast and the noisy observations are properly weighed.
Hybrid sample Kalman filters for weather forecasting.
You can learn the effects... of these small scale processes.
takeaway: The core lesson is that prediction begins with state estimation. For chaotic physical systems, learning the forecast rule and learning how to set up its starting state are inseparable.

title: Sergei Tretiak: Machine Learning For Materials And Chemical Dynamics
speaker: Sergei Tretiak
one_sentence: This lecture shows how machine learning models can stand in for expensive materials and chemical simulations, using smart data collection to find where the model is uncertain and dealing with the fact that what happens at a distance away can matter.
core_problem: Getting precise answers from quantum and molecular simulations is costly, but finding new materials means running thousands of these simulations across different structures and conditions. Machine learning can predict how a structure's properties relate to its shape, but it fails when the training data are missing important cases or when the model only looks at each atom's immediate neighbors and ignores effects from distant atoms—like electric charge spread across the system, how the charge redistributes, attraction between far-off molecules, or excited electronic states.
first_principles_model: A molecular ML model takes the positions of atoms and predicts the energy, forces, or properties. Local models—where each atom's energy comes mostly from atoms nearby—run fast and scale to large systems, but real chemistry includes effects that bridge across the whole molecule. Active learning works by having the model make predictions, spotting configurations where it is least confident, running expensive reference simulations at those points, retraining with the new data, and repeating.
