To capture longer-range effects, some models add layers that let atoms talk to each other step by step, use cycles where predictions feed back in, or add charge-equilibration (a way to spread charge across the system to match what electrostatics demands).
key_claims: Machine learning builds surrogate models trained on reference chemical or materials data.
The quality of training data sets a hard limit on accuracy, because the model can learn only the configurations it has seen.
Active learning grows the dataset automatically wherever the model is most unsure.

Assuming each atom is predicted mainly from its nearby neighbors makes atomistic ML fast but can miss charge transfer, charge redistribution, electrostatic effects, van der Waals attraction, and excited electronic states.
Distant interactions can be captured with layers that pass information step by step, self-consistent feedback loops, and charge-equilibration schemes.
Simulating chemistry over time requires the model to stay stable as atomic configurations change, not just to predict static properties accurately.

important_terms.meaning: A trained model that predicts molecular energies and forces from the positions of atoms.
A loop that picks new configurations for expensive reference simulations where the model is most uncertain, then retrains.
Treating each atom's energy or behavior as if it comes mostly from atoms in its neighborhood, not from distant parts of the molecule.
A physical effect where distant atoms or the overall charge distribution in a molecule influence what happens at one location.
A step that computes how charge spreads across a molecular system to satisfy electrostatic forces and long-range effects.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties to data-focused scientific machine learning: choosing which data to gather is as important as the model architecture itself.
It also connects to multiscale modeling because the rules that apply to single atoms must add up to reliable predictions at the material scale.
It reinforces the series theme that when extrapolation is risky, built-in knowledge about how the physics works is often needed.
practical_caution: A model that performs well on a test set can fail once you run it in a live simulation if that simulation explores configurations the training data never included or enters a regime where distant atoms and global charge effects dominate.
selected_evidence: Machine learning... provides a surrogate model trained on the dataset of some reference data.
Designing high-quality training data sets is crucial to overall model accuracy.
Active learning strategy... new data are automatically collected for atomic configurations that produce large ML uncertainties.
A major drawback of the current machine learning framework... is locality.
Overcome nonlocality... interaction layers, self-consistent cycles, or charge equilibration schemes.
takeaway: The underlying lesson is that molecular ML is a controlled substitute for quantum or molecular physics. Whether it works depends on where you collected training data and what physical interactions—whether distant or not—the model's design can represent.

title: Kaushik Bhattacharya: Multi-Scale Modeling And Neural Operators
speaker: Kaushik Bhattacharya
one_sentence: This lecture explains neural operators as function-to-function approximators that can carry fine-scale material physics into efficient coarse-scale multiscale models.
core_problem: Material behavior emerges from interacting physics across electronic, atomistic, defect, domain, and continuum scales. Directly resolving every fine-scale detail inside engineering-scale simulations is often impossible, while simple averaging can lose the details that control performance.
first_principles_model: Multiscale modeling splits the problem into an ordered hierarchy of scales. The coarse scale provides boundary conditions or loading to the fine scale, and the fine scale returns effective responses. A neural operator learns this map between function spaces rather than between fixed-size vectors. If trained as a controlled approximation to the fine-scale operator, it can be embedded at the coarse scale with high accuracy and lower cost.
key_claims: Materials involve coupled physics across many length and time scales.
Multiscale modeling uses a divide-and-conquer hierarchy in which coarser scales control and filter finer-scale details.
The practical bottleneck is repeatedly solving expensive fine-scale problems inside coarse-scale computations.
Neural operators approximate maps from one function space to another, which matches the mathematical structure of many physical solution operators.
Operator learning is different from ordinary supervised learning on fixed-size vectors because the input and output are functions.
Neural operators can preserve small-scale detail while making coarse-scale implementation computationally efficient.

important_terms.meaning: A modeling strategy that links physical descriptions across different spatial or temporal scales.
A neural model that learns a map between function spaces, such as from a coefficient field to a solution field.
A set whose elements are functions, making the learning problem infinite-dimensional before discretization.
The larger-scale representation used for engineering simulation or system-level prediction.
The smaller-scale physics, such as atomistic or microstructural behavior, that informs effective large-scale response.

stanford_connections: This lecture is central to the playlist's neural-operator thread and complements talks on FNOs, DeepONets, and ROMs.
It connects operator learning to classical multiscale mechanics rather than treating it as a generic surrogate method.
It also links to uncertainty and reliability because coarse-scale predictions inherit approximation errors from learned fine-scale closures.
practical_caution: A neural operator is only useful if it approximates the right operator over the right distribution of functions. Good interpolation on one discretization does not guarantee multiscale validity under new microstructures, loads, or boundary conditions.
selected_evidence: The behavior of materials involve physics at multiple length and time scales.
Multiscale modeling seeks to understand this complexity with a divide and conquer approach.
The maps we are interested in learning is from one function space to another.
We are trying to learn a non-linear operator.
Capture all the details of the small scale but can be directly implemented at the coarse scale.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that operator learning succeeds when the learned object matches the physics object: a map between fields, scales, and boundary-conditioned responses.

title: Lexing Ying: Prony's Method, Analytic Continuation, And Quantum Signal Processing
speaker: Lexing Ying
one_sentence: This lecture uses Prony's method—a technique for extracting exponential frequencies and amplitudes from signal samples—to unify three problems: noisy analytic continuation and stable factorization in quantum signal processing.
core_problem: Many scientific computing problems ask us to recover hidden spectral or exponential structure from limited samples. This is hard because noise, finite sampling, and ill-conditioning (where tiny data errors cause huge errors in the answer) can make frequency identification and analytic continuation unstable. Quantum signal processing adds a related factorization problem where stable phase recovery is essential.
first_principles_model: Prony's method starts from the assumption that a sampled signal is a sum of exponentials. If that model is right, the frequencies and amplitudes are encoded in algebraic relationships among equally spaced samples. The broader lesson is to exploit latent analytic structure: convert a hard inverse problem into identifying the parameters of a structured representation, while respecting noise and conditioning.
key_claims: Prony's method identifies frequencies and amplitudes from equally spaced samples of exponential sums.
The method is old but underappreciated relative to its usefulness in scientific computing.
Noisy analytic continuation can be approached using ideas from Prony-style structured signal recovery.
Quantum signal processing requires stable factorization of phase factors.
The same algebraic insight can connect classical signal processing, complex analytic continuation, and quantum algorithms.
Stability is the central practical issue because the inverse problems are sensitive to noise.

important_terms.meaning: A classical algorithm for recovering frequencies and amplitudes in a signal modeled as a finite sum of exponentials.
Extending a function beyond the region where it is directly known, often an ill-posed problem when data are noisy.
A technique for transforming spectra of quantum operators through sequences of controlled phase factors.
Estimating the exponential or oscillatory components that generate observed samples.
A situation where small data errors can cause large errors in the recovered solution.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to inverse problems in the series: extracting hidden structure from limited measurements is a recurring theme.
It also complements Koopman and spectral methods because all rely on finding useful frequency or eigen-structure.
It adds a numerical-analysis perspective to the ML-heavy playlist: not every data-driven method is a neural network.
practical_caution: Structured recovery can yield accurate answers, but if the assumed exponential model is wrong or the data are too noisy, Prony-style methods can amplify errors rather than reveal structure.
selected_evidence: Prony's method is a powerful algorithm for identifying frequencies and amplitudes from equally spaced signals.
How many frequencies do you have in the signal... can you figure out what is... the weights.
Applying Prony's method to do noisy analytic continuation.
Stable factorization of the phase factors for quantum signal processing.
The classical solution... goes back more than 200 years.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that good algorithms exploit structure before optimizing. Prony's method works because it turns samples into a parametric spectral model.

title: Ming Zhong: Machine Learning Of Self Organization From Observation
speaker: Ming Zhong
one_sentence: This lecture builds a method for learning the interaction rules in self-organizing collective systems directly from measured motion trajectories.
core_problem: Self-organization happens in systems such as flocking, crowds, crystals, superconductivity, and social behavior. The large-scale pattern is visible, but the microscopic interaction rule among individual agents is unknown. The challenge is to infer physically meaningful dynamical laws from observations rather than only predict future motion.
first_principles_model: A collective system can be modeled as interacting agents whose velocities or accelerations depend on distances between them, agent states, and agent types through interaction kernels (functions that describe how one agent influences another). Given trajectory data from multiple starting conditions, the learning problem is to estimate those kernels so the resulting dynamical system reproduces observed behavior and predicts new collective motion. Theory studies how well we can recover the kernels as we gather data from more starting conditions.
key_claims: Self-organization can be studied through observed motion of interacting agents.
The goal is to derive interpretable dynamical systems and interaction rules, not only accurate predictions without understanding.
Learning interaction kernels can validate and improve existing models of collective behavior.
Convergence analysis depends on data from multiple starting conditions and on how trajectory data are discretized.
The method extends from identical agents to heterogeneous systems such as predator-prey interactions.
Steady-state observations can also contain information about interaction kernels, though the inverse problem requires regularization.

important_terms.meaning: Collective behavior where large-scale order emerges from local interactions among components or agents.
A function describing how one agent influences another as a function of distance, state, or type.
Agents governed by the same interaction laws.
Agents of different types with different interaction rules, such as predators and prey.
Time-indexed observations of agent states used to infer the governing interaction laws.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to equation discovery and symbolic modeling because it learns governing laws from data.
It also links to nonlocal kernels and graph-based physics: collective behavior depends on relational interactions.
It complements forecasting talks by emphasizing interpretable dynamics over pure motion extrapolation.
practical_caution: Inferring interaction laws from observation is an inverse problem. Good trajectory fit does not guarantee a unique or physically correct kernel, especially when you have limited starting conditions or only steady-state observations.
selected_evidence: Self-organization... can be found in studying crystal formation, superconductivity, social behaviors.
Can we actually derive from observation data... the interaction rules between all the agents.
Develop a learning framework to derive physically meaningful dynamical systems.
Analyze the convergence... from various different initial conditions.
Handle a system of heterogeneous agents.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that collective patterns are compressed evidence about interaction laws. Scientific machine learning should recover the laws, not just repeat the pattern.

title: Alice Cicirello: Interpretable, Explainable And Non-Intrusive Uncertainty Propagation
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to find the range of possible outputs from an expensive computer model when inputs might vary, using machine learning to pick which model runs matter most, while keeping the process understandable to engineers.
core_problem: Engineering choices need to know whether a system will work under changing conditions, but running realistic physics models can take hours or days. Finding the full range of outputs usually means running the model thousands of times or changing how the solver works, which may not be practical for real-world simulations.
first_principles_model: Uncertainty propagation means tracking how variations in inputs become variations in outputs as they flow through a computational model. If you treat the simulator as a black box (you run it but don't change its code), you need to pick a few runs wisely. Machine-learning optimization can search for which input combinations give the highest and lowest outputs, and then explain why those extremes happen by building a simple mathematical model (called a surrogate) that approximates the expensive one.
key_claims: Uncertainty quantification helps engineering decisions by computing how variations in inputs ripple into variations in performance.
For models that take a long time to run, the main challenge is picking as few model runs as possible.
Non-intrusive methods don't modify the simulator's code or simplify the underlying physics.
Interpretability means a human can trace through how a result was calculated.
Explainability means presenting results in a form engineers can actually use and reason about.
Machine-learning optimization can search for output extremes (highest and lowest values) instead of densely testing the entire input space.

important_terms.meaning: Tracking how ranges or variations in model inputs flow through to ranges or variations in outputs.
A method that treats the simulator as a black box—you run it but don't change or rewrite its code.
Uncertainty expressed as ranges ("between 10 and 20") rather than full probability distributions.
A method that uses a simple statistical model to predict which runs will be most informative, then picks those runs instead of trying everything.
A limit (upper or lower) on how well a system performs when inputs can vary within their ranges.

stanford_connections: This talk addresses the series' uncertainty theme by showing how to handle variability in real engineering problems.
It connects to active learning—both use strategies to pick which experiments or model runs matter most when testing is expensive.
It builds on interpretability talks by showing that explaining uncertainty results is essential for engineers to trust and use them.
practical_caution: If your sampling strategy misses certain input regions or your surrogate doesn't capture the full behavior, you might miss the true extremes. Treat output bounds as reliable only after checking that your search strategy and surrogate actually covered the important parts of the input space.
selected_evidence: Uncertainty models are used in conjunction with a computational model to compute the effects of uncertainties on a system performance.
Interpretable: a human can understand how a prediction was made.
Explainable: the results are presented in a format that is understandable by humans.
Non-intrusive: no modifications of the computational model are carried out.
Select the minimum number of physics based models to run in order to get performance bounds.
takeaway: The core idea is that uncertainty quantification is a problem with limited computing budget. You must pick your runs smartly to find the bounds you care about, then show engineers clearly why those bounds are what they are.

title: Yannis Kevrekidis: No Equations, No Variables, No Parameters, No Space And No Time
speaker: Yannis Kevrekidis
one_sentence: This lecture argues that modern data-driven modeling can sometimes skip explicit equations, variables, parameters, space, and time by finding useful high-level observables and computational representations straight from observations.
core_problem: Classical modeling starts with observations, then defines variables, writes equations, picks parameters, and analyzes. Complex systems often block this path because the right high-level variables stay hidden, the microscopic simulator may exist without closed equations, and the effective geometry or time scale may be buried inside high-dimensional data.
first_principles_model: The first-principles move is to separate the scientific goal from the traditional symbolic box. If your goal is prediction, continuation, bifurcation analysis (how system behavior changes as a parameter shifts), or control, you can sometimes build the needed computational operators directly from data or short bursts of simulation. Manifold learning (finding low-dimensional curved structure inside high-dimensional data), diffusion maps, autoencoders (neural networks that compress data into smaller representations), recurrent nets, neural ODEs (neural networks that describe change over time), and operator learning can identify low-dimensional coordinates, high-level observables, or evolution rules without first writing a closed-form high-level equation.
key_claims: Many modern neural architectures have older roots in nonlinear dynamical-system identification.
Equation-free modeling keeps the analysis goal but swaps explicit high-level equations for computational experiments on data or microscopic simulators.
The right variables can be learned from data rather than chosen by intuition alone.
Manifold learning can reveal low-dimensional curved structure inside high-dimensional observations.
Diffusion maps are one way to learn coordinates on data manifolds that serve as high-level observables.
The phrase no equations, variables, parameters, space, or time points to learning the representation needed for the task rather than assuming it in advance.

important_terms.meaning: A computational method that performs high-level analysis using data or microscopic simulators without closed-form high-level equations.
A reduced variable that summarizes the large-scale state of a complex system.
Methods that discover low-dimensional curved structure inside high-dimensional data.
A manifold-learning method that uses diffusion geometry on data to construct useful low-dimensional coordinates.
A computational operator that advances high-level variables by lifting them to microscopic states, simulating briefly, and restricting back.

stanford_connections: This talk links directly to Petros Koumoutsakos' effective dynamics lecture and later data-driven dynamics talks.
It also connects to ROMs (reduced-order models, simplified versions of complex systems) and neural operators because both search for lower-dimensional or operator-level descriptions.
It reframes scientific ML as representation discovery: first learn what variables or coordinates make the problem solvable.
practical_caution: Learning coordinates from data works only if the data cover the relevant curved structures. A beautiful low-dimensional embedding can break when you encounter new operating conditions, rare transitions, or parameters you didn't see during training.
selected_evidence: No equations no variables no space no time.
Obtaining predictive dynamical equations from data lies at the heart of science and engineering modeling.
Operate directly on observations -data-.
Machine learning on the data to find out what the right macro observables are.
Diffusion Maps... learn low dimensional curved manifolds passing through the data.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that equations are one way to represent dynamics, not the only way. The deeper goal is to find the coordinates and operators that make prediction and analysis possible.

title: Weinan E: Machine Learning And Multi-Scale Modeling
speaker: Weinan E
one_sentence: This lecture explains how machine learning helps multiscale modeling by learning mathematical functions that can capture complex behavior—the kind classical hand-built models cannot express by hand.
core_problem: Multiscale modeling aims to connect quantum, atomistic, coarse-grained, continuum, and turbulence-level descriptions into practical simulations that predict real-world properties. The idea is powerful, but a real challenge remains: the effective models and closure relations (equations that account for what smaller scales do) can be too complicated to write down or parameterize by hand.
first_principles_model: Each scale has a model that works well in its own range. The multiscale task is to move information between scales: fine-detailed models supply effective laws, closures, potentials, or constitutive relations (how a material responds to forces) for coarser models. Machine learning expands what models can be expressed for these connections between scales, making room for learned potentials, coarse-grained dynamics, non-Newtonian constitutive models, and reduced PDE models.
key_claims: Multiscale modeling connects physical models across scales to build accurate simulation tools.
Its practical success has been limited because the functions and models needed are too hard to write by hand.
Machine learning offers flexible ways to represent closures and effective models.
Applications include molecular dynamics, coarse-grained molecular dynamics, non-Newtonian fluid dynamics, and PDE model reduction.
The hierarchy of physical models spans quantum mechanics, density functional theory, molecular dynamics, coarse-grained models, continuum mechanics, and turbulence models.
The central promise is not replacing physics, but learning the pieces that connect physical descriptions across scales.

important_terms.meaning: A process of linking models defined at different physical scales to predict large-scale quantities of interest.
An approximate relation that captures the effects of small-scale details that a coarser model cannot represent directly.
A molecular simulation that groups many small degrees of freedom into fewer, larger effective units.
A fluid whose stress-strain relationship cannot be described by a constant viscosity, unlike simple Newtonian fluids.
A model at one scale that captures the essential effects of more detailed physics at smaller scales.

stanford_connections: This lecture pairs naturally with Kaushik Bhattacharya's work on neural operators for multiscale mechanics.
It also connects to materials machine learning because learned potentials are one concrete way to bridge between scales.
It reinforces a theme that returns throughout the seminar: machine learning is most useful when it fills a gap in what a physics-based tool can express.
practical_caution: A learned closure can be accurate inside its training regime and still break conservation, stability, or transfer across scales if it is not built into the larger simulator in a consistent way.
selected_evidence: Multi-scale modeling... aims at unifying the different physical models at different scales.
Practical success on really challenging problems has been limited.
Limited ability to represent complex models and complex functions.
Machine learning has emerged as a promising tool for overcoming the difficulty.
A hierarchy of physical models... quantum mechanics... molecular dynamics... continuum mechanics.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that multiscale machine learning is about learning the interfaces between different physical descriptions. The model is valuable when it lets a trusted simulation reason across scales.

title: Daniel Floryan: Charting Dynamics From Data
speaker: Daniel Floryan
one_sentence: This lecture uses maps of curved surfaces (manifolds) and overlapping local coordinate systems (atlases and charts) to build small dynamical models directly from time-series data.
core_problem: Many systems are high-dimensional, nonlinear, and hard to write down as first-principles equations, yet their trajectories often live on lower-dimensional surfaces. A single global coordinate system may twist that surface or fail to work, so the modeling problem is to find local coordinate systems and dynamical laws that together cover the entire state space.
first_principles_model: A curved surface (manifold) can be described by an atlas: overlapping local coordinate systems with maps between local coordinates and the ambient state. From time-series data, you can cluster trajectories into patches, learn coordinates on each patch, learn local dynamics, and stitch the patches into a global dynamical description. The result is a minimal model in the true dimensionality of the system rather than the dimensionality of the measured state.
key_claims: Data-driven model discovery is motivated by unknown equations and high-dimensional equations we do know.
Natural systems often evolve on low-dimensional surfaces inside high-dimensional state spaces.
An atlas of coordinate systems provides local ways to cover a curved surface.
Time-series data can be clustered into overlapping patches that become coordinate domains.
Learning local coordinate systems can produce dynamical models in the lowest useful dimension.
Local coordinate systems can separate the true shape of state space from coordinate artifacts and improve prediction or control.

important_terms.meaning: A space that may be curved overall but looks locally like ordinary flat space.
A set of overlapping local coordinate systems that together describe a curved surface.
A local coordinate system describing one patch of a curved surface.
The true number of degrees of freedom needed to describe the system's state.
Sequential observations of a system used to learn its shape and how it changes over time.

stanford_connections: This lecture complements Kevrekidis' work on discovering structure in data with a concrete geometric method.
It also connects to reduced-order models because both aim to find low-dimensional descriptions of how systems evolve.
It bridges manifold learning, nonlinear dynamics, and control-focused model discovery.
practical_caution: Local coordinate systems require good coverage and overlap. If the data miss parts of the surface or transitions between patches, the learned atlas can produce jumps or misleading dynamics.
selected_evidence: Learn minimal dynamical models directly from time series data.
Natural systems tend to live on small or low dimensional manifolds.
A manifold is... an atlas of charts.
Time series data... lie on or near a manifold.
Cluster the data into overlapping patches.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that dimension reduction is not just compression. For dynamical systems, the learned coordinates must support a valid evolution rule.

title: Petros Koumoutsakos: Artificial Intelligence And Scientific Computing For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Petros Koumoutsakos
one_sentence: This lecture argues for mixing AI and scientific computing carefully for complex flows, using learned reduced models and multi-agent reinforcement learning while separating real progress from hype.
core_problem: Fluid mechanics combines nonlinear dynamics, structure at many scales, turbulence, flow-structure interaction (how fluids push and pull on solid objects), and control. AI methods are widely promoted as replacements for traditional simulation, but learning algorithms alone cannot be trusted for complex flows. The problem is how to combine data, numerical solvers, physical insight, and learning algorithms into systems that predict and control flows better than either piece alone.
first_principles_model: Scientific computing provides discretized physical laws, numerical solvers, and stability constraints. AI provides flexible approximation, representation learning, and control policies. A hybrid system is one where each component does what it is structurally good at: solvers generate or constrain dynamics, learned models approximate the effective low-dimensional behavior, and reinforcement learning (learning by trial and environmental feedback) explores control strategies under physical simulation feedback.
key_claims: AI has benefited from massive hardware and data growth, but fluid-mechanics claims require careful separation of what is proven from what is speculation.
Complex flow prediction and control should use combinations of AI and simulations rather than AI alone.
Learning reduced models is one hybrid approach: detailed or high-resolution simulations inform a smaller dynamical description.
The equation-free method is an important ancestor of learned reduced dynamics.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning can be combined with scientific computing for flow-structure interaction and control.
Successes and failures both matter because they reveal when the underlying physics structure is necessary.

important_terms.meaning: A hybrid system that joins scientific computing, models, solvers, and machine learning into one calculation.
A reduced description that captures how a complex system behaves at the scale you care about.
Coupled motion between a fluid and solid bodies that can move or change shape.
A method where multiple agents learn by interacting with an environment and each other, adjusting their actions based on rewards.
Numerical methods and algorithms that solve math models of physical systems on computers.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly extends ideas from Kevrekidis about equation-free methods and effective dynamics into fluid mechanics.
It connects to later talks about surrogate acceleration because the goal is not speed alone but accurate prediction and control.
It also links to reinforcement learning in scientific control, where the simulation becomes the training environment.
practical_caution: For fluids, a learned model that looks impressive on one test run can fail when conditions change, when predictions drift over long times, or when control feeds back into the system. Mixing AI and solvers must include numerical and physical checks to catch these failures early.
selected_evidence: There is an ever-increasing amount of hype... regarding the capabilities of learning algorithms.
Forming alloys of AI and simulations for the prediction and control of complex flow systems.
Models and numerics and... machine learning tools... I call this computing alloys.
Learning the effective dynamics of complex systems.
Equation free framework... simulations in the microscales.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that AI for fluids should be built as a hybrid scientific-computing system. The right question is not AI or solvers, but which mixture is stable, accurate, and can be controlled.

title: Benjamin Peherstorfer: Neural Galerkin Schemes With Active Learning
speaker: Benjamin Peherstorfer
one_sentence: This lecture presents Neural Galerkin schemes that solve high-dimensional evolution equations by fitting neural-network states over time and actively choosing training samples based on where the current solution approximation fails most.
core_problem: High-dimensional time-dependent PDEs are difficult because sampling uniformly across the time-space domain wastes data, while neural networks need well-chosen training points to use their approximation power well. A fixed training set may miss moving localized structures such as waves, fronts, or concentrated features that travel across the domain.
first_principles_model: Galerkin methods approximate a PDE solution inside a chosen trial space by measuring how much the guess violates the differential equation and reducing that error. Neural Galerkin replaces the classical trial basis with a neural-network representation whose parameters evolve sequentially in time. Instead of drawing all training points blindly, the method uses this error measurement to actively collect samples where the current approximation performs worst.
key_claims: Estimating how well a model will work on new data is hard in science and engineering when informative samples are scarce.
Neural Galerkin schemes fit network parameters by minimizing the PDE error sequentially over time.
Residual-based sampling provides a self-guided active-learning mechanism.
Active data collection is needed to make neural approximation strengths practical in high dimensions.
The approach works especially well for evolution equations with moving concentrated features.
The method treats training data generation as part of the numerical solver rather than a separate preparation step.

important_terms.meaning: A numerical method that approximates a solution in a chosen space and reduces how much the guess violates the governing equation.
A Galerkin-style PDE solver where the chosen space is parameterized by a neural network.
The amount by which an approximate solution violates the governing differential equation.
A data-selection strategy that chooses new training samples based on what would most improve the model's performance.
A differential equation describing how a system changes over time.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to PINNs through error minimization, but adds a sequential time-stepping and active-learning view aligned with numerical solvers.
It also connects to ROMs and high-dimensional PDE methods because the neural trial space is an adaptive reduced representation.
It reinforces the series' data-generation theme: where you sample can matter as much as what architecture you use.
practical_caution: Minimizing the equation error can hide the truth if the sampling distribution skips important regions or if the equation error stays small while the actual solution error grows large. Active learning reduces this risk but does not guarantee the answer is correct without outside checking.
selected_evidence: Fitting parameters... requires accurately estimating the population loss from training data.
Few informative training samples are available.
Neural Galerkin schemes... generate training data samples with active learning.
Fit network parameters by minimizing the residual sequentially over time.
Active form of gathering training data... is key.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that neural PDE solvers should adapt their samples to track the dynamics. The training set is part of the numerical method, not just preparation before it begins.

title: Ishan Khurjekar: Uncertainty-Aware Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
speaker: Ishan Khurjekar
one_sentence: This lecture explains how ensemble learning and probabilistic methods can make guided-wave structural health monitoring more reliable when temperature, loading, and model errors introduce uncertainty.
core_problem: Guided-wave SHM systems detect and locate damage by comparing acoustic wave signals across sensor arrays. Real structures experience temperature, loading, and environmental shifts that change how waves travel, so damage-like signal changes can appear even when the structure is healthy. Standard neural networks often become overconfident under these shifts.
first_principles_model: A guided-wave monitoring system sends sound waves through a structure and records what comes back. Damage changes those signals, but non-damage factors like temperature also change them. Uncertainty-aware learning treats detection and localization as probabilistic inference: ensembles, variational autoencoders (neural networks that learn a probability distribution over compressed signals), adversarial perturbations, and anomaly detection estimate both predictions and confidence when conditions vary.
key_claims: Structural health monitoring is essential for buildings, bridges, aircraft, oil rigs, and other structures that need inspection.
Guided waves work well for damage detection and localization because sensor arrays can send and receive sound waves.
Temperature and loading shifts create uncertainty by changing how waves travel, even when there is no damage.
Deep learning methods need to handle uncertainty because ordinary networks can fail or become overconfident when conditions change.
Ensembles of variational autoencoders can improve reliability when temperature varies.
Training on simulated perturbations can improve reliability when sound-wave properties are uncertain.

important_terms.meaning: Sensing and analysis methods for detecting, locating, and describing damage in structures.
An acoustic wave trapped and moved by the structure itself, often sent through it to look for damage over distance.
Estimating where damage is located in a structure.
Combining multiple models to improve reliability and estimate how confident we should be in predictions.
A neural network that learns a probability distribution over compressed versions of data, and can spot when new data looks different from training data.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to uncertainty propagation and reliable surrogate modeling through engineering decision-making and risk.
It also links to active learning and data augmentation because environmental variation must be included in training data.
It is a real-world example of why uncertainty estimates matter for actual engineering use.
practical_caution: Damage detection is safety-critical. A model must tell the difference between damage and environmental shift, and must say when it is uncertain about inputs outside what it saw during training.
selected_evidence: Guided wave systems consist of an array of sensors that can transmit and receive waves.
Guided waves are sensitive to external variations such as temperature and loading conditions.
There is uncertainty in damage detection and localization.
Can we cast damage detection as an anomaly detection problem.
Ensemble learning... train an ensemble of variational auto encoders.
takeaway: The core lesson is that monitoring is not just classification. It is inference under environmental variation, and uncertainty must be part of what the system outputs.

title: Tailin Wu: Learning To Accelerate Large-Scale Physical Simulations
speaker: Tailin Wu
one_sentence: This lecture presents learned simulators for large-scale fluid and plasma systems, using graph networks, U-Nets, and multi-step training to predict long-term evolution and capture behavior at many different scales.
core_problem: Large-scale fluid and plasma simulations can involve millions of cells and take days or weeks to run. Machine learning models trained to copy these simulations promise to run faster, but they must handle uneven geometry, local and global dynamics, behavior at different scales coupled together, and errors that grow as you run them forward in time.
first_principles_model: A physical simulator updates a field state over time. A learned simulator approximates that update map. For subsurface flow, local water-oil dynamics can be represented by graph neural networks over mesh cells, while pressure has more global structure better captured by U-Net-like field models. Training on multi-step losses exposes the model to its own prediction errors, improving long-term stability compared with training on just the next single step.
key_claims: Classical numerical solvers for fluids and plasmas require days of computation for large systems.
Machine learning models trained to copy these simulations can make them faster but must overcome long-term evolution and behavior-at-different-scales challenges.
Hybrid simulators combine graph networks for local dynamics with 3D U-Nets for global pressure dynamics.
Graph neural networks handle irregular or mesh-based local interactions where information flows along connections.
Training on multiple future steps improves accuracy over long runs compared with training on only the next step.
The method scales to very large systems, handling millions of cells in the subsurface example.

important_terms.meaning: A machine learning model trained to copy how a physical simulator updates a system forward in time.
A neural network that sends information along graph edges, designed for mesh or particle systems where connections matter.
An encoder-decoder convolutional architecture that reads a field as input and writes a field as output.
A training goal that penalizes prediction errors over several time steps ahead, not just the next one.
Running a learned simulator forward by applying its update rule repeatedly to predict many future time steps.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the learned-surrogate idea with a concrete graph-based simulator for large systems.
It connects to Petros Koumoutsakos' work by combining different neural architectures where the physics suggests each one fits.
It also connects to neural operators and reduced-order models because the learned model approximates an evolution operator.
practical_caution: A learned simulator that predicts the next step accurately may accumulate large errors when run forward many steps. Long-term stability must be tested directly, especially when the surrogate (learned copy) is used for control or inverse design.
selected_evidence: Simulating the time evolution of large-scale physical systems is crucial.
How to learn faithful long-term evolution, and how to model multi-scale dynamics.
Introduce a hybrid graph network simulator.
Graph network to model the dynamics of the water and oil and also a 3d unit... pressure.
Multi-step loss can really help the long-term rollout.
takeaway: Learned simulation is repeated operator application. Stability over many steps is what really matters, not next-step prediction alone.

title: Molei Tao: Trustworthy Learning Of Mechanical Systems And Stiefel Optimization
speaker: Molei Tao
one_sentence: This lecture shows how embedding geometric structure such as symplecticity (a way energy stays constant when it should) into learned mechanical dynamics improves predictions far into the future, and connects dynamics ideas to optimization on the Stiefel manifold (the mathematical space of orthonormal frames).
core_problem: Mechanical systems preserve geometric structures: energy stays constant when it should, momentum follows conservation laws, and the flow lives on a special kind of mathematical surface called symplectic. Standard neural networks can fit short trajectories while breaking these rules, causing predictions to drift farther and farther from truth as you extend them into the future. Optimization on constrained spaces such as the Stiefel manifold faces a similar problem: algorithms should respect the curved geometry they're moving on instead of pretending the space is flat.
first_principles_model: A mechanical system is not just a list of states; it is a flow with preserved geometric structure. Symplectic learning embeds this preservation directly into the model so the learned time evolution stays correct over long horizons. For Stiefel optimization, the variable sits on the manifold of orthonormal frames (matrices with columns that are perpendicular unit vectors), so gradient steps and momentum acceleration must be designed to stay on the manifold rather than treating it like unconstrained flat space.
key_claims: Physics embedded directly into deep learning models can improve trustworthy prediction of mechanical dynamics.
Mechanical systems preserve structures such as energy, momentum, and symplecticity.
Symplecticity is an underlying geometric property of Hamiltonian dynamics.
Embedding symplectic structure can provably improve how far into the future you can predict accurately.
The connection between dynamics and machine learning also informs optimization algorithms.
Momentum-accelerated gradient descent can be built on curved mathematical spaces, with the Stiefel manifold as a key example.

important_terms.meaning: A geometric structure where flow preserves area and energy-like quantities; a property of Hamiltonian mechanical dynamics.
A formulation of mechanics based on position, momentum, and an energy-like function called the Hamiltonian.
Forecasting a dynamical system over many time steps where small structural errors compound and grow.
The set of matrices whose columns are perpendicular unit vectors; the mathematical space where constrained problems sit.
Optimization methods designed to move on curved mathematical surfaces instead of flat spaces.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to the structure-preserving thread across physics-informed neural networks, neural ODE solvers, and scientific machine learning.
It complements talks on uncertainty and trustworthiness by showing one path to safer extrapolation: preserve geometry and conservation laws.
It also links dynamics and optimization, a pattern that recurs in neural PDE solvers and learning on curved spaces.
practical_caution: Embedding structure helps only when the assumed structure matches the system. If you force symplecticity on systems that lose energy through friction or get pushed by external forces, the model will preserve the wrong geometry and predictions will fail.
selected_evidence: Trustworthy learning of mechanical systems & Stiefel optimization.
How to make symplectic predictions.
Mechanical system... has structures... conservation of energy... momentum.
Underlying geometric notion called symplecticity that is preserved by the dynamics.
Hardwire this... in our learning model.
takeaway: The core lesson is that trustworthy dynamics learning starts by respecting the geometry of the system. Accurate prediction over time follows from preserving the right conservation laws and symmetries.

title: Dirk Hartmann: Machine Learning And Physics-Based Simulations For Industrial Digital Twins
speaker: Dirk Hartmann
one_sentence: This lecture shows industrial digital twins as hybrid systems where machine learning and physics-based simulation must work together closely to reach the accuracy, speed, and automation that real decisions need.
core_problem: Industrial assets, products, systems, and infrastructure need digital models that are accurate enough for decisions and fast enough for design, engineering, and operations. Pure high-fidelity simulation is often too slow and demands manual expert effort to set up, while pure machine learning can give wrong answers outside the range of data it learned from. Scaling digital twins across many assets also hits a wall: manual expert modeling effort is expensive and takes time.
first_principles_model: A digital twin is a computer representation tied to a real asset or process. In industry, it must answer operational questions inside hard constraints: speed, accuracy, ease of upkeep, and cost to deploy. Physics-based models provide structure that makes sense when data runs out; machine learning supplies fast predictions, automatic calibration, and adaptation to new data. What wins in practice is the hybrid workflow—neither pure simulation nor pure machine learning alone gets the job done.
key_claims: Linking the digital and real world demands digital models that are fast enough and accurate enough.
Only by tightly joining machine learning and physics-based methods can you reach the speed and accuracy required.
Hybrid digital twins are necessary across design, engineering, and operations for complex industrial systems.
Industrial deployment asks for the right balance between accuracy and speed rather than the highest accuracy at any cost.
Manual expert effort is the main bottleneck stopping faster production of more digital twins.
Research should be judged on what matters in the full industrial lifecycle, not only on academic test scores.

important_terms.meaning: A computer model of a real asset, product, system, or infrastructure that you use to predict or guide what happens.
A digital twin that combines physics-based simulation (rules from natural laws) with machine learning (learning patterns from data).
Putting a method to real use in production with hard limits on cost, speed, maintenance, and who is responsible when things go wrong.
The practical choice between how exact a model is and how fast it runs.
The limit you hit when you need scarce experts to manually build, tune, or fix models, slowing everything down.

stanford_connections: This talk grounds the series' hybrid physics-machine-learning theme in a concrete industrial systems problem.
It ties to surrogate modeling, reduced-order models, active learning, and uncertainty because digital twins need all of them when deployed.
It also shows why interpretability and automation matter: they determine whether you can build and maintain many twins at scale.
practical_caution: An impressive demo twin is not the same as an industrial digital twin that works in real production. Industrial use demands full integration across the system's lifetime, testing against real assets, ways to update the model when things change, and clear responsibility when model predictions guide decisions.
selected_evidence: Sufficiently accurate and fast digital models of assets, products, systems, and infrastructures are required.
Tightly integrating machine learning and physics-based methods (hybrid digital twins).
Industrial challenges from design & engineering up to operations.
Achieve the right model accuracy and speed.
Without requiring significant manual expert efforts.
takeaway: The core lesson is that industrial scientific machine learning is constrained engineering: solve real decisions with real limits. The model that wins is the one that solves the decision problem with enough physics, enough data, and enough automation to deploy and keep running.

title: Ricardo Vinuesa: Modeling And Controlling Turbulent Flows Through Deep Learning
speaker: Ricardo Vinuesa
one_sentence: This lecture covers deep learning applied to turbulent flows: wall-based sensing to predict hidden flow patterns, transfer learning to adapt across flow speeds, nonlinear reduced models, GAN-based image sharpening, and reinforcement learning to find better control strategies.
core_problem: Turbulent flows are high-dimensional, nonlinear, and change at many scales at once. They are expensive to measure or simulate accurately. For flows bounded by walls, the flow away from the wall is difficult to observe without sensors that disturb it. Meanwhile, control strategies need fast, accurate estimates of the swirling structures (coherent structures) that drive the flow.
first_principles_model: Turbulent flows contain flow properties that vary through space but are never fully visible from any one spot. Sensors, computer simulations, and neural networks each give partial views. Convolutional neural networks can use wall measurements to predict velocity (speed and direction) patterns away from the wall. Transfer learning reuses patterns learned at one flow speed to work at another. Autoencoders (neural networks that compress and decompress data) build simplified nonlinear models. GANs (generative adversarial networks, systems where two neural networks compete to generate realistic data) can fill in high-resolution flow details from low-resolution or sparse data. Reinforcement learning can search for control strategies by trial and reward in simulation.
key_claims: Deep learning is now widely used in computational fluid dynamics and turbulent-flow analysis.
Non-intrusive sensing can predict flow away from the wall using only wall measurements, avoiding sensors that would disturb the flow.
Convolutional neural networks outperform traditional linear models at predicting turbulent flows.
Transfer learning can move trained representations from one flow speed to nearby flow speeds.
Autoencoders can build simpler nonlinear models of turbulent flows.
GANs and reinforcement learning can create high-resolution flow images and find control strategies, but need careful real-world testing.

important_terms.meaning: Turbulent flow shaped by solid boundaries such as pipes, aircraft wings, or building surfaces.
Estimating flow properties without placing physical sensors in the flow that would alter what you are trying to measure.
Reusing a neural network trained on one situation (such as flow at one speed) to work better on a related situation (such as flow at a different speed).
A simplified model built by compressing flow patterns into a small set of hidden numbers and then reconstructing full patterns from those numbers.
Actively changing a flow to achieve goals such as reducing drag or improving mixing.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds on Petros Koumoutsakos' work on AI and fluid mechanics by showing specific neural network tools for predicting flow and designing controls.
It connects to talks on reduced-order models because autoencoders offer a nonlinear alternative to traditional linear methods like POD (proper orthogonal decomposition).
It reinforces a core theme across the seminar: physical measurements are always partial and incomplete, so models must infer the full flow state from what we can actually observe.
practical_caution: Machine learning for turbulent flows often overfits to one flow speed, one geometry, or one simulation setup. Claims about transfer learning, control, and super-resolution need to be tested in conditions different from the training data: different flow speeds, different shapes, and different real-world conditions.
selected_evidence: Modeling and controlling turbulent flows through deep learning.
Non-intrusive sensing... measure at the wall so that we can predict what happens above the wall.
Outperforming traditional linear models.
Transfer learning... reuse what we learn in one task for another.
Using... autoencoders to build non-linear reduced order models.
takeaway: The core lesson is that turbulence learning is about inferring hidden flow properties and finding control strategies in a world where flow changes at multiple scales. Deep learning succeeds when the way it represents patterns matches what your sensors measure and what your control needs to do.

title: Santi Adavani: Industrial Grade Scientific Machine Learning
speaker: Santi Adavani
one_sentence: This lecture explains why scientific machine learning in production must solve ambiguity, scalability, and deployability problems before it can replace or work alongside traditional PDE solvers (equations that model how systems change over time) in real applications.
core_problem: SciML research has produced many papers and open-source tools, but industrial practitioners still face domain-specific constraints: unclear requirements, integrating with existing solvers, scaling to real problem sizes, deployment infrastructure, validation, and uncertainty over when a neural network approach is better than a traditional forward solver (one that predicts outcomes from known inputs) or inverse solver (one that finds unknown inputs from observed outcomes).
first_principles_model: An industrial solver is not just an algorithm; it is a production artifact embedded in workflows, hardware, data pipelines, domain constraints, and verification practices. SciML must therefore be evaluated along three axes: whether the problem formulation is unambiguous, whether the method scales to industrial sizes and compute environments, and whether it can be deployed, monitored, and maintained.
key_claims: SciML applies modern deep learning to engineered systems represented by PDEs (equations that model how systems change over space and time).
There is strong academic and industrial interest, but practical adoption faces major barriers.
Industrial users need a clear path to move from traditional forward and inverse PDE solvers to SciML-based solvers.
Ambiguity, scalability, and deployability are central industrial challenges.
Open-source packages and publications are not enough for domain-specific production use.
The research community can contribute by addressing real deployment-facing constraints, not only method novelty.

important_terms.meaning: Scientific machine learning designed for production reliability, scale, integration with existing systems, and maintainability.
A solver that predicts what a system will do given known starting conditions, geometry, and material properties.
A solver that figures out unknown starting conditions or material properties by working backward from what was observed.
The ability to install, run, check on, and maintain a model inside a real operational workflow without breaking.
The ability of a method to work with realistic industrial problem sizes, data volumes, and available computing power.

stanford_connections: This lecture complements Dirk Hartmann's industrial digital-twin talk by focusing on the obstacles to turning SciML into production software.
It connects to every discussion in the series about replacing traditional solvers: accuracy alone is not enough for people to adopt it.
It also provides a practical lens for evaluating PINNs (physics-informed neural networks), neural operators, and differentiable solvers.
practical_caution: Do not mistake a research prototype for an industrial solver. Industry needs clear problem definitions, scaling behavior, deployment plans, and validation procedures before moving away from trusted numerical workflows.
selected_evidence: Industrial Grade Scientific Machine Learning: Challenges and Opportunities.
Several challenges for practitioners in the industry to apply this new paradigm.
Transition from traditional forward/inverse PDE solvers to SciML-based solvers.
Ambiguities scalability and deployability problems.
Practical applications.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that industrial SciML is judged by how well it fits into an existing system. A method becomes useful when it can be specified, scaled, deployed, and trusted.

title: Ben Erichson: Continuous Networks For Sequential Predictions
speaker: Ben Erichson
one_sentence: This lecture treats recurrent neural networks for time-series prediction as discretized dynamical systems (equations describing how a system changes over time) and shows how numerical integration methods, stochastic differential equations, and multiscale ODEs (ordinary differential equations with fast and slow dynamics) improve accuracy and long-term sequential modeling.
core_problem: Sequential prediction models are deployed in scientific settings such as fluid dynamics and climate modeling, where accuracy and reliability matter. Standard recurrent units can be sensitive to small changes in the input and may not capture the continuous-time structure of the underlying physical system.
first_principles_model: A recurrent network can be understood as a time-discretized dynamical system (a rule for evolving a system broken into discrete time steps). Once viewed this way, numerical analysis becomes architecture design: forward Euler resembles a simple residual update, higher-order integrators such as explicit midpoint can improve accuracy by evaluating slopes at intermediate points, adding stochastic differential equations adds random forcing for stability, and multiscale ODEs can represent long-term dependencies that evolve at different speeds.
key_claims: Time-series neural networks can be analyzed through the lens of dynamical systems (equations describing how a system evolves).
Out-of-the-box deep networks may not be suitable for mission-critical scientific applications because they can be sensitive to small input changes.
Continuous-time recurrent neural networks can be more reliable and accurate than traditional recurrent units.
Classical numerical time integration methods can improve neural sequential prediction.
Explicit midpoint integration can outperform simpler forward Euler discretization by using more slope information.
Connections to stochastic differential equations (equations with random terms) and multiscale ODEs support reliable long-term sequence modeling.

important_terms.meaning: A recurrent architecture based on an underlying continuous-time dynamical system before it is broken into discrete time steps.
A first-order numerical time integration method that advances a state using one slope evaluation per time step.
A higher-order time integration method that evaluates the slope at the midpoint of a time step to improve accuracy.
A differential equation that includes random or diffusion terms in addition to deterministic changes.
An ordinary differential equation representation where dynamics operate across multiple time scales, with some changes happening quickly and others slowly.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects neural architecture design to numerical methods, a recurring theme in physics-informed neural networks and neural ODE talks.
It also complements structure-preserving mechanics and differentiable programming by treating learning models as dynamical systems.
It gives a stability-focused alternative to purely empirical sequence-model design.
practical_caution: A recurrent model's time discretization is part of the model itself. Changing the time step size, the integration method, or the noise level can change stability and robustness, so sequential models need numerical validation before deployment.
selected_evidence: View neural networks for time series prediction through the lens of dynamical systems.
Continuous-time recurrent neural networks... more robust and accurate.
Higher-order explicit midpoint time integrator.
Compared to using the simpler one-step forward Euler scheme.
Connection between recurrent neural network and stochastic differential equations.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that sequence models are numerical dynamical systems. Better scientific architectures come from better discretization (breaking continuous dynamics into time steps) and stability thinking.

title: Benjamin Sanderse: Structure-Preserving Learning Of Embedded Discrete Closure Models
speaker: Benjamin Sanderse
organization: CWI, Dutch National Institute for Mathematics and Computer Science
one_sentence: This lecture explains how neural closure models for PDEs should be learned while embedded inside discretized solvers, with structure preservation such as kinetic-energy conservation to avoid instability.
core_problem: Closure models represent the effect of unresolved small scales on resolved large scales in LES (Large Eddy Simulation), ROMs (Reduced Order Models), and other simplified descriptions. Neural networks can fit closures accurately when trained in isolation, but once inserted into a numerical PDE solver they can become unstable because the training environment differs from where they actually operate.
first_principles_model: A closure is not a standalone prediction task; it is a piece of a time-stepping numerical method. Learning it outside the solver optimizes the wrong situation. Embedded differentiable training places the closure inside the discrete PDE solver during learning so gradients show how closure errors affect future states. Adding structure-preserving forms, such as kinetic energy conservation, provides stability guarantees even when errors occur.
key_claims: The closure problem is a fundamental challenge in fluid flow and reduced-order modeling.
Neural networks can construct highly accurate closure models, but directly inserting them into physics models is prone to numerical instability.
Instability arises partly because the training environment does not match the prediction environment.
Closure models should be learned while embedded in the discretized PDE solver.
Differentiable programming enables gradients through the solver but creates adjoint and time-integration challenges.
Preserving kinetic energy conservation can provide stability guarantees.

important_terms.meaning: A model that captures the effect of unresolved small scales on resolved large-scale variables.
Training a learned component while it sits inside the numerical solver where it will be used.
A closure designed for the discretized PDE system rather than only the continuous equation.
The backward sensitivity calculation used to compute gradients through a solver or time-stepping process.
A structure-preserving property that prevents artificial energy growth in certain fluid models.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly connects to reduced-order model closures, Large Eddy Simulation, differentiable programming, and structure-preserving learning.
It also clarifies a recurring failure mode: a neural component trained in isolation may fail when coupled to physics.
It complements talks on PINN failures by focusing on solver-embedded stability rather than residual loss alone.
practical_caution: Do not train a closure as a standalone supervised prediction model and assume it will remain stable when running forward in time. The closure must be tested and preferably trained in the numerical environment where it will operate.
selected_evidence: The closure problem... represents the effect of the small scales on the large scales.
Neural closure models... prone to numerical instabilities.
The training environment does not match the prediction environment.
Learning closure models while they are embedded in a discretized PDE solver.
Preserve structure, namely kinetic energy conservation.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that closure learning is coupled numerical modeling. Stability comes from embedding the learned object in the solver and preserving the right invariants.

title: Jan Drgona: Differentiable Programming For Modeling And Control Of Dynamical Systems
speaker: Jan Drgona
one_sentence: This lecture combines model predictive control, differentiable physics models, scientific machine learning, and offline policy optimization into a single method for building and training control systems.
core_problem: Classical model predictive control can enforce constraints and physical laws but runs slowly on devices with limited compute. Reinforcement learning can train control policies but needs huge amounts of data and often struggles with hard constraints. Energy and industrial systems need control methods that work fast, learn from small amounts of data, respect physical and safety constraints, and run on embedded hardware.
first_principles_model: Differentiable predictive control treats the control law (the rule for choosing actions) as a trainable computation built from differentiable physics models and constraint equations. It keeps the classical MPC idea: simulate future states, choose actions that minimize cost, enforce constraints. The difference is that it pre-computes the policy offline using differentiable programming, so real-time execution just runs the learned policy instead of solving an optimization problem during operation.
key_claims: Differentiable programming gives a useful way to think about optimal control of systems that change over time.
Differentiable predictive control merges classical MPC with scientific machine learning methods.
The method uses custom differentiable physics models to train control policies before deployment.
Nonlinear constraints can be included directly during policy training.
Case studies show results in building temperature control and electrical grid scheduling.
Embedded demonstrations show the method can run fast and efficiently for control deployed as a service.

important_terms.meaning: A method for training control policies where the controller learns using differentiable (smoothly-varying) models of how the system behaves and differentiable representations of constraints.
A strategy where the control system repeatedly predicts future behavior over a short time window, finds the best actions under that prediction, and applies them.
Training a control strategy in advance (using models or simulations) so it can run fast without solving new optimization problems during operation.
A limit or rule (such as 'power output cannot exceed this value') expressed using curved or bent mathematical functions.
A way to package and deploy control algorithms so they can be reused across multiple systems or embedded into other applications.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects differentiable programming directly to control, fitting within the DDPS seminar's focus on differentiable methods.
It complements reinforcement learning and flow-control talks by showing how to combine learned models with classical optimization principles.
It also relates to digital twins because real-world control systems need fast, accurate models tied to the physical systems they operate.
practical_caution: Policies trained offline can fail if the physics model is inaccurate or constraints are implemented only as soft penalties instead of hard limits. Real deployment needs testing against unexpected conditions and built-in safety fallbacks.
selected_evidence: Differentiable programming perspective on optimal control of dynamical systems.
Differentiable predictive control (DPC).
Integrates the principles of classical model predictive control (MPC) with scientific machine learning.
Offline policy optimization subject to nonlinear constraints.
Building control and dynamic economic dispatch problems.
takeaway: The core insight is that differentiability makes control design a trainable problem, but the controller is only as reliable as the physics model underneath it, how strictly constraints are enforced, and the care taken during deployment.

title: Eric de Sturler: Cheap And Robust Adaptive Reduced Order Models For Nonlinear Inversion And Design
speaker: Eric de Sturler
one_sentence: This lecture explains how randomization and adaptive reduced-order models can reduce the cost of nonlinear inverse and PDE-constrained optimization problems while checking that the stand-in model stays accurate.
core_problem: Nonlinear inverse problems and design optimization often need many repeated large linear, nonlinear, and adjoint solves. Smaller models built from a family of full models (parametric ROMs) can cut cost, but building and running them can still be expensive, and they often have no cheap way to check if they are giving right answers during optimization.
first_principles_model: Using a stand-in model for optimization only works if the optimizer knows when the stand-in is trustworthy. Randomization can cheaply build reduced bases or check errors and gaps in how well the objective got better. Adaptive ROMs update the smaller model when checking shows it no longer gives right answers, and trust-region logic (an optimization method that takes steps only where the model is believed to be accurate) keeps steps the size the surrogate says is safe.
key_claims: Nonlinear inverse and PDE-constrained optimization problems need many repeated solves.
Newton-type methods also need adjoint or transpose-system solves.
Smaller models built to approximate a full model across different parameters can greatly cut computation.
Computing smaller models online can itself be expensive for these problems.
Smaller models built across parameters often have no cheap way to check error.
Randomization can help compute smaller models cheaply and check accuracy or how much the objective improved for trust-region methods.

important_terms.meaning: A problem of estimating unknown parameters or structures from observations when the relationship between the parameters and what you see is not linear.
Optimization where the things you are adjusting must obey a differential equation model.
A smaller model built to stand in for a full model across a range of different parameter settings.
Using randomized numerical methods to cut cost, check error, or pick informative subsets or directions.
An optimization method that limits steps to areas where the model is believed to be accurate.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects smaller models to inverse design and optimization rather than only running simulations forward.
It also ties to checking and controlling errors because using stand-in models requires ways to know if they are reliable.
It adds to science and machine learning in industry by asking how smaller models can be made cheap and reliable enough for repeated design loops.
practical_caution: A reduced model can speed up optimization but steer it the wrong way if its errors are not being watched. Trust-region checks or randomized error tests are part of the algorithm, not optional add-ons you can skip.
selected_evidence: Nonlinear inverse problems and other PDE-constrained optimization problems... require the repeated solution of many discretized large linear systems.
For Newton-type methods we also need solutions for the adjoint problem.
Parametric model reduction or other surrogate models as well as by randomization.
Reduced order models do not come with (cheap) error bounds.
Monitor the difference between the reduced model and full model objective function improvement.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that optimization needs trustworthy cheap models, not just cheap models. The stand-in must know when it is safe to guide the next step.

title: Zorin Mitran: Data-Driven Information Geometry For Stochastic Model Reduction
speaker: Zorin Mitran
organization: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
one_sentence: This lecture extends reduced-order modeling from flat straight subspaces to curved statistical manifolds, using data-driven information geometry for systems with randomness and variation.
core_problem: Standard ROMs often project data onto linear subspaces using Euclidean least squares. For stochastic systems, what we care about are probability distributions, and their natural geometry may be curved rather than flat. In systems far from equilibrium, we may not even know a clean parametric distribution family to start with.
first_principles_model: Information geometry treats families of probability distributions as manifolds with metrics and curved paths (geodesics). Instead of projecting vectors onto a flat linear subspace, stochastic model reduction projects or transports distributions along curved statistical manifolds. When no parametric family is given, we can build local normal distributions from the data using SVD, and their envelope forms a data-driven statistical manifold.
key_claims: Standard ROMs project onto subspaces and minimize Euclidean distance in flat linear spaces.
Stochastic systems can be modeled on manifolds of probability distributions.
Information geometry studies statistical manifolds of parametrized probability distributions.
For systems far from equilibrium, an explicit parametrized distribution may not be available.
A data-driven statistical manifold can be built from envelopes of local normal distributions extracted from SVD of the data.
Reduced models are obtained by moving along geodesics, where paths are curved rather than straight Euclidean lines.

important_terms.meaning: The study of probability distributions as geometric objects; how probability distributions sit on curves and surfaces.
A curved surface whose points each represent one probability distribution.
The shortest or most natural path between two points on a curved surface; generalizes the idea of a straight line.
A bell-curve (Gaussian) approximation built around small neighborhoods in the data.
Reducing the complexity of models whose states or outputs include randomness and variation.

stanford_connections: This lecture broadens the ROM theme from deterministic state reduction to probabilistic distribution reduction.
It connects to uncertainty quantification because model states are treated as distributions rather than single point values.
It also links to manifold learning talks: the reduced object may sit on a curved learned geometry rather than flat space.
practical_caution: A Euclidean projection can distort the statistical structure of probabilities. For stochastic systems, the choice of geometry affects the reduced model, so the manifold we construct must match how distributions actually behave in the data.
selected_evidence: Reduced-order models are often obtained by projection onto a subspace.
Extension... from flat spaces to curvilinear manifolds of probability distributions.
Information geometry is the study of statistical manifolds.
Envelope of local normal distributions obtained from the singular value decomposition of data.
Reduced-order models are obtained by geodesic transport.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that stochastic reduction depends on geometry. If what you are modeling are distributions, the reduced space should respect how those distributions sit and move.

title: Michael Brenner: Scientific Uses Of Automatic Differentiation
speaker: Michael Brenner
one_sentence: This lecture argues that the biggest scientific opportunity from the machine learning revolution isn't ML itself, but automatic differentiation plus large-scale optimization—a new way to formulate and solve scientific problems.
core_problem: Many scientific problems hide inside optimization: solve a PDE (partial differential equation, which describes how things change in space and time), design a material with the right properties, find an unstable flow state (a water or gas flow that doesn't stay put), tune a kinetic pathway (the sequence of steps a molecule takes during assembly), infer developmental rules (how organisms grow), or design a nonequilibrium protocol (driving a system far from balance to achieve something). Traditionally, each domain needs hand-derived gradients (how to calculate the direction to change inputs for a better result), specialized adjoints (customized tricks for computing gradients backward), or brute-force search. That limits the size and flexibility of the problems scientists can attack.
first_principles_model: Automatic differentiation turns a computation into a differentiable object (something you can take gradients of). If a simulator, loss function (a number measuring how far you are from a goal), or scientific protocol is written as a differentiable program, gradients can be propagated through it and used for large-scale optimization.
