This makes optimization a general scientific language: propose an objective, encode the physical computation, differentiate it, and search for designs, hidden states, or governing structures.
key_claims: The tools underlying machine learning, especially automatic differentiation, can be more scientifically important than the ML models themselves.
Automatic differentiation enables large-scale optimization for scientific discovery.
Automatic differentiation can support new algorithms for solving PDEs.
The same approach can design energy landscapes and kinetic pathways for self-assembly.
Optimization can discover unstable solutions that organize fluid instabilities.
Automatic differentiation-based scientific computation can extend to organismal development, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, fluid rheology, and protein self-assembly.

important_terms.meaning: A computational technique that exactly differentiates programs by applying the chain rule (a calculus rule for derivatives of composite functions) through their operations.
Solving optimization problems with many variables, often made possible by efficient gradient computation (calculating the direction and slope to move toward a better solution).
A function describing the energy of a system across all possible configurations, shaping which states are stable and how transitions between them happen.
A sequence of dynamical states through which a system evolves, such as the steps a cluster of molecules takes during assembly.
A mathematically valid state or trajectory that is not stable under small disturbances but can still organize nearby dynamics.

stanford_connections: This lecture is a conceptual foundation for differentiable programming, embedded closure learning, DPC, and inverse design talks.
It reframes machine learning infrastructure as scientific infrastructure: differentiability makes scientific workflows optimizable.
It also connects to equation discovery and digital twins because differentiable programs can search over mechanisms and designs.
practical_caution: Differentiating a computation does not guarantee the objective is scientifically meaningful or numerically stable. Automatic differentiation gives you gradients; scientists still need valid models, constraints, and real-world validation.
selected_evidence: A primary opportunity is not machine learning per se.
The tools underlying the ML revolution yield significant opportunities for scientific discovery.
Primary among these tools is automatic differentiation.
Automatic differentiation and large scale optimization to solve science problems.
Developing new algorithms for solving partial differential equations.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that differentiability changes what can be optimized. Automatic differentiation turns scientific computation into a design and discovery engine.

title: Andrea Manzoni: Deep Learning For Reduced Order Modeling
speaker: Andrea Manzoni
one_sentence: This lecture explains how deep neural networks can improve reduced-order modeling by learning non-intrusive ROMs and neural operators to approximate parametrized PDEs quickly.
core_problem: Classical ROMs speed up parametrized PDE solves for real-time simulation, uncertainty quantification, control, monitoring, and digital twins. But nonlinear time-dependent problems often stay expensive because reducing the dynamics, compressing terms carefully, and accessing the original solver code can be hard to build or deploy in practice.
first_principles_model: A ROM approximates high-resolution solutions in a low-dimensional representation. Deep learning can replace or add to several ROM parts: encoders map full-resolution snapshots to latent coordinates, decoders reconstruct high-resolution fields, neural maps evolve or parameterize reduced states, and POD-enhanced variants mix classical linear bases with neural nonlinear approximation. The goal is fast simulation without requiring full access to modify the solver.
key_claims: ROM techniques such as reduced basis methods are essential for efficient approximation of parametrized differential equations.
ROMs enable real-time simulation and repeated scenario evaluation for uncertainty quantification, control, monitoring, data assimilation, and digital twins.
Deep neural networks can build ROMs from full-resolution model snapshots in a fully non-intrusive way.
Deep-learning ROMs use neural networks as core building blocks for parametrized PDE approximation.
POD-enhanced deep-learning ROMs combine classical projection structure with neural nonlinear maps.
Deep learning can also approximate nonlinear ROM operators and improve selective compression of reduced terms.

important_terms.meaning: A lower-dimensional approximation of a high-resolution model used to speed up simulation.
A stored high-resolution solution sample used as training or basis data for a ROM.
A deep-learning-based reduced-order model that uses neural networks to learn reduced coordinates, reconstruction, or dynamics.
A ROM that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (a classical method to find the simplest basis vectors) with deep neural networks.
A reduced model built without modifying or deeply accessing the code of the original high-resolution solver.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the ROM thread and bridges classical reduced basis and POD methods with neural surrogates.
It connects to industrial digital twins because real-time parametrized simulation is a core twin capability.
It also links to CUR decomposition, adaptive ROMs, and neural operators as different answers to the same compression-and-speed problem.
practical_caution: A neural ROM trained on snapshots inherits the limits of what those snapshots cover. Non-intrusive convenience does not remove the need for error checks when the model runs on new parameters, geometries, or transient regimes it hasn't seen before.
selected_evidence: Reduced order modeling... efficient approximation of parametrized differential problems.
Real-time simulation... data assimilation... predictive digital twins.
Exploit deep neural networks... to build ROMs for parametrized PDEs in a fully non-intrusive way.
Deep learning-based ROMs (DL-ROMs).
POD-enhanced DL-ROMs.

title: Ralph Smith: Parameter Subset Selection And Active Subspaces
speaker: Ralph C. Smith
one_sentence: This lecture explains how to find which parameters and combinations of parameters matter most in high-dimensional engineering and biological models, making it possible to calibrate them, build fast approximations, and estimate uncertainty.
core_problem: Engineering and biological models often have dozens or hundreds of parameters, but the measurements you can actually make don't give you enough information to pin down all of them. Running high-fidelity simulations millions of times to explore what happens is too expensive. The real problem: Which parameters or combinations of parameters actually change the outputs you care about?
first_principles_model: A parameter space with many dimensions can hide a much smaller structure that actually drives the outputs. Parameter subset selection finds individual parameters you can reliably measure or estimate from data. Active subspaces (low-dimensional directions, or combinations, of parameters) capture how most of the output changes happen along just a few directions. Once you identify these directions, you can build fast approximations, tune Bayesian calibration to focus on what matters, and compute how uncertainties flow through the model in a much smaller space.
key_claims: Most engineering and biological model parameters cannot be uniquely pinned down from the measurements available.
The cost of running high-fidelity simulations many times makes direct Bayesian calibration and full uncertainty propagation impractical.
Global sensitivity analysis can rank which inputs have the strongest effect, but has limits.
Parameter subset selection provides a direct way to pick out which parameters are most influential.
Active subspace techniques find important directions in parameter space (combinations and patterns), not just single parameters.
Bayesian calibration done on active subspaces can estimate the uncertainty in physical parameters.

important_terms.meaning: When the data available cannot pin down model parameters to a unique answer, because different parameter choices give nearly the same output.
A set of methods that measure how uncertainty in the inputs causes uncertainty in the outputs.
Choosing a smaller group of parameters that are most changeable from data or have the most effect on outputs.
A low-dimensional space of parameter combinations that accounts for most of the variation in outputs.
Estimating what values and ranges parameters must have by combining prior assumptions, model predictions, and observed measurements.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together uncertainty quantification, inverse problems (finding parameters from measurements), and surrogate modeling by reducing the number of parameters to track.
It complements reduced-order model talks by shrinking the number of inputs instead of the number of states.
It also gives a practical path for digital twins: figure out which parameters the data can actually teach you about, then calibrate only those.
practical_caution: Ranking parameters by importance can mislead you if they interact in nonlinear ways or if the metric you care about shifts with different data. Active subspaces must be checked carefully for the exact quantity of interest and the regime of data you're working with.
selected_evidence: Parameters which are nonidentifiable... not uniquely determined by measured responses.
Computational cost of high-fidelity simulation codes often precludes their direct use.
Isolate influential parameters for subsequent surrogate model construction.
Parameter subset selection and active subspace techniques.
Bayesian calibration on active subspaces.
takeaway: The core insight is that not all parameters are equally important. Good calibration starts by finding which directions the data and the model outputs can actually reveal.

title: Ajay Harish: Uncertainty Quantification And Deep Learning For Water-Hazard Prediction
speaker: Ajay Harish
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to use uncertainty quantification and deep learning to predict storm surge and water hazards, where water flow, floating debris, building structure, and infrastructure unknowns all shape how much damage occurs.
core_problem: Storm surges, tsunamis, and coastal flooding exert severe forces on urban buildings and roads. The damage depends on more than just water height; it also depends on the uncertain starting conditions, how waves and surge interact, floating debris, sediment movement, material properties of structures, and how buildings respond under load. To make sound decisions about protection, we must measure these uncertainties and their effects.
first_principles_model: A water-hazard model takes uncertain inputs (surge start, structure properties) and computes uncertain damage outputs. Bayesian calibration (updating uncertain model numbers using measured data) estimates parameters from observations; neural networks and surrogate models (fast replacements for slow simulations) speed up repeated simulations; uncertainty propagation (tracking how input uncertainty flows through the model) produces a range of possible damage values, not just one prediction. The goal is to forecast not just a single impact, but a distribution—the full range of possible damage—so decision-makers know the true risk.
key_claims: Storm surge is the rise in sea level above normal tides, caused by wind and pressure from a storm system.
Surge combined with waves and high tides can greatly raise average water levels and flood coastal cities.
Modeling urban infrastructure damage is made harder by uncertainty in both water flow and building behavior.
Major uncertainty sources include starting conditions, floating debris, sediment movement, and how solid materials behave under stress.
Bayesian calibration and neural networks can help measure and understand extreme-event impacts quantitatively.
Water-hazard prediction requires damage estimation, not just water-flow simulation.

important_terms.meaning: An abnormal rise in sea level caused by storm winds and low air pressure, above regular tide levels.
A damaging water-driven event such as storm surge, tsunami, coastal flood, or wave impact.
Estimating the likely physical or economic harm caused by a hazard event.
Updating uncertain model parameters using measured data and prior assumptions.
The exposure of buildings, roads, utilities, and coastal assets to harm from hazard events.

stanford_connections: This lecture is an applied uncertainty-quantification case study that builds on uncertainty propagation and structural health monitoring talks.
It connects to digital twins because making good infrastructure decisions needs fast calibrated hazard models that run in real time.
It also links to surrogate modeling: extreme-event uncertainty quantification requires many model simulations under different conditions.
practical_caution: A single-value flood map can hide the true risk because it ignores uncertainty. Real hazard decisions must account for unknown starting conditions, random debris, structure variability, and errors in model calibration itself.
selected_evidence: Storm surge... difference in the observed and regular sea level.
Storms coincide with the periodic high tides.
Modeling the impact of storm-surge events on urban infrastructure are extremely complicated.
Uncertainties in the flow... and in the structure.
Bayesian calibration, Neural networks... quantify the impact of such extreme events.
takeaway: The core lesson is that hazard prediction is uncertainty propagation feeding into decisions. Deep learning helps when it lets us measure and communicate risk faster and more accurately.

title: Spencer Bryngelson: Competitive Physics-Informed Networks
speaker: Spencer Bryngelson
one_sentence: This lecture introduces competitive PINNs, an adversarial method where a discriminator (a separate network trained to spot errors) learns to highlight where the solution network fails, letting the system reach much higher PDE-solution accuracy than standard PINNs that minimize squared residuals.
core_problem: Standard PINNs train by squaring PDE residuals and adding them up, but they often stop improving around modest accuracy even on simple PDEs. One reason is conditioning: when you square residuals, you're also squaring the condition numbers from PDE discretization, which makes the optimization numerically unstable and hard to push to high accuracy.
first_principles_model: Competitive PINNs turn PDE solving into a two-player game. The solution network tries to minimize how much the PDE is violated, while a discriminator is rewarded for finding mistakes the solution network makes. The exact PDE solution is the best strategy both players can reach in this game. This adversarial approach changes which errors are penalized most and sidesteps some of the conditioning problems that come from squaring residuals.
key_claims: PINNs use PDE residuals as loss functions but typically hit accuracy ceilings on most problems.
Competitive PINNs add a separate adversarial network that is trained to spot where the PINN makes mistakes.
The two networks form a competition where the best strategy either can find matches the exact PDE solution.
The method avoids the numerical instability from squaring large condition numbers in PDE discretization.
On a Poisson problem (a standard test), Competitive PINNs achieved errors ten-thousand times smaller than strong baseline PINNs.
The method produced errors at single-precision machine accuracy with steady improvement each training step.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to match observed data and to satisfy the residuals of a differential equation (the rule governing how a system evolves in space and time).
An adversarial form of PINN where a second network is taught to find errors in the first network's solution.
A learned network in Competitive PINNs that is trained to point out where the solution network is wrong.
A competitive setting where if one player gains something, the other player loses exactly that amount, so their interests are completely opposite.
A number that measures how sensitive a calculation is to small changes in input; large values mean the calculation will be noisy and fragile.

stanford_connections: This talk directly builds on earlier lectures about why PINNs fail, and offers an adversarial fix.
It ties conditioning problems in optimization to why physics losses can stop improving, making numerical stability central to the story.
It also pairs with Neural Galerkin and structure-preserving closure talks as other ways to make neural PDE solvers more numerically trustworthy.
practical_caution: Adversarial training adds its own stability and tuning challenges. Competitive PINNs should be judged on whether they converge reliably across different PDEs, not just on one carefully-chosen example.
selected_evidence: PINNs... currently cannot produce high-accuracy solutions.
Competitive PINNs (CPINNs).
Train a discriminator that is rewarded for predicting mistakes the PINN makes.
Discriminator and PINN participate in a zero-sum game.
Errors four orders of magnitude smaller than the best-performing PINN.
takeaway: The core lesson is that how you write the loss function for physics matters. If squaring residuals causes bad conditioning, changing the game setup can change whether the method learns well.

title: Soledad Villar: The Passive Symmetries Of Machine Learning
speaker: Soledad Villar
one_sentence: This lecture explains passive symmetries as invariances that come from arbitrary choices in how we write down data, and shows that respecting these symmetries can help machine-learning models generalize better.
core_problem: Every time we write down data, we make choices: which coordinates to use, which units to measure in, how to label nodes in a graph, which gauge convention to pick, or which basis vectors to start with. None of these choices are part of the real-world process that generated the data. A model that shifts its predictions when we make different choices is learning artifacts of how we wrote things down, not the real structure of what's happening.
first_principles_model: A passive symmetry is a change between two different ways of writing the same real object. When we rotate coordinates, convert units, apply a gauge transformation, or relabel nodes in a graph, the model's inputs and outputs should change in matching ways without changing what the model actually predicts. Group equivariance (a mathematical property where transforming an input causes a predictable change in the output) is one way to build this matching directly into neural networks.
key_claims: Representation choices create exact symmetries because the same real object can be written down in many different ways.
Passive symmetries include coordinate freedom, gauge symmetry, unit transformation, and permutation symmetry.
These symmetries come from our choices of notation, not from the data-generating process itself, yet they affect how well machine learning works.
Some passive symmetries can be built into neural networks as group equivariances.
Respecting passive symmetries is especially useful for making predictions on data the model has never seen.
This topic connects what machine-learning practitioners do to ideas from physics and causal reasoning.

important_terms.meaning: A symmetry that arises when we change how we write something down while the actual thing we're describing stays the same.
The fact that the same object or system can be described using different coordinate systems without changing what it is.
A redundancy in notation where multiple different mathematical descriptions represent the exact same physical state.
Quantities change in a consistent, predictable way when measurement units are switched.
A property of a model where transforming the input causes the output to transform in a matching way.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to equivariant neural networks, graph models, and structure-preserving learning throughout the series.
It shows why symmetries matter for actual machine learning—not just as physics decoration, but because models need to ignore arbitrary choices in how data is written down.
It ties into making models work on new kinds of data: generalization improves when models ignore representation choices that don't matter.
practical_caution: Not every symmetry should be forced onto a model without thought. A model should respect symmetries that come from representation choices, but it must not erase real asymmetries that actually exist in the process generating the data.
selected_evidence: Any representation of data involves arbitrary investigator choices.
Each choice leads to an exact symmetry.
Passive symmetries... include coordinate freedom, gauge symmetry and units' covariance.
Implemented as group equivariances.
Valuable when the goal... is to generalize out of sample.
takeaway: The core lesson is that machine-learning models should give the same answer regardless of arbitrary representational choices. Passive symmetries tell us what the model must treat as truly equivalent.

title: Victor Zavala: Bayesian Optimization With ML Models, Physics, And High-Throughput Experiments
speaker: Victor M. Zavala
organization: University of Wisconsin-Madison / Argonne National Laboratory
one_sentence: This lecture presents Bayesian optimization methods—a way to search for good answers when experiments are expensive—that combine physics models, learned corrections to those models, uncertainty estimates you can scale up, and designs for running many experiments at once.
core_problem: Bayesian optimization is useful when experiments or simulations cost time or money. But standard methods based on Gaussian processes struggle when your model is large, when you have physics knowledge to use, or when you can run many experiments in parallel. The challenge is how to use physics and parallelism while still keeping your search guided by uncertainty—how confident you are in your predictions.
first_principles_model: Bayesian optimization picks the next experiment by optimizing an acquisition function: a formula that scores each possible choice using a surrogate (a fast substitute model) and uncertainty estimates. If physics gives you a reference model (a rough first guess based on known laws), you can split performance into two parts: what the physics model predicts plus the residual (what's left over). Training a Gaussian process—a statistical model that assigns probabilities to different functions—on just the residual focuses your limited experiments on catching what physics misses. The reference model also lets you divide up the design space so parallel searches don't waste effort, and it helps build acquisition functions that work on large models.
key_claims: Bayesian optimization can use large-scale ML models, physical knowledge, and experiments run in batches together.
You can split what happens into two parts: a physics-based reference model plus a learned correction model.
Training a Gaussian process on just the correction speeds up your search.
Reference models can split up the design space so you run parallel experiments without duplication.
Running many experiments at once requires Bayesian optimization methods that choose groups of points, not one at a time.
Scalable acquisition functions can extend Bayesian optimization to large parametric models using simple uncertainty counts.

important_terms.meaning: A search method that uses statistical models to make quick guesses about good choices and only runs the experiments most likely to teach you something new.
A starting model, often built from physics or simple science, that captures the basic shape of how performance changes.
A learned model that captures the errors or corrections the reference model misses.
A statistical tool that assigns probabilities to different possible functions, letting you estimate both what will happen and how sure you are about it.
A scoring formula that Bayesian optimization uses to decide which experiment or simulation to try next.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to active learning and experimental design across the playlist, and to how you build and tune digital copies of real systems.
It extends the idea of hybrid physics-ML modeling by treating physics as a starting point rather than the complete answer.
It shows the optimization side of building surrogate models while thinking carefully about how sure you are in your predictions.
practical_caution: A weak physics model can send your search in the wrong direction. When using physics-informed Bayesian optimization, watch how well the residual behaves and how sure your uncertainty estimates are, rather than trusting the reference model everywhere.
selected_evidence: Bayesian Optimization... exploiting machine learning models, physics and high throughput experiments.
Decomposes the performance function into a reference model... and a residual model.
Learning the residual from data using a Gaussian Process.
Partition the design space and enable parallel search.
Acquisition function.
takeaway: The core idea is that Bayesian optimization is smart experimentation when you're unsure. Physics works best when it points your search in the right direction while still letting you learn what it gets wrong.

title: Hassan Babaee: CUR Matrix Decomposition For Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Hassan Babaee
one_sentence: This lecture uses CUR matrix decomposition to make reduced-order models with time-evolving bases scalable for nonlinear PDEs while cutting down the complexity of putting the method into code.
core_problem: Dynamical low-rank approximation with time-evolving bases can solve high-dimensional PDEs by tracking a low-rank representation that changes, but for generic nonlinear PDEs the cost savings disappear. For nonlinearities (terms where input changes produce non-proportional changes in output) that aren't polynomials, computing the reduced equations can cost as much as solving the original full-size model, and putting the method into code is difficult.
first_principles_model: DLRA represents a solution that starts high-dimensional and evolves by keeping low-rank factors that change over time. Those factors get updated by minimizing how far the model's prediction misses the actual PDE answer. CUR decomposition picks the most informative rows and columns to approximate large matrices using just a few entries, allowing smart selection of how to evaluate nonlinear terms. This lets time-evolving-basis reduced models handle generic nonlinear PDEs at their promised reduced cost.
key_claims: DLRA pulls out correlations from high-dimensional PDE solutions.
Time-evolving bases are built from minimizing prediction error rather than extracted from data computed beforehand.
DLRA stays efficient for linear or quadratic PDEs, but generic nonlinearities force full-size costs.
Nonlinearities that aren't polynomials create especially difficult challenges for time-evolving-basis equations.
Smart sparse selection based on CUR decomposition makes time-evolving-basis reduced models scale for nonlinear PDEs.
The method reduces how much code rewriting is needed to apply time-evolving-basis reduced models to new PDEs.

important_terms.meaning: A way to approximate a large matrix by picking a few columns, a few rows, and computing a small connecting matrix from their overlap.
A method for handling evolving high-dimensional systems by keeping track of time-changing low-rank factors.
A shrunk set of directions that evolves during a simulation instead of staying fixed after being learned from precomputed data.
A way to approximate nonlinear terms by computing them only at carefully picked informative points or entries.
A nonlinear term that cannot be written as a polynomial, which typically makes computing reduced versions much harder.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the reduced-model lineage with a scalable computational method for nonlinear PDEs.
It connects to learning-based reduced models and adaptive reduced models as another path to making reduced simulation work in practice.
It also links to active sampling and data-selection methods like CUR: pick the rows and columns that do the real computational work.
practical_caution: Smart sparse selection must keep low-rank error under control. If the picked rows or columns skip important nonlinear behavior, the reduced model runs fast but gives wrong answers.
selected_evidence: CUR Matrix Decomposition for Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling.
Dynamical low-rank approximation... high-dimensional partial differential equations.
Time-dependent bases.
Residual minimization.
Adaptive sparse interpolation algorithm based on CUR matrix decomposition.
takeaway: The core lesson is that fast reduced models need both low-rank structure and cheap nonlinear evaluation. CUR provides the selective sampling that keeps nonlinear reduced models actually reduced.

title: Jian Cao: Physics-Based AI-Assisted Design And Control In Flexible Manufacturing
speaker: Jian Cao
one_sentence: This lecture shows how physics-based and machine-learning methods together support design, sensing, prediction, and real-time control in flexible manufacturing processes such as metal additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming.
core_problem: Flexible manufacturing aims to produce three-dimensional parts without dedicated tooling for each shape, but the process physics is hard: material properties depend on long production histories, geometric features are complex, and the design and control space has many dimensions. Pure physics models can be too slow or incomplete, while purely machine-learning models may miss the actual mechanics and control constraints.
first_principles_model: A manufacturing process connects design choices and control inputs through the physics of how material moves, solidifies, and hardens into microstructure, material state, shape, and mechanical behavior. Physics supplies conservation laws (energy and mass balance), mechanical principles, and what the process allows; machine learning supplies fast prediction, active sensing (choosing what to measure during production), and adaptive control. The control target is local and during production: measure what is happening right now as the part is being made and adjust inputs before flaws lock into the final part.
key_claims: Flexible manufacturing improves when physics-based and machine-learning approaches work together.
Metal powder-based additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming show production without dedicated tooling for each shape.
Basic process physics, process control, and machine learning can be combined to predict mechanical behavior during manufacturing.
Machine learning can guide active sensing—deciding what to measure—to enable effective real-time local process control.
Long history-dependent properties are a central difficulty in manufacturing prediction.
Complex geometries and high-dimensional design spaces make purely manual or exhaustive search approaches impractical.

important_terms.meaning: Manufacturing methods that can produce many different shapes or products without needing dedicated tooling for each design.
Building parts layer by layer, often using metal powder and laser heat in this talk's examples.
A forming process for three-dimensional parts that does not require a dedicated die or mold for each geometry.
Using trained models and measurements to decide what process information to collect during production.
Adjustments made during manufacturing based on real-time measurements of the process as it happens.

stanford_connections: This talk connects industrial digital twins to actual manufacturing control loops that act during production.
It also links to active learning and sensing because the model must choose what to measure during the process.
It complements materials microstructure talks by showing how production history shapes material behavior.
practical_caution: A manufacturing machine-learning model that ignores production history can miss the real source of material properties. Control needs history-aware state estimation—tracking how material changed from its start—not just static prediction from geometry to property.
selected_evidence: Flexible processes... metal powder-based additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming.
Without geometry-specific tooling.
Integration of the fundamental process mechanics, process control, and techniques including machine learning.
Machine learning for active sensing.
Effective in-situ local process control.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that manufacturing with scientific machine learning is closed-loop process modeling. Prediction, sensing, and control must be learned by understanding the physics of how parts are made.

title: Matthias Chung: Big Data Inverse Problems
speaker: Matthias Chung
one_sentence: This lecture explains sparse inverse problems at big-data scale and shows how variable projection and neural networks can help choose regularization—adjustments that keep solutions stable when working backward from noisy measurements.
core_problem: Inverse problems recover hidden causes from indirect measurements, but they are often ill-posed: many different solutions fit the data equally well, noise gets amplified, and large datasets make traditional statistical methods too slow. Sparsity—assuming the answer has only a few large values—helps, but L1-regularized problems require difficult choices about regularization strength and how to optimize.
first_principles_model: An inverse problem trades off data match against prior structure. Sparsity says the unknown quantity is simple in some vector space or dictionary, so L1 regularization (a penalty on absolute coefficient values) encourages sparse reconstructions. Variable projection reduces coupled optimization by analytically or implicitly eliminating variables, while learned regularization uses deep neural networks to infer stabilizing adjustments from data or problem features.
key_claims: Modern data analytics, machine learning, and uncertainty quantification depend on efficient inverse-problem solvers.
Growing model size and data volume exceed the limits of many existing statistical methods.
Many inverse problems aim to reconstruct quantities with sparse representations.
L1 regularization is widely useful in compressed sensing, dictionary learning, and imaging.
Variable projection provides a new route for sparse inverse optimization.
Deep neural networks can infer regularization parameters for solving inverse problems.

important_terms.meaning: A problem of inferring unknown causes, fields, or parameters from observed effects.
A problem where solutions may not exist, may not be unique, or may change wildly when data shifts slightly.
A representation where only a small number of coefficients are nonzero or matter.
A penalty on absolute coefficient values that encourages solutions with many coefficients equal to zero.
An optimization technique that removes some variables to reduce or stabilize the remaining problem.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to inverse scattering, adaptive reduced-order models, and Bayesian calibration across the series.
It clarifies why regularization is not an afterthought; it is how prior assumptions stabilize inverse inference.
It links scientific machine learning with classical computational mathematics rather than replacing regularization theory.
practical_caution: Learning a regularization parameter does not eliminate the need to understand the prior. A network-selected parameter can still encode the wrong bias if the training inverse problems differ from the ones you apply it to.
selected_evidence: Big Data Inverse Problems... Promoting Sparsity and Learning to Regularize.
Reconstruct quantities with a sparse representation.
Optimization problems with L1 regularization.
A new method based on variable projection.
Deep neural networks (DNNs) to obtain regularization parameters.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that inverse problems need stabilizing assumptions. Sparsity and learned regularization are ways to encode those assumptions at scale.

title: Ameya Jagtap: Scientific Machine Learning Through The Lens Of PINNs
speaker: Ameya Jagtap
one_sentence: This lecture surveys physics-informed neural networks (PINNs—a method that teaches neural networks to solve equations by including physics constraints alongside data) as a scientific machine learning tool, emphasizing their strengths, limitations, scalable variants, and causal time-decomposition strategies.
core_problem: Traditional scientific computing requires known physics, boundary and initial conditions, meshes, and long simulations. PINNs offer mesh-light integration of physics and data, but vanilla PINNs face scaling and trainability limits for big data, large domains, long time horizons, and parameterized PDEs.
first_principles_model: A PINN represents a solution with a neural network and trains it with data and PDE residual constraints. Scalable PINN variants decompose the problem: conservative PINNs enforce conservation across subdomains, extended PINNs split large domains, and causal or temporal sweeping trains time-dependent problems in an order that respects physical causality rather than treating all time points equally.
key_claims: Scientific machine learning has emerged as an alternative to workflows requiring precise laws, meshes, and long simulations.
PINNs are a central method for solving forward and inverse problems (predicting what happens next, or inferring hidden causes from observations) with noisy data.
PINNs have useful capabilities but also important limitations.
Conservative PINNs and extended PINNs are scalable extensions for big data or large models.
Temporal decompositions help scale PINNs over long time horizons.
Causal sweeping provides a unified strategy for training time-dependent PINN problems in physically meaningful order.

important_terms.meaning: Machine learning that incorporates physical laws, constraints, or data from scientific systems so the model respects the science it learns.
A neural network trained to satisfy differential-equation residuals (how well it solves the equation) and data constraints at the same time.
A PINN variant designed to respect conservation laws (like energy or mass staying constant) across decomposed subdomains rather than globally.
A domain-decomposition PINN method that splits a large or complex spatial region into smaller pieces to train more efficiently.
A training strategy for temporal problems that trains the neural network to predict earlier times before later times, matching how causality works in physics.

stanford_connections: This lecture synthesizes many early PINN-focused talks: vanilla PINN promise, failure modes, and scalable repairs.
It connects to CPINNs (conservative PINNs) because both try to address limitations of standard residual training.
It also links to operator learning and Neural Galerkin schemes as alternative responses to PINN scaling problems.
practical_caution: PINNs can be effective in selected applications, but the training strategy matters. Large time-domain problems can fail if trained without decomposition, causality, or conservation structure.
selected_evidence: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).
Current capabilities and limitations of PINNs.
Conservative PINNs (cPINNs) and extended PINNs (XPINNs).
For big data and/or large models.
Causal sweeping strategies for PINNs and their temporal decompositions.
takeaway: The core lesson is that PINNs are a suite of strategies, not one algorithm. Scaling them requires breaking down physics, space, time, and training dynamics into smaller pieces.

title: Anima Anandkumar: Neural Operators On Function Spaces
speaker: Anima Anandkumar
one_sentence: Neural operators learn to predict output fields directly from input fields for PDEs and multiscale scientific systems, generalizing across resolutions and achieving thousands-of-times speedups over traditional numerical solvers.
core_problem: Scientific systems such as weather, climate, deep earth, materials, and quantum-to-planetary-scale processes involve mappings between fields, not fixed-size vectors. Standard neural networks are tied to one specific mesh size and struggle to work on different resolutions, different geographical areas, or different boundary conditions.
first_principles_model: A PDE solver takes input functions (like initial conditions or forcing) and produces output functions (like solutions). A neural operator learns this input-to-output mapping directly on function spaces. Because the learned map does not depend on a specific mesh size, it can work on new grids and naturally handles multi-scale (small and large features together) field-to-field structure better than ordinary neural networks tied to one discretization.
key_claims: Neural operators learn the mappings between input and output fields that PDEs define.
Function-space learning works especially well for scientific applications across many scales.
Applications include weather and climate, deep earth, and other scientific simulations.
Well-designed neural operators can generalize to new problems without retraining, going beyond the training data.
Neural operators can run thousands of times faster than numerical weather models and similar simulations.
The advantage comes from learning the right mathematical object: an operator (a function-to-function map), not just using neural networks.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network that learns mappings from input functions to output functions, rather than from fixed-size vectors to fixed-size vectors.
A mathematical collection of functions, such as temperature or pressure fields defined over a region.
Working correctly on new problems or new conditions without seeing training examples from those specific cases.
A system where behavior depends on interactions happening at many different scales of size or time, all at once.
Training a model to learn the map that converts input conditions into solution fields for a family of related problems.

stanford_connections: This talk anchors the neural-operator concept and connects to Kaushik Bhattacharya's work on operators across multiple scales.
It relates to reduced-order models because both aim to build fast, reusable maps, but operators work directly on fields rather than vector snapshots.
It also ties to talks on weather and data assimilation because both need fast field predictions for atmospheric systems.
practical_caution: Zero-shot generalization (working on new problems never seen during training) must be tested against real cases, not assumed from the architecture alone. Operator learning can fail when the new problem has different physics or boundary conditions than the training set.
selected_evidence: ML for solving PDEs: neural operators on the function spaces.
Learn mappings between function spaces.
Ideal for capturing multi-scale processes.
Zero-shot generalization beyond the training domain.
4-5 orders of magnitude speedups.
takeaway: The key lesson is that learning should target the operator that maps between field solutions, not individual solution snapshots. The architecture should match what you are actually trying to learn: a function-to-function map.

title: Lori Graham-Brady: ML-Driven Models For Material Microstructure And Mechanical Behavior
speaker: Lori Graham-Brady
one_sentence: This lecture shows how ML can generate realistic material microstructures and learn fast mappings from microstructural images to local stress, strain, damage, and material behavior.
core_problem: Material failure is governed by microstructural features, but real microstructures are random, high-dimensional, and difficult to simulate exhaustively. Experiments may provide limited 2D images, while engineering design needs collections of realistic 3D microstructures and rapid property or damage predictions.
first_principles_model: A material's large-scale mechanical behavior emerges from its microstructure. The workflow has two learned components: generate digital microstructures that preserve important experimental features, and use limited physics-based simulations on those microstructures to train ML surrogates (fast mathematical models that replace slow simulations) for properties and local fields. Transfer learning (using learned patterns from one task to help another related task) can help compare or generate microstructures when handcrafted correlation descriptors (manually designed measurements of how microstructural features relate to each other) are insufficient.
key_claims: Material behavior leading to failure is often tied to microstructural features.
Random microstructural variability creates uncertain material response.
Digital microstructure generation must capture important experimental features, not only simple statistical correlations.
Translating 2D experimental microstructure images into realistic 3D microstructures is crucial.
Transfer learning can support rapid generation or comparison of different microstructure families.
ML models can map microstructural images to properties and local stress, strain, and damage fields many times faster than physics simulations.

important_terms.meaning: The small-scale internal structure of a material that influences its mechanical behavior.
A microstructure with variability across samples, leading to uncertain material response.
Using learned patterns or features from one task or dataset to improve another related task.
Concentration of stress, strain, or damage in particular microstructural regions.
The high-dimensional collection of possible material structures, processing choices, and resulting properties.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects materials ML to uncertainty and stochastic (random) mechanics.
It complements manufacturing talks because process and microstructure together determine behavior.
It also links to generative modeling and surrogate acceleration for high-dimensional scientific images.
practical_caution: A generated microstructure is useful only if it preserves the features that control mechanics. Matching visual texture or simple statistical correlations (which capture only relationships between nearby features) may not be enough for failure prediction.
selected_evidence: Material behavior leading to failure is often associated with microstructural features.
Random variability of these microstructures leads to uncertain material response.
Digitally generating ensembles of microstructures.
Transfer learning approach to rapid generation of three-dimensional microstructures.
Local stresses, strains and damage accelerate the analyses by orders of magnitude.
takeaway: The key lesson is that material ML must preserve the microstructural features that drive mechanics. The surrogate is only as good as the generated and simulated microstructure collection.

title: Ying Liang: Data-Assisted Algorithms For Inverse Random Source Scattering
speaker: Ying Liang
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to combine boundary measurements with machine learning to find the statistical properties of random sources in inverse scattering problems, needing far fewer random trials than traditional methods.
core_problem: Inverse source scattering appears in antenna design, medical imaging, earthquake monitoring, and similar work. When the source varies randomly and the surrounding medium is not fully known, standard approaches need many trials and must know the medium's properties in detail to accurately find what the source's statistics are.
first_principles_model: The physical problem starts with boundary measurements created by wave equations or scattering equations. Integral equations (mathematical statements where unknowns appear within integrals) give a first guess at the source. Machine learning then improves that guess by learning the mapping from these equation-based approximations to the true source statistics. The goal is not to replace physics but to use observed data to cut down the number of trials needed.
key_claims: Inverse random source scattering is an inverse problem with many real-world uses.
Standard methods require many trials and need to know the medium's properties in detail.
Combining boundary measurement data with machine learning can find the statistical properties of a random source.
Machine learning can improve the first approximation from integral equation methods.
This method achieved better reconstruction using only one tenth the number of trials that standard approaches need.
Among the image translation models tested, pix2pix worked best when inclusions were far apart and their positions were accurately known.

important_terms.meaning: Finding the properties of a source by observing the waves it scattered.
An inverse problem where the source, medium, or measurements involve randomness.
Data collected at the edge of a region, used to figure out what is inside.
A type of equation where unknowns appear inside integrals; commonly used to solve scattering problems.
A machine learning model that learns to translate one type of image to another, used here to map measurement data to source properties.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together inverse problems, uncertainty in data, and machine learning-aided reconstruction.
It shows how the ideas from inverse problems work in a specific scattering example that includes randomness.
It also relates to earthquake monitoring and medical imaging, where measurements at a boundary must reveal sources hidden inside.
practical_caution: Image translation models help only when the data they trained on matches the actual physics and geometry of your inverse problem. Treat these models as data-assisted aids that improve initial results, not as proof that the answer is unique or certain.
selected_evidence: Inverse source scattering problems are essential... antenna synthesis, medical imaging, and earthquake monitoring.
Stochastic inverse problems.
Boundary measurement data to reconstruct the statistical properties of the random source.
Better reconstruction with only 1/10 of the realizations.
The pix2pix method outperforms others.
takeaway: The key lesson is that observed data can lower the cost of sampling in inverse problems involving randomness, if that data is anchored to the physics equations.

title: Paul Atzberger: Generative Machine Learning For Data-Driven Modeling And Reductions
speaker: Paul Atzberger
one_sentence: This lecture covers machine-learning models that create compact representations of complex dynamical systems, using geometric VAEs (a type of neural-network encoder that preserves shape and structure) to capture physically meaningful patterns and stochastic dynamic GANs (two-network systems trained competitively to model random time-evolving processes) to encode randomness in dynamics.
core_problem: Simulations of soft materials, complex fluids, and biological systems involve many length and time scales plus random fluctuations. Reduced models need to capture nonlinear dynamics and account for randomness, but standard machine-learning models that compress data into hidden layers may ignore geometric structure, smoothness properties, conservation laws, and the numerical stability needed to run simulations over many steps.
first_principles_model: A generative reduction learns a simulator by extracting patterns from observations or detailed simulations. Geometric VAEs add built-in rules so that the hidden representation respects shape, curvature, and physical laws. SDYN-GANs learn random dynamics as stochastic differential equations (rules for how systems evolve when subject to random forces), including the smooth drift term, the noise scale, and numerical methods that keep multi-step simulation stable. The result is not just compressed data; it is a learned dynamical model you can run forward in time.
key_claims: Machine learning creates opportunities to build reduced-order models and multiscale models of nonlinear scientific simulations.
Physical principles and existing scientific knowledge should be added as built-in biases that guide what the model learns.
Geometric variational autoencoders can learn representations that preserve shape, topology, smoothness, and adherence to physical laws.
Geometric VAEs can build reductions of high-dimensional time-evolving systems and nonlinear partial-differential equations.
SDYN-GANs learn random dynamical models from data collected from stochastic systems.
SDYN-GAN models use stochastic differential equations and stable numerical methods for multi-step simulation.

important_terms.meaning: A system that learns to create samples or time sequences resembling the actual data.
A neural-network encoder that learns compressed representations while preserving shape, topology, smoothness, and physical structure.
A two-network system where one generates and one criticizes random dynamical representations, trained competitively.
A rule for how a system evolves when subject to random forces; includes smooth drift plus random noise.
A numerical method that advances random dynamics forward multiple time steps while maintaining accuracy and stability.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects machine learning with reduced-order models, stochastic model reduction, and learning curved spaces from data.
It builds on information-geometry and charting-dynamics talks by focusing on structure in learned hidden spaces.
It also relates to uncertainty quantification because random dynamics require probabilistic reduced models, not just deterministic approximations.
practical_caution: A generative model can produce trajectories that look plausible while violating conservation laws or breaking down numerically. Scientific reductions need structural constraints built in, not just visual or statistical similarity.
selected_evidence: Generative Machine Learning Approaches for Data-Driven Modeling and Reductions.
Incorporate... inductive biases including physical principles.
Geometric Variational Autoencoders... topological information, smoothness, and adherence to physical principles.
Stochastic Dynamic Generative Adversarial Networks (SDYN-GANs).
SDEs and stable m-step stochastic numerical integrators.
takeaway: The core lesson: generative machine learning for science should learn structured dynamics, not just generate samples. The hidden representation must enable simulation.

title: Eduardo Gildin: Guided Deep Learning Manifold Linearization Of Porous Media Flow
speaker: Eduardo Gildin
one_sentence: This lecture presents physics-aware manifold linearization for porous-media flow, using non-intrusive reduction, autoencoders, and Koopman-style lifting to speed up reservoir digital twins (fast computational copies used for monitoring and control).
core_problem: Reservoir simulators are expensive because nonlinear porous-media equations require iterative solves at each time step. Running fast closed-loop simulations, optimizations, and control systems in real time needs a quicker proxy—but full access to the simulator's internal equations is often unavailable or impractical.
first_principles_model: The core idea is to learn a transformed space where nonlinear reservoir dynamics behave more like linear systems. E2CO (Embed to Control and Observe) combines data-driven model reduction and neural networks to copy both the time evolution of the state and how the system responds to inputs, without needing simulator internals. A second path augments the state space and uses an autoencoder (a neural network that compresses and decompresses data) to map reservoir equations to a lower-dimensional surface where a Koopman operator (a linear operator that describes evolution in a transformed space) approximates the dynamics, cutting down on expensive nonlinear iteration.
key_claims: Reservoir digital twin operations require fast simulation to enable real-time closed-loop management, drilling decisions, and optimization.
Physics-aware machine learning can give proxy models properties related to material balance and conservation laws (rules about what cannot be created or destroyed).
E2CO uses data-driven reduction and neural networks for simultaneous matching of state trajectories and input-output behavior.
The non-intrusive method does not require access to the reservoir simulator's internal equations or structure.

POD (proper orthogonal decomposition, a data-driven compression method) can be extended by adding extra state dimensions to create a bilinear system (one where the nonlinearity comes only from interactions between state and input).
Autoencoders can linearize reservoir equations on a reduced manifold by treating the Koopman operator (a linear map in a transformed space) as the evolution rule.

important_terms.meaning: Movement of fluids (oil, gas, water) through materials that contain pores, such as rock in underground reservoirs.
A fast computational copy of a reservoir used for monitoring changes, testing decisions, and running control systems.
Embed to Control and Observe—a non-intrusive method that combines model reduction and machine learning to match both state evolution and input-output response without accessing simulator internals.
A linear operator that describes how observables (measurable properties) of a nonlinear dynamical system evolve in time.
Learning a transformed lower-dimensional space where the nonlinear dynamics become closer to linear evolution.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together Koopman theory, autoencoder-based reduced-order models, and industrial digital twins applied to reservoirs.
It also complements talks on learned simulators by showing how to deploy fast models non-intrusively alongside existing simulators.
It reinforces the seminar's theme that the most useful learned representation is one where control and prediction become computationally efficient.
practical_caution: A learned linear manifold only stays accurate within the operating conditions present in the training data. Real closed-loop reservoir control needs monitoring to catch when the latent linearization stops matching the simulator's behavior or actual field measurements.
selected_evidence: Digital Twin operations for closed-loop reservoir management.
Embed to Control and Observe method (E2CO).
State and input-output matching.
Non-intrusive method does not need to have access to reservoir simulation internal structure.
Linearize the reservoir equations in a reduced manifold by means of a Koopman operator.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a digital twin needs a representation where the control problem becomes cheap to solve. Manifold linearization (learning a transformed space where dynamics are closer to linear) is one way to turn nonlinear reservoir physics into something operational.

title: Yexiang Xue: Scaling Up AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
speaker: Yexiang Xue
one_sentence: This lecture tackles computational bottlenecks in AI-driven scientific discovery by building differentiable PDE solvers into end-to-end learning and using random projection and hash-based tricks to speed up sparse physics updates.
core_problem: Learning first-principles physics models from experimental data requires a loop where data, simulation, gradients, and model discovery all feed back into each other. The bottleneck is computational: running large-scale PDE simulations is expensive in the forward pass (computing what happens next), and sending gradients backward through them can be even more expensive.
first_principles_model: The key idea is to treat a PDE solver as a differentiable layer (a step you can send gradients backward through) inside a learning pipeline. This lets the model learn PDE structure directly from experimental data while gradients flow backward through the physics simulation. Scaling then depends on exploiting structure: only updating parts of the state that change meaningfully, using locality in how elements affect their neighbors, and applying random projection or locality-sensitive hashing (a trick that groups elements with similar temporal patterns) to speed up which pieces to compute.
key_claims: AI-driven scientific discovery is held back by the lack of end-to-end pipelines that embed large-scale physics simulation into learning.
Backward gradient propagation through physics models is often more computationally expensive than running the simulation forward.
PDE solvers can be written as fully differentiable layers in neural networks.
Differentiable solver layers allow large-scale physics simulations to be embedded into learning workflows.
Locality-sensitive hashing can speed up sparse PDE updates by grouping elements with similar local neighborhoods.
Random projection and symbolic regression can support efficient discovery of sparse and decomposable PDEs.

important_terms.meaning: A learning loop where model discovery, simulation, and gradient-based optimization are all connected into one differentiable pipeline.
A PDE solver built so that gradients can be sent backward through its computations.
A hashing method that groups similar objects together; used here to find and speed up computing on PDE elements with similar local neighborhoods.
An update pattern where only a subset of state elements changes in an informative way at each time step.
A dimensionality-reduction technique that projects data into a lower-dimensional random subspace while roughly preserving the structure.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly connects automatic differentiation, differentiable programming, and PDE discovery.
It also complements neural solver and operator talks by emphasizing how to scale both forward and backward computation.
It extends the equation-discovery thread from symbolic search to differentiable simulation pipelines.
practical_caution: End-to-end differentiable physics has real limits: memory constraints, numerical stiffness (when equations resist stable computation), and biased experimental data. Fast gradients help only if the embedded solver and the discovered PDE stay physically meaningful.
selected_evidence: Lack of end-to-end frameworks embedding large-scale simulation of physics models into learning.
Backward gradient propagation.
PDE solvers are formulated as fully differentiable neural network layers.
Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH).
Sparse updates of PDE models.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scaling scientific discovery requires making physics differentiable and computationally sparse enough to learn from.

title: Dongbin Xiu: Data-Driven Modeling Of Unknown Systems With Deep Neural Networks
speaker: Dongbin Xiu
one_sentence: Deep neural networks can learn the hidden rule—the evolution operator, or map from one system state to the next—from measurement data alone, then use that learned map to predict how an unknown system will behave.
core_problem: Many dynamical systems (systems that change over time) are only partially observed: the equations that govern them are unknown, some variables are not measured, some parameters are hidden, and the structure of partial differential equations (PDEs—equations with multiple variables and rates of change) may not be available. The question is whether you can build a model that predicts the future just from the measured history.
first_principles_model: Instead of trying to learn the differential equation directly, flow map learning finds the evolution operator—the rule that maps a current observed state to a future observed state. A deep neural network (a flexible mathematical model with many layers) learns this map from data. Once trained, the learned map can predict how the observed system will evolve and answer questions about the system, even when you don't have complete measurements or know what hidden variables exist.
key_claims: Predictive modeling of unknown systems can be reframed as finding the evolution operator (the rule that advances the system in time) behind the data.
The evolution operator is the flow map: it takes the system state now and gives you the system state later.
Deep neural networks can learn this flow map by training on measurement data.
A well-trained learned flow map becomes a working predictive model for the unknown system.
Flow map learning works for dynamical systems, systems with missing variables, systems with hidden parameters, and PDEs.
The method can predict the measured variables even when the full system dimension (the total number of variables, hidden and visible) is unknown.

important_terms.meaning: The rule that shows how a system state at one time changes to a new state at a later time.
A rule that describes how a system advances forward through time.
Unobserved parts of the system state that affect how it moves but are not directly measured.
Numbers that control the system's behavior but are not known or not measured.
A mathematical tool that forecasts what the system will do next based on what you know right now or recently.

stanford_connections: This approach builds on Koopman operator theory, charting of dynamics, and equation-free modeling—other methods that learn how systems evolve from data without needing the equations.
It differs from equation discovery (which tries to recover the actual differential equations) by focusing on learning the time-advance map instead.
It also relates to reservoir computing, manifold linearization, and operator learning because all of these learn maps from data.
practical_caution: A flow map trained only on the variables you can observe may miss effects from variables you cannot see. The prediction might work well for nearby conditions but fail when hidden states shift the way the observed system behaves.
selected_evidence: Discover/approximate the unknown evolution operator, i.e., flow map, behind the data.
Deep neural network (DNN) is employed to construct such an approximation.
Serves as a predictive model for the unknown system.
Systems with missing variables and hidden parameters.
Partial differential equations (PDEs).
takeaway: A system can be modeled by learning how it advances through time—the evolution operator from one state to the next—even when you don't have its governing equations.

title: Peng Chen: Derivative-Informed Neural Operators
speaker: Peng Chen
one_sentence: This lecture introduces derivative-informed neural operators—learned approximations that predict both PDE solutions and their sensitivities to input changes—for use in Bayesian inference (inferring unknown values from uncertain data), optimal experiment design (choosing measurements that give the most information), and stochastic optimization (finding best choices under uncertainty).
core_problem: Optimization and inference problems governed by large-scale PDEs (partial differential equations—rules describing how quantities change over space and time) with high-dimensional random parameters require many expensive PDE solves. Classical methods become impractical because each sampling step or optimization iteration needs not only state predictions but also statistical measures, derivatives, and sensitivities.
first_principles_model: A neural operator learns to map from parameters and controls to a PDE solution. For optimization to work well, you also need the derivative of that map—how the output changes when inputs shift slightly. A derivative-informed neural operator trains a reduced-basis architecture (a neural network that represents outputs in a smaller-dimensional space for speed) to learn both the solution and its derivative, cutting down the number of expensive PDE solves while keeping sensitivity information intact for downstream algorithms.
key_claims: Large-scale PDE optimization with high-dimensional random parameters comes up in Bayesian inverse problems (finding unknown values from data), optimal experimental design (picking which measurements give the most information), and stochastic optimization (finding good answers when parameters are uncertain).
Classical approaches cost too much in computation because statistical measures require solving the PDE many times.
Derivative-informed neural operators learn to approximate both the PDE solution map and how it responds to small changes in input variables.
Reduced-basis architectures (neural networks that work in a compressed space) make the operator practical for high-dimensional problems.
Training with only a limited amount of data can achieve high accuracy for both the PDE solution and the optimization solution.
Derivative information makes neural operators useful for optimization, not just for predicting forward.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to approximate both a PDE solution map and how that solution changes with respect to input variables.
Finding unknown values by inferring them from observed data, treating the unknowns as random variables with probabilities.
Choosing how and where to collect data so that you learn the most about the system.
Finding the best choice for something when some quantities are uncertain or random.
A neural network design that compresses outputs into a smaller set of dimensions for faster and more accurate training and prediction.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends neural operators into inverse problems and design, where sensitivities—how outputs respond to changes—matter.

It connects to active subspaces (finding the most important input directions), Bayesian calibration (adjusting parameters to match data), and differentiable programming (writing code that computes gradients automatically) because all three depend on understanding how outputs shift with inputs.
It also builds on reduced-order model talks by using compressed bases inside neural operators.
practical_caution: A neural operator that predicts states accurately may still produce wrong derivatives. If those wrong sensitivities guide your optimization, decisions will be poor. You must validate derivatives when the learned surrogate is making real choices.
selected_evidence: Derivative-informed neural operators.
Approximate not only the mapping... to the PDE state, but also its derivative.
Reduced basis architecture.
Limited number of training data.
Bayesian inverse problems... optimal experimental design... stochastic optimization.
takeaway: Optimization needs more than fast predictions of what will happen. It needs trustworthy derivatives—accurate answers to 'if I change this input a little, how much does the output shift?'—from the learned physics model.

title: Alvaro Coutinho: Enhancing Data-Driven Workflows For Complex Simulations
speaker: Alvaro Coutinho
organization: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
one_sentence: This lecture shows that data-driven workflows for large simulations must handle I/O bottlenecks by analyzing, reducing, and updating data while simulations run.
core_problem: Complex PDE simulations produce high-dimensional state vectors on fine meshes. Modern computers can generate data faster than disk storage and I/O systems can write it. If workflows wait until after simulation to save and analyze everything, the data bottleneck—the slow speed of moving information between computer memory and disk—becomes the limiting factor in the science.
first_principles_model: A simulation workflow is a coupled computation-and-data pipeline. Data-driven methods such as model discovery, reduced-order models (simpler stand-in models that capture the essential behavior), physics-informed neural networks (ML models trained to respect physics equations), and control all need snapshots from the simulation. But large simulations cannot always save every snapshot. The solution is to analyze data while the simulation runs and reduce data before writing it to disk: update models during runtime, reduce data before writing, steer simulations based on intermediate results, and combine simulation workflows with machine-learning workflows.
key_claims: Data-driven methods are widely used in engineering and scientific simulations.
Large transient nonlinear PDE simulations produce high-dimensional data that stress storage systems.
The gap between computation speed and I/O speed makes it hard to save large data to disk for later analysis.
Data should be analyzed while the simulation is running or reduced before being saved.
Algorithms running during simulation can update data-driven models as new snapshots arrive.
In situ tools can merge simulation workflows and machine-learning workflows.

important_terms.meaning: Analyzing data while a simulation is running, rather than after writing all output to disk.
A slowdown caused by the speed at which data can be read from and written to disk, relative to how fast the computation produces data.
An algorithm that updates during simulation as new data arrive, without waiting for the simulation to finish.
Compressing or summarizing simulation data to use less storage and require less time to analyze.
Changing simulation behavior or analysis choices during runtime based on intermediate results.

stanford_connections: This talk complements large-scale simulation and machine-learning talks by focusing on how to move data efficiently through the workflow, not just how to build better models.
It connects to reduced-order models because reduction can happen during simulation to avoid saving full state vectors.
It also links to real-world machine-learning deployment: whether methods work depends on whether you can actually get data to them.
practical_caution: If a workflow cannot move data efficiently, a better model will not fix the bottleneck. Scientific ML pipelines must be designed around compute, storage, and I/O constraints.
selected_evidence: One must be cautious regarding I/O operations.
Disparity between computing and I/O speed.
Large simulations to output to disk a large amount of data.
Data should be analyzed while the simulation is running.
Merge... simulation workflow and the Machine learning workflow.
takeaway: Data-driven simulation is also systems engineering. The model cannot learn from data the workflow cannot afford to move.

title: Thomas Beckers: Physics-Enhanced Gaussian Processes For Electromechanical Systems
speaker: Thomas Beckers
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to combine physics-enhanced Gaussian processes (a way to learn probability distributions over functions) with Port-Hamiltonian systems (models that respect energy conservation) so you can learn how electromechanical machines behave from data while keeping uncertainty estimates and staying physically correct without adding penalty tricks.
core_problem: Data-driven models for nonlinear electromechanical systems struggle with two problems: they need a lot of training data, and they can make physically impossible predictions if you don't tell them about known physics like energy conservation. Adding soft penalties during training can help, but the model can still violate physics or need a lot of tuning to behave well.
first_principles_model: Gaussian processes describe a distribution over all possible functions and give you uncertainty estimates for any prediction. Port-Hamiltonian systems are a way to write down dynamics (how things change over time) that automatically respect energy flow, losses, and how parts connect. Combining them means building a Bayesian distribution over possible systems that obey Port-Hamiltonian structure, rather than treating dynamics as a single opaque learned function. Physics-enhanced variational autoencoders (models that learn compressed hidden representations) go further by putting a Gaussian process prior (a built-in guess about what dynamics should look like) with Green's-function structure (a way to encode how linear systems respond) on the hidden dynamics.
key_claims: Data-driven electromechanical models should encode basic physical principles to use data efficiently and avoid impossible predictions.
Physics-enhanced Gaussian processes let you learn nonparametric Bayesian models (models that use data directly without assuming a fixed number of parameters) and track uncertainty.
Gaussian Process Port-Hamiltonian systems enforce physical correctness in their structure, not by penalizing violations during training.
GP-PHS uses data to form a probability distribution over different possible Port-Hamiltonian systems.
Physics-enhanced variational autoencoders use Gaussian process priors with Green's-function structure on hidden-layer dynamics.

Green's functions (which describe how a linear system responds to a sudden input) can encode prior knowledge about linear behavior into the process kernel (the mathematical object that defines distances between functions).

important_terms.meaning: A Bayesian method that treats functions as random objects, giving you a distribution over possible functions and uncertainty for each prediction.
A way to write dynamics that explicitly tracks energy storage, dissipation (energy lost), and how subsystems connect to each other.
A model built so that physical laws are wired into its structure, rather than added as penalties or soft constraints.
A mathematical function showing how a linear system responds when you give it a single brief input; used to embed physics knowledge into the similarity measures that Gaussian processes use.
The behavior that happens in a learned hidden layer or compressed representation, such as the code space of a variational autoencoder.

stanford_connections: This lecture joins uncertainty-aware learning with dynamics that preserve physical structure.
It builds on symplectic and Hamiltonian learning talks in the series by adding Bayesian uncertainty estimates.
It also connects to talks on physics-informed kernels and Green's-function views elsewhere in the seminar series.
practical_caution: A physics-based structure only works if the real system actually follows that structure. If your physical assumptions don't match the true system, the model can be very confident in predictions that are systematically biased in the same wrong direction every time.
selected_evidence: Physics-enhanced Gaussian processes.
Gaussian Process Port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-PHS).
Physically correct by design.
Distribution over all possible Port-Hamiltonian systems.
Green's function... included in the kernel function.
takeaway: The key insight is that you can bake both Bayesian uncertainty and physical structure into the model architecture itself, instead of bolting physics on as a penalty after training.

title: H. S. Udaykumar: Data-Driven Multi-Scale Simulations For Energetic Materials
speaker: H. S. Udaykumar
one_sentence: This lecture describes data-driven multiscale simulation for energetic materials, using machine-learning closures, surrogate models, deep learning, transfer learning, and multifidelity strategies to build structure-property-performance design loops.
core_problem: Energetic material sensitivity and performance depend on physics at nano, micro, meso, and macro scales. Atomistic simulations must inform mesoscale models, and mesoscale models must provide closures for macroscale response. Directly resolving all scales in practical design loops is impossible.
first_principles_model: Materials-by-design requires a structure-property-performance map: the link from material structure to properties to final performance.
