Multiscale simulation works upward: atomistic mechanisms inform mesoscale localization, mesoscale ensembles define closures (how to represent unresolved small-scale effects in the larger-scale model), and macroscale models predict performance. Machine learning supplies data-driven closures and surrogates that upscale unresolved localization physics and enable optimization over microstructures.
key_claims: Energetic material sensitivity requires upscaling physics from nano-, micro-, and meso-scales to macro-scale response.
Atomistic simulations must inform mesoscale models; mesoscale models must provide closures (learned models of unresolved effects) for macroscale simulations.
Machine-learning algorithms can provide data-driven closures for unresolved subgrid localization physics.
Materials-by-design depends on structure-property-performance relationships.
Surrogate modeling with ensembles of mesoscale calculations is one route to structure-property-performance design.
Deep learning, transfer learning, and multifidelity modeling (combining simulations of different accuracy and cost) can accelerate learning across related energetic materials.

important_terms.meaning: A material that stores and releases chemical energy rapidly, used in propellants, explosives, and related systems.
Passing information from simulations at one physical scale to models at a larger scale.
A learned model that represents unresolved small-scale effects in a larger-scale simulation.
The chain from material structure to material properties to final performance.
Combining data or simulations of different accuracy levels and computational costs.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects materials microstructure machine learning with multiscale closure learning.
It complements industrial digital-twin and manufacturing talks by focusing on design loops for materials.
It reinforces the closure theme: unresolved physics must be summarized accurately at each step up for higher-scale prediction.
practical_caution: Transferring knowledge between energetic materials is useful but risky. Similar material families can still differ in sensitivity mechanisms, so transfer learning needs validation across all scales.
selected_evidence: Telescoping physics from the nano- and micro- and meso-scales.
Meso-scale models must provide closure to macro-scale simulations.
Data-driven closures which upscale key (localization) physics.
Structure-property-performance (S-P-P) relationships.
Transfer learning and multi-fidelity modeling strategies.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that materials-by-design is a multiscale closure problem: you must represent unresolved small-scale physics accurately at each step up. Machine learning is most valuable when it carries the right unresolved physics upward.

title: Amir Arzani: A Flexible And Generalizable XAI Framework For Scientific Deep Learning
speaker: Amir Arzani
one_sentence: This lecture presents an interpretable XAI method for scientific deep learning that probes trained networks, fits sparse integral-equation models, and improves how well models work on new data outside their training set.
core_problem: Scientific deep learning often lacks interpretability and fails when given inputs unlike those in the training data, because training data rarely cover the full range of features the model might encounter. Models that predict well on familiar data often give little explanation or guidance on how to extrapolate to new conditions.
first_principles_model: The method treats a trained neural network as a source of learned local patterns. First, probe the network within the feature space it saw during training. Then fit an interpretable substitute model from a library of integral equations (equations that sum up effects using kernels and nonlinearities), using sparse regression to select a small, compact model. This interpretable model can be used when building a system or after training to explain what a network learned, and works like a simpler, more understandable version of operator learning (mapping inputs to outputs using learned rules).
key_claims: Interpretability and generalization are central challenges in scientific deep learning.
Out-of-distribution inference errors grow because physics-based learning tasks often cannot generate exhaustive datasets.
The proposed XAI method can be used at design time or after training with trained networks.
The method probes a trained neural network within the input space it saw during training.
A sparse library of integral equations is fitted to produce an interpretable model.
The approach relates to neural operators but trades some prediction power for analytical interpretability.

important_terms.meaning: Methods that make model predictions understandable to humans so we can see why the model makes its choices.
Prediction on inputs that fall outside the range of the data the model trained on.
An explanation method applied after a trained model has already been built to show what it learned.
A collection of candidate integral-equation forms used to build interpretable rules that map inputs to outputs.
A regression method that picks out only the most important terms from a large list of possible predictors.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects explainability with neural operators, Green's functions (solutions to differential equations that show how effects spread), and sparse regression methods that pick important terms.
It complements Miles Cranmer's scientific-debt talk by offering a path to write down equations that match what a network learned.
It also links to out-of-distribution reliability, a recurring issue in surrogate models and digital twins (virtual copies of real systems).
practical_caution: An interpretable substitute explains what the probed network learned, not necessarily the true physical system itself. The explanation should be tested against real physical measurements and physical rules that must hold true.
selected_evidence: Lack of interpretability and generalization are key challenges.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inference.
Applied in either by-design or post-hoc fashions.
Library of integral equations.
Sparse regression similar to SINDy.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific explanation can be learned as a sparse operator approximation of a trained network, but it must still be tested against actual physics.

title: Khalid Jawed: Reduced Order Modeling And Inverse Design Of Flexible Structures
speaker: Khalid Jawed
one_sentence: This lecture creates reduced models for highly deformable structures and solves inverse design problems for shape-morphing systems using neural networks and neural ODE ideas.
core_problem: Highly deformable structures involve nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material behavior. Full fine-grained simulations can be expensive, while inverse design for target 3D shapes requires finding which design choices or actuations work—a search that can take many cycles across complex local decisions.
first_principles_model: A flexible structure may have a lower-dimensional representation that captures its dominant deformation. For a slinky, the helix axis can serve as a reduced state instead of the full helical rod. A neural network trained on Discrete Elastic Rod simulations stores the effective elastic forces in that reduced representation. Neural ODE ideas then let the reduced dynamics be simulated efficiently. For morphing structures, neural networks map design or actuation choices to target shapes for inverse design.
key_claims: Highly deformable structures require simulation tools for nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material behavior.
Neural networks can reduce variables and accelerate simulation by orders of magnitude.
A slinky's deformation can often be captured by its helix axis as a reduced-order representation.
Neural networks can store elastic forces in the reduced representation.
Training data can come from fine-grained Discrete Elastic Rod simulations.
Shape-morphing structures motivate inverse design from planar patterns to target 3D shapes.

important_terms.meaning: A structure that undergoes large shape changes requiring nonlinear mechanics.
A lower-dimensional description that captures the dominant structural state.
A neural model representing continuous-time dynamics through differential equations.
A method for simulating slender elastic structures such as rods, ropes, and helices.
Finding design variables that produce a desired target behavior or shape.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects reduced-order models, neural ODEs, and inverse design in a tangible mechanics setting.
It complements manufacturing and materials talks because geometry, fabrication, and mechanics interact.
Good reduced variables often come from physical insight, not only from data compression.
practical_caution: A reduced structural coordinate is valid only when it captures the deformation modes used in deployment. If the structure bends, twists, contacts, or buckles outside the training regime, the learned reduced force law may fail.
selected_evidence: Highly deformable structures... nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material.
Reduce the number of variables and speed up the simulation by orders of magnitude.
The axis of the helix is a reduced-order representation.
Neural ordinary differential equations.
Discrete Elastic Rods (DER).
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that inverse design of flexible structures starts with the right reduced mechanical coordinates. Neural networks accelerate the force law once the representation is physically meaningful.

title: Eleni Chatzi: Twinning And Model Discovery For Engineered Systems
speaker: Eleni Chatzi
one_sentence: This lecture frames structural health monitoring and digital twinning as hybrid model-discovery problems where data-driven sensing must be integrated with mechanics to assess, forecast, and act on engineered structures.
core_problem: Modern engineered structures are interconnected, exposed to variable loads, and operated in harsh environments. Basic SHM—structural health monitoring, a sensing and analysis method to detect damage—can alert you to problems, but higher-level tasks such as measuring damage size, predicting how long a structure will last, and planning maintenance require more than fitting numbers to sensor data, because the monitored structure must be represented as it actually is now and under future stresses.
first_principles_model: A structural twin is a live representation of a physical asset. Sparse sensors provide measurements, while mechanics-based models spread that information to unmeasured locations and future conditions. Model discovery identifies damage, material properties, or structural states that make the model match reality. The twin becomes actionable when it can detect damage, locate it, measure it, predict future performance, and suggest maintenance decisions.
key_claims: SHM tasks form a hierarchy: first detect damage, then locate it, then measure it, then predict remaining useful life.
Purely data-driven methods fall short for higher-level SHM tasks such as damage measurement and remaining-life prediction.
Digital twins of monitored structures require physics-based representations grounded in mechanics.
Hybrid SHM can represent a structure as it actually is rather than only as it was designed.
Augmented twin representations can anticipate performance under future stressors.
A useful twin should recommend preventive and repair actions, not only display measurements.

important_terms.meaning: Sensing and modeling methods for detecting, locating, measuring, and predicting damage in structures.
A digital twin updated with data from sensors and built on physics-based representations of the actual structure.
The remaining useful time a system has before degradation or failure becomes unacceptable.
Estimating structural response across the entire object from a small number of sensor measurements.
Learning model parts, states, or properties that explain the observed behavior of a structure.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects digital twins, SHM, uncertainty, and model discovery in a deployment-oriented structural setting.
It complements guided-wave SHM by moving from damage detection and location toward prediction and action.
It also links to ROM and surrogate model talks because twins need fast but mechanics-aware representations.
practical_caution: A dashboard displaying sensor data is not a digital twin. Higher-level SHM needs mechanics, uncertainty accounting, and future-load reasoning before it can reliably support maintenance decisions.
selected_evidence: SHM comprises a hierarchy... detect, localize and quantify damage.
Offer a prognosis over the system's residual life.
Purely data-driven methods are found to be lacking.
Furnishing a digital twin of a monitored structure.
Augmented twin representations... anticipating performance under future stressors.
takeaway: The core lesson is that twinning combines three things: state estimation (what is the structure now), mechanics (how will it behave), and decision support (what should we do). Sensors alone do not create a useful twin.

title: Lu Lu: Deep Neural Operators With Reliable Extrapolation
speaker: Lu Lu
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to build neural operators (neural networks that learn transformations between functions, not just numbers) that work well beyond the data they learned from, especially for problems involving multiple physical systems and different scales.
core_problem: Neural operators can learn how to solve complex systems, but deep learning tends to work best when guessing answers for data similar to what it saw during training. Real science needs to predict what happens in new regimes—different physical conditions, different accuracy levels, new kinds of inputs, and problems where different physical laws interact—where a simple neural operator might give wrong answers without warning.
first_principles_model: DeepONet builds operators by using two separate networks: one that reads in the input function and one that evaluates at specific locations, then combines their answers. Variants of this idea extend it to handle problems where multiple physical systems interact, use reduced representations (proper orthogonal decomposition, which picks out the most important patterns), handle multiple inputs at once, use patterns from Fourier analysis, and combine data that has different levels of cost and accuracy. To make extrapolation trustworthy, you need to understand how hard it is to move outside the training regime and create checks that catch or reduce that risk.
key_claims: Neural networks can learn nonlinear operators—transformations between functions—not just mappings from numbers to numbers.
DeepONet can learn operators that represent both deterministic equations (rules with no randomness) and stochastic equations (rules with randomness).
DeepM&Mnet extends operator learning to problems where different physical systems interact.
POD-DeepONet combines proper orthogonal decomposition (a method to find the most important patterns in data) with operator learning.
MIONet handles multiple-input operators, while multifidelity DeepONet mixes data from sources that have different costs and accuracies.
For science to trust these models, you need to measure how hard extrapolation is and build workflows that detect problems or improve predictions outside the training range.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network designed to learn transformations from functions to functions, using a branch network that encodes inputs and a trunk network that encodes evaluation points.
A version of DeepONet that first uses proper orthogonal decomposition (a method to compress data by keeping only the most important patterns) before applying the operator network.
A neural operator network built to handle operators with multiple inputs.
Training a model using data from different sources that have different costs (some cheap and approximate, some expensive and accurate).
A measurement or description of how hard it is for a model to make correct predictions when it encounters data or situations outside its training domain.

stanford_connections: This talk adds depth to neural-operator discussions beyond Fourier neural operators, specifically covering the DeepONet family of methods.
It connects to Anima Anandkumar's operator talk through learning in function spaces, with a focus on whether predictions stay reliable beyond training data.
It also ties to other talks in the series on multifidelity methods, multiscale problems, and situations where multiple physical systems interact.
practical_caution: Learning operators does not automatically solve the extrapolation problem. A model can work perfectly on the functions it learned from but fail when it meets new physics, new scales, or interactions it wasn't trained on.
selected_evidence: Deep operator network (DeepONet).
DeepM&Mnet for multiphysics problems.
POD-DeepONet.
Multifidelity DeepONet.
Quantify the extrapolation complexity.
takeaway: The real lesson is that neural operators should be judged not just by how well they fit known data, but by which types of new problems they can handle correctly.

title: Krishna Garikipati: Fokker-Planck Inverse Reinforcement Learning
speaker: Krishna Garikipati
one_sentence: This lecture connects inverse reinforcement learning (inferring why an agent behaves as it does) with Fokker-Planck mean-field dynamics (how probability spreads in random systems) to infer both reward and transition functions from observed noisy trajectories.
core_problem: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer a reward function from observed agent behavior, but most IRL methods assume the transition function (the rule for how states change) is already known. In many scientific and biological systems, such as cancer cell dynamics, the transition rules themselves are hidden and must be figured out at the same time as the reward.
first_principles_model: An MDP (Markov Decision Process: a model with states, actions, probabilities of state changes, rewards, and decision rules) describes how an agent makes choices. If agent motion in state-action space follows SDEs (stochastic differential equations: rules with random noise), then the resulting probability density (the likelihood of being in each state) evolves according to a Fokker-Planck equation (a differential equation for probability flow). The lecture proposes that time-discrete Fokker-Planck dynamics and MDP structure are mathematically equivalent, allowing FP-IRL to simultaneously infer the transition rules, reward values, and decision policy from observed trajectories using variational system identification (fitting a model by optimizing an objective function based on weak mathematical forms).
key_claims: IRL estimates an unknown reward function from observed agent trajectories.
Most IRL methods require a transition function that is known or estimated beforehand.
When transition dynamics are unknown, inferring both reward and dynamics becomes much harder.
Random motion in state-action space can be represented at the average level by the Fokker-Planck equation.
A time-discrete Fokker-Planck to MDP correspondence can enable physics-aware IRL.
FP-IRL can simultaneously infer transition and reward functions from observed trajectories.

important_terms.meaning: Finding the reward function that explains why an agent chooses the actions it does.
A model with states (current situation), actions (choices), transition probabilities (odds of moving to the next state), rewards, and policies (rules for picking actions).
A differential equation that describes how a probability density (the spread of likely outcomes) changes over time in a random system.
The rule that says, given your current state and action, what are the odds of reaching each next state.
Discovering system rules by adjusting parameters to minimize a math objective based on weak forms of the equations.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects stochastic dynamics (random motion over time), inverse problems (inferring hidden inputs from outputs), and reinforcement learning (learning to act) in a science-driven setting.
It complements talks on Fokker-Planck equations, SDEs, and stochastic model reduction elsewhere in the seminar series.
It demonstrates a key theme: using physics structure to make a learning problem solvable when otherwise it would be ambiguous.
practical_caution: Inferring reward from behavior is inherently ambiguous—multiple different rewards can produce the same actions. Physics constraints can reduce this ambiguity, but the inferred reward should not be treated as the true cause without checking it against real-world knowledge from the field.
selected_evidence: Inverse Reinforcement Learning... revealing the rationale underlying the behavior of autonomous agents.
Estimate the unknown reward function... from observed agent trajectories.
IRL needs a transition function.
Fokker-Planck (FP) equation.
Simultaneously infer the transition and reward functions using only observed trajectories.
takeaway: The core lesson is that behavior inference requires knowing both the goal (reward) and the rules (dynamics). Fokker-Planck structure gives IRL the missing part: it models how the system's state spreads over time.

title: Alice Cicirello: Integrating Physics Knowledge In Machine Learning Strategies
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This lecture organizes physics-informed machine learning around four ways to inject physics: through the data itself, through the model's built-in structure, through how you train it, and through a separate model that captures what the physics equations got wrong, using friction-force identification as an example.
core_problem: ML models trained only from data often fail when predicting new situations, make unrealistic predictions that violate physics, and work poorly with limited measurements. Real engineering problems have partial physics knowledge—some equations you know, some you don't—plus noisy measurements and limited data. The question is: where and how should you feed physics knowledge into your learning process?
first_principles_model: Physics knowledge can enter machine learning in four places. Observational bias changes the data by selecting or creating measurements that physics tells you matter. Inductive bias builds physics constraints, symmetries, conservation rules, or boundaries directly into the model's structure. Learning bias modifies the training procedure—the loss function (what you tell the model to minimize), hard constraints it must satisfy, or how you search for the best model. Discrepancy bias adds a separate model that captures known gaps between your partial physics equations and what you actually observe. Friction identification shows how sparse system identification (finding which forces matter most) and Gaussian processes (a method that represents uncertainty in predictions) can use all four types of bias.
key_claims: Physics knowledge improves prediction on new data when you have small to medium amounts of training data and can enforce that predictions stay physically consistent even with large data.
Training only on data without physics can introduce observational bias (the data you have is misleading) and physically impossible predictions.
Observational bias can be controlled by using physics-informed data sources or artificially creating new training examples that physics tells you should exist.
Inductive bias embeds prior knowledge such as boundaries, conservation laws (like energy or momentum), and symmetries (unchanged behavior under transformations) into the model's structure.
Learning bias changes the training process: the loss function you minimize, hard rules the model must obey, or the algorithm you use to find the best model.
Discrepancy bias uses partial physics knowledge or corrects for known gaps between idealized equations and real data, as shown through friction-force identification.

important_terms.meaning: Physics-informed choices about which data to collect, which to create artificially, or which to emphasize when training a model.
A built-in restriction or assumption that the model carries from the start, baked into its structure or how it represents information.
Physics information introduced through the loss function (what you minimize), hard constraints the model must satisfy, or the optimization method itself.
A separate model trained to correct for known gaps or errors between an imperfect physics model and real observations.
Estimating friction forces or friction laws in a moving system from data and physics constraints, often when friction is the main unknown.

stanford_connections: This lecture provides a clear taxonomy that unifies earlier talks on physics-informed machine learning, physics-guided machine learning, and physics-enhanced machine learning.
It connects to PINNs (physics-informed neural networks), sparse system identification (finding the few most important forces), Gaussian-process methods with physics priors, and discrepancy modeling.
It gives precise language for deciding where physics should enter a model, moving beyond vague advice to simply 'add physics'.
practical_caution: Adding physics knowledge the wrong way can fail or mislead. For example, adding a penalty term (a soft rule) in your loss function may be much weaker than building a hard constraint into the model's structure when a physical law must absolutely never be broken.
selected_evidence: Four different biases... observational, inductive, learning, and discrepancy.
Poor generalization performance and extrapolation.
Physically inconsistent or impossible prediction.
Friction forces in a dynamical system.
Sparse system identification... Gaussian Processes.
takeaway: The core lesson is that physics can enter at four points: the data, the model's structure, how you train it, and the discrepancy model. Good physics-informed machine learning (SciML) chooses where to insert physics knowledge deliberately rather than adding it everywhere.

title: Jinlong Wu: Data-Driven Closure Modeling Using Derivative-Free Kalman Methods
speaker: Jinlong Wu
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to use derivative-free Kalman methods (techniques that update estimates without computing derivatives) to learn what happens to a system's large-scale variables when small-scale details can't be tracked, using limited and indirect measurements.
core_problem: Real systems like turbulent flows and cloud formation have far too many moving parts to track every single one. Instead, you have to describe what the small-scale details do to the large-scale flow you can see—this description is the closure model. But making good closures is hard: traditional methods don't capture the real physics well enough, they need to be tuned by hand for each case, and learning from data gets even harder when measurements are indirect, sparse, or noisy.
first_principles_model: A closure takes what you can observe directly—the large-scale variables—and predicts what the unobserved small-scale motion does to them. Kalman inversion methods treat the unknown parts of the closure as hidden states and update them using ensemble-based data assimilation, which means combining many parallel estimates to gradually fit them to the data without ever computing derivatives. This lets you learn closures from measurements that don't directly show what you want to learn, and it extends the method from simple deterministic closures to richer ones that include randomness and sparsity.
key_claims: Closure models are essential in complex systems because simulating every tiny motion is impossible.
Current closure models are not good enough, partly because they can't capture enough detail and partly because hand-tuning each one is impractical.
Derivative-free Kalman methods can learn closure models even from measurements that don't directly show closure behavior.
This approach works for simple deterministic closures.
The same method also handles sparse identification—picking out which terms in the equations actually matter.
Derivative-free Kalman inversion can even learn closures with randomness built in, from indirect measurements.

important_terms.meaning: A description of how the small-scale motion you can't track affects the large-scale motion you can see.
A way to update estimates using many parallel copies of the system, comparing them to real data, without ever calculating derivatives.
Measurements of one thing that you use to infer something else—like measuring wind speed at one height to understand turbulence you can't see directly.
Learning what equation or closure describes a system by finding which terms are active and which can be ignored.
A closure model that includes randomness—describing not just the average effect of small-scale motion, but its unpredictable part too.

stanford_connections: This lecture builds on the closure ideas from LES (large-eddy simulation), reduced-order models, and structure-preserving closures discussed earlier in the seminar.
It uses data assimilation—the practice of blending measurements with models—in the same way that Kalman filters do, but to learn closure parameters instead of just estimating state.
It connects to SINDy and sparse system identification, which are methods to learn simple, interpretable equations and closures from data.
practical_caution: Derivative-free methods skip the work of computing derivatives, but they don't fix the deeper problem of identifiability: if your indirect measurements are weak, many completely different closure models might fit the data equally well. You need to check whether the learned model is actually unique.
selected_evidence: Closure problems are critical in predicting complex dynamical systems.
Derivative-free Kalman methods.
Learn closure models from indirect and limited amount of data.
Sparse identification of dynamical systems.
Learning of stochastic closures.
takeaway: The underlying principle is this: closure learning is really just inference from incomplete evidence. Kalman-based methods give you a way to do that inference without gradients—useful when your data never directly show the closures you're trying to learn.

title: Christopher Rackauckas: Generalizing SciML And Differentiable Simulation Beyond Continuous Models
speaker: Christopher Rackauckas
organization: JuliaHub / Pumas AI / MIT Julia Lab
one_sentence: This lecture argues that scientific machine learning and differentiable simulation should go beyond ordinary differential equations (equations describing how things change smoothly over time) and partial differential equations to include jump processes (sudden discrete events), stochastic simulations (random outcomes), agent-based models (many actors following rules), particle filters (methods for tracking uncertainty), and differentiable Bayesian computation (computing probabilities while recording how to improve them).
core_problem: Much scientific machine learning has focused on continuous models—ordinary and partial differential equations where change happens smoothly. But real scientific simulation also includes discontinuities (sudden changes), stochastic events (random outcomes), agents (independent actors), particle filters (sequential probability tracking), MCMC (Markov chain methods for exploring probability distributions), and hybrid forms mixing discrete and continuous parts. Differentiating through these systems (computing how to adjust them to match data) introduces mathematical, numerical stability, and practical coding challenges that differ from the adjoint methods (reverse-mode calculation) used for smooth differential equations.
first_principles_model: Differentiable simulation means building a simulator you can train—adjusting unknown functions or numbers inside it to match observed data. If a scientific model has unknown pieces, you can swap them for neural networks or other trainable pieces, as long as you can compute gradients (the calculus that shows how to adjust the unknown pieces to improve fit). Extending this beyond smooth models means computing gradients through randomness, events that happen at specific moments, discrete choices, chaotic behavior, and algorithms that do inference (estimate hidden states from data).
key_claims: Scientific machine learning has successfully incorporated ordinary and partial differential equations into deep learning through differentiable simulation.
Scientific simulation also includes jump diffusions (processes combining random drift with sudden events), agent-based models, and other non-continuous forms.
Differentiable simulation can be generalized to chaotic simulations (sensitive to initial conditions) and stochastic simulations (involving randomness).
Particle filters and agent-based models require specific differentiation approaches not available for smooth equations.
Bayesian inverse problems (inferring unknown parameters from data) can require differentiating MCMC methods themselves.
As differentiable programming spreads to new domains, numerical stability and implementation issues become central concerns.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation built so you can compute gradients through it—the calculus showing how to adjust unknown parameters to improve fit to data.
A stochastic process that combines smooth random drift (diffusion) with sudden discrete events (jumps).
A simulation of many interacting actors, each following their own local rules, producing collective behavior.
A sequential method for estimating hidden states in random systems by maintaining many sample trajectories and reweighting them as new data arrives.
Treating Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms or their results in a way that allows gradients to flow through them for learning.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends the automatic differentiation and differentiable programming thread from earlier sessions.

It connects to FP-IRL (inverse reinforcement learning from data), stochastic generative models, and Bayesian inverse problems because all require computing gradients through non-standard simulation loops.
It also offers a software perspective on making scientific machine learning general and practical rather than limited to differential equations only.
practical_caution: A gradient through a stochastic or discrete simulator can give biased results, become numerically unstable, or depend on implementation choices. You must match your differentiation method to the mathematical object you're actually trying to optimize.
selected_evidence: Generalizing scientific learning and differentiable simulation beyond continuous models.
Jump diffusions, agent-based models.
Differentiating stochastic simulations like particle filters.
Differentiation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods.
Numerical stability issues, implementation issues.
takeaway: The foundational insight is that scientific machine learning must differentiate through scientific computation in all its forms, not only smooth differential equation solvers.

title: Elnaz Rezaian: Data-Driven Balancing Transformation For Predictive Model Order Reduction
speaker: Elnaz Rezaian
one_sentence: This lecture covers balanced truncation and data-driven methods for building small models from big systems for control, focusing on error bounds and the challenges when you have many inputs and outputs.
core_problem: Small predictive models can run fast but often break in real engineering if they miss how inputs connect to outputs or don't guarantee how wrong they are. Balanced truncation gives you mathematical promises about accuracy, but computing it directly or from data can be slow when your system has many inputs and outputs.
first_principles_model: Balanced truncation finds states that are reachable (the system can get there from inputs) and observable (you can see them in the outputs), then deletes states that barely affect input-output behavior. Data-driven versions like ERA build small models by measuring how the system responds to impulses. The result is a model tuned for control goals and comes with mathematical error bounds, but making it scale up needs techniques like tangential interpolation (asking the system about specially chosen directions), output decomposition (breaking the outputs into smaller pieces), and gappy POD-style approximations (filling in missing data).
key_claims: Balanced truncation grows from control theory and is built specifically for steering systems.

Data-driven balancing uses measured Gramians (matrices that capture reachability and observability from data) and minimum realization theory (finding the smallest model that matches the input-output measurements).
Mathematical error bounds let balanced models work reliably for actual predictions.
The eigensystem realization algorithm is a direct data-driven approach to balanced truncation.
ERA predicts well on stiff fast-burning chemical flows and sound-driven systems.
Many input-output channels mean more computation, so you need tangential interpolation, output decomposition, and gappy POD.

important_terms.meaning: A model reduction method that deletes states with low combined reachability (how far the system can be steered from inputs) and observability (how much they show up in outputs).
A matrix that measures how reachable or observable a dynamical system is based on its structure and properties.
A data-driven method that builds a small state-space model by analyzing how the system responds to impulse inputs.
A number in the sequence of impulse-response values used to reconstruct what a system does.
A method to reconstruct fields from partial or scattered measurements using basis vectors derived from proper orthogonal decomposition.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds a control-theory perspective on small models to the broader model reduction sequence.
It connects to predictive models, reverse engineering, and digital twins because error bounds are needed before you can trust the model in real use.
It also builds on CUR and adaptive ROM talks by emphasizing input-output balancing instead of only compressing which states matter.
practical_caution: A small model can still predict badly if it removes states that matter for outputs or for steering the system. Reduction should focus on the input-output task you actually care about, not just which states have the most energy.
selected_evidence: Balanced truncation and data-driven variations.
Empirical system Gramians.
Theoretical error bounds.
Eigensystem realization algorithm (ERA).
Gappy POD approach to address this bottleneck.
takeaway: The core lesson is that small predictive models should keep track of what the system can be pushed toward and what you can see, not just what vibrates the loudest.

title: Michael Glinsky: A Physics-Based ROM Capturing The Topology Of Dynamical Manifolds
speaker: Michael E. Glinsky
one_sentence: This lecture presents a physics-based reduced-order model (a fast approximation of expensive simulations) inspired by scattering transforms, renormalization ideas, and projections that preserve the geometric structure of dynamical manifolds (the low-dimensional surfaces on which dynamics evolve).
core_problem: High-energy-density physics simulations like pulsed power liner implosions are expensive and highly nonlinear, yet practical work needs fast surrogates. A model that only interpolates state vectors (numbers describing the system at one moment) may miss the manifold topology (the qualitative shape of the low-dimensional surface) and scale-dependent structure of how the dynamics evolve.
first_principles_model: The proposed Heisenberg Scattering Transformation applies a structured deep convolutional transform inspired by Mallat's scattering transform (a wavelet-based method that builds stable hierarchical representations) and a Hamiltonian generating functional (a physics-based mathematical object encoding how the system evolves). It projects dynamics into a renormalization or S-matrix basis (coordinates where scales of physics appear naturally) where the evolution stays confined to a low-dimensional complex linear subspace (a flat space of lower dimension). PCA (Principal Component Analysis, finding the main directions in data) identifies this subspace, and an encoder-decoder neural network quantifies topology through an analytic function (a function smooth enough that calculus works on it) on that space.
key_claims: The approach is inspired by Mallat's scattering transformation (a wavelet-based hierarchical method) and a canonical Heisenberg-style perspective on how dynamics work.
A logarithmic generating functional of the Hamiltonian (a physics-based mathematical tool) operates on the system state or statistical distribution.
The transform projects dynamics onto a renormalization or scattering-matrix basis (coordinates where different scales of physics appear naturally).
The low-dimensional complex linear subspace can be identified with PCA (Principal Component Analysis).
Topology is quantified using a neural network with decoder/encoder structure that approximates an analytic function (a smooth, well-behaved mathematical function) on the subspace.
The method is applied as a fast surrogate for 2D pulsed power liner implosions, including MagLIF (Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion).

important_terms.meaning: A structured wavelet-based convolutional transform that builds stable hierarchical representations by repeated filtering at different scales.
This talk's proposed physics-based transform for representing dynamics in a renormalization or scattering basis where scales appear naturally.
A set of coordinates where the structure of physics at different scales (how solutions look across small and large distances) appears naturally.
The qualitative geometric structure of the low-dimensional surface on which the system's evolution happens, including how it twists and folds.
Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion; a pulsed-power approach to fusion where an imploding metal cylinder compresses fuel at extreme density.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects manifold learning (finding low-dimensional representations of data), reduced-order models (fast approximations), topology (geometric structure), and physics-based transforms.

It complements earlier work on charting dynamics and information geometry (the geometry of probability distributions) by showing that the reduced space has real geometric structure, not just coordinates.
It also links to high-energy-density surrogate modeling (creating fast approximations of expensive simulations), where preserving structure matters for predictions to stay accurate.
practical_caution: Topology-aware transforms are effective but specialized. The assumed transform structure must match the actual physics; otherwise the model can preserve the wrong geometric features and fail in realistic scenarios.
selected_evidence: Physics-based reduced order model capturing the topology of dynamic manifolds.
Scattering Transformation.
Renormalization Basis.
Principal Component Analysis.
Fast surrogate model for 2D pulsed power liner implosions (MagLIF).
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that some models must preserve dynamical topology (the actual geometric shape where dynamics live) and scale structure, not just minimize projection error (the gap between the original and simplified versions).

title: Mengwu Guo: Probabilistic Methods for Data-Driven Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Mengwu Guo
one_sentence: This lecture explains how probabilistic reduced-order modeling can make data-driven digital twins fast while also quantifying uncertainty.
core_problem: Digital twins and multi-query simulations need models that run much faster than full-order solvers. A deterministic surrogate can be fast but overconfident, especially when the online input leaves the region covered by offline simulations.
first_principles_model: A reduced-order model shrinks a high-dimensional physical system into a lower-dimensional representation. Probabilistic ROMs add uncertainty to this shrinking and prediction process. Gaussian process regression treats the full-order solver as an offline tool and builds a simulation-free online surrogate. Deep kernel learning uses neural networks inside manifold Gaussian processes to discover low-dimensional latent dynamics from noisy high-dimensional images. Bayesian operator inference estimates reduced operators from data while keeping the projected reduced-state equation form and adding regularization and uncertainty estimates.
key_claims: Probabilistic ROMs are useful when fast simulation must also report computational credibility.
Gaussian process reduced-order surrogate modeling uses full-order solvers offline for data generation and avoids simulation online.
Deep kernel learning can combine neural representation learning with Gaussian process uncertainty.
Bayesian reduced-order operator inference is a method that estimates reduced operators without requiring full-order solver internals, and its estimates come with uncertainty bounds.
Bayesian inference naturally embeds penalty-based regularization and uncertainty quantification.
The three methods span different levels of access to physics structure, from treating the solver as unknown, to partially visible, to fully known.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that represents uncertainty in predictions, operators, latent states, or model error.
A probabilistic regression method that gives both a mean prediction and predictive uncertainty.
A hybrid method that uses neural networks to learn features or latent coordinates used by a kernel model.
A method for estimating reduced dynamical operators from data using Bayesian priors and posterior uncertainty.
A penalty-based regularization method that stabilizes ill-posed inverse or regression problems.

stanford_connections: This talk connects ROMs, surrogate modeling, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins.
It complements operator inference and neural operator lectures by asking how much physics structure the learner should retain.
It also links to active learning and experimental design because posterior uncertainty can guide where new simulations are most valuable.
practical_caution: A posterior distribution is only as credible as the model class, priors, and training coverage. A simulation-free online surrogate can produce incorrect predictions when the input falls outside the region where training data existed.
selected_evidence: Gaussian process regression.
The online stage is entirely simulation-free.
Bayesian reduced-order operator inference.
A naturally embedded Tikhonov regularization together with a quantification of modeling uncertainties.
Deep kernel learning.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a useful ROM for deployment should be fast, structurally grounded when possible, and honest about uncertainty.

title: Nicolas Boulle: Elliptic PDE Learning Is Provably Data-Efficient
speaker: Nicolas Boulle
one_sentence: This lecture explains why learning to predict solutions of elliptic PDEs (steady-state physics equations) can work well with surprisingly little training data.
core_problem: PDE learning often appears data-efficient in practice, but without theory it is hard to know whether this is an accident of the test cases or a consequence of mathematical structure in the equations themselves. The question is: why can a model learn an unknown physical solution map from relatively few input-output examples?
first_principles_model: For an elliptic PDE, the object being learned is not one solution but a solution operator: a map from source terms, coefficients, or inputs to solutions. Elliptic operators (steady-state equations like those describing heat distribution at equilibrium) have smoothing and compactness properties that make their solution maps lower-complexity than arbitrary function-to-function maps. The lecture explains how PDE regularity (smoothness guaranteed by the equation type and boundary conditions) and randomized numerical linear algebra (algorithms that use random sampling to approximate large matrix operations) can be combined to recover these operators with error dropping exponentially as the number of training examples increases.
key_claims: PDE learning can be viewed as approximating solution operators—maps between function spaces—rather than fitting a single function to points.
Elliptic PDEs provide structure that makes this operator-learning problem much more data-efficient than generic regression.
The theoretical result explains why error shrinks exponentially with respect to training dataset size.
The proof combines prior PDE theory with randomized numerical linear algebra.
The theory may inform better dataset construction and neural operator architecture design.
The result should be read as structure-specific, not as a universal guarantee for all PDE learning.

important_terms.meaning: A class of partial differential equations, often describing steady-state or equilibrium phenomena, with strong smoothness and damping properties.
The mapping from a PDE input such as a forcing function to the corresponding solution.
Error reduction that improves exponentially fast as a resource—here, training examples—increases.
Algorithms that use random sampling or projections to approximate large matrix and operator computations efficiently.
Mathematical smoothness properties of PDE solutions implied by the equation class and boundary conditions.

stanford_connections: This talk is a theoretical counterpart to neural operator and operator-learning lectures.
It connects sample efficiency to physical structure rather than only to network size.
It also reinforces the recurring theme that the right starting assumption for the learning problem can turn a high-dimensional problem into a tractable operator approximation task.
practical_caution: The guarantee is tied to elliptic PDE assumptions. Hyperbolic, chaotic, discontinuous, or poorly observed systems may not inherit the same data efficiency.
selected_evidence: We aim to approximate solution operators.
We want to reach an exponential convergence rate.
The proof technique combines prior knowledge of PDE theory and randomized numerical linear algebra techniques.
Improving dataset and neural network architecture designs.
PDE learning is provably data-efficient.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that data efficiency often comes from structure in the physical operator itself, not from the learning algorithm alone.

title: Dimitrios Giannakis: Quantum Information and Data Science for Modeling Classical Dynamics
speaker: Dimitrios Giannakis
one_sentence: This lecture applies ideas from quantum information theory to extend operator-based methods for modeling classical dynamics.
core_problem: Koopman and transfer operators can turn nonlinear dynamics into linear equations by working in spaces of observables (quantities you measure) and probability densities (how likely different states are). But traditional classical methods rely on algebras where multiplying A then B gives the same result as B then A. The lecture asks: what do we gain by representing classical dynamics through quantum ideas, where the order of multiplication matters?
first_principles_model: A dynamical system changes states over time, but it also changes what we measure and how likely each outcome is. Koopman operators describe how the things we observe change, while transfer operators describe how the probability density changes. The talk rewrites these using multiplication operators and density operators—tools borrowed from quantum mechanics—which lets us handle data fitting and model closure in the same operator language. This approach enables numerical schemes that preserve physical meaning, like keeping densities nonnegative, and lets us build approximations from data using kernel methods.
key_claims: Koopman and transfer operators let you use linear techniques on nonlinear dynamics.
Quantum information provides a way to generalize how you represent observables and densities when multiplication order matters.
Probability densities can be written as density operators, which are mathematical objects borrowed from quantum mechanics.
Data fitting and dynamical closure fit into the same operator-based language.
Keeping densities and states nonnegative is crucial because they must stay physically valid.
Kernel methods provide a way to build the required operators directly from data.

important_terms.meaning: A linear operator that evolves observables (quantities you measure) in a nonlinear dynamical system.
An operator that evolves probability densities (how likely different states are) through dynamics.
An operator that represents a statistical state; borrowed from quantum mechanics and used here to describe classical distributions.
A set of mathematical rules where the order of multiplication matters—if you multiply A then B, you may not get the same answer as B then A.
A numerical method that keeps densities and state representations nonnegative so they stay physically meaningful.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends the operator-based approach across Koopman analysis, model closure, and kernel-based learning.
It bridges physics-informed machine learning with information geometry and quantum-inspired mathematical tools.
It also connects to weather and climate through assimilation examples and subgrid-scale closure problems.
practical_caution: The quantum analogy is a mathematical model, not a statement that the classical system behaves like a quantum one. The real value comes from whether the operator form preserves the right mathematical properties and makes computation faster or more accurate.
selected_evidence: Koopman and transfer operators.
Density operators.
Positivity-preserving function approximation.
Kernel methods for operator approximation.
Applications to data assimilation and subgrid-scale modeling.
takeaway: The core lesson is that switching how you represent observables and densities can make nonlinear dynamics appear more linear, organized, and easier to compute.

title: Jan Christoph: Predicting Heart Rhythm Disorders from Spatio-Temporal Imaging Data Using AI
speaker: Jan Christoph
one_sentence: This lecture explains how AI can infer hidden electrical waves in the heart from observable images of tissue motion.
core_problem: Heart rhythm disorders come from abnormal electrical waves moving through cardiac tissue. Current imaging cannot easily resolve the full three-dimensional pattern of electrical activity inside the heart wall. Doctors and researchers need a way to infer dangerous hidden electrical patterns from measurements that are easier to obtain, like motion or deformation images.
first_principles_model: Cardiac cells are electrically excitable nonlinear oscillators (cells that generate electrical pulses and respond by changing state). Their coordinated electrical pulses create reaction-diffusion waves (patterns that spread through tissue via local reactions and diffusion), and these electrical waves trigger mechanical contraction and deformation. If electrical activity leaves a measurable mechanical signature, then a model can learn the inverse map (work backward) from high-speed fluorescence or ultrasound imaging of deformation back to electrical dynamics. Ex vivo isolated-heart experiments (hearts removed from the body and kept functioning in controlled conditions) provide paired training data where both the hidden electrical state and visible mechanical motion can be measured.
key_claims: Heart rhythm disorders can be understood as abnormal nonlinear wave activity in cardiac tissue.
Electrical excitation and mechanical deformation are coupled, so motion images can contain information about electrical activity.
AI models can learn to predict electrical dynamics from spatiotemporal imaging data.
High-speed fluorescence and ultrasound imaging provide complementary data sources.
Ex vivo isolated-heart training enables supervised learning with paired electrical and mechanical measurements.
The goal is to better predict and understand the mechanisms of arrhythmia.

important_terms.meaning: The study of electrical activity in biological tissue, specifically in the heart.
A system where local chemical or electrical reactions and spatial spreading combine to create propagating waves or patterns.
Imaging that captures both spatial structure and how it changes over time.
A medical imaging technique that uses sound waves to observe tissue motion and structure.
Collection of training data using organs or tissue outside the living body in controlled experimental conditions.

stanford_connections: This talk connects physics-informed learning, inverse problems, and biomedical imaging.
It exemplifies a broader DDPS theme: inferring hidden states from observable proxy measurements.
It links nonlinear waves and reaction-diffusion dynamics to real clinical prediction problems.
practical_caution: A model trained ex vivo may not transfer directly to in vivo clinical settings. Differences in tissue conditions, imaging quality, patient variability, and medical interventions must be tested and validated.
selected_evidence: Predicting heart rhythm disorders from spatial temporal Imaging data using artificial intelligence.
Mechanical deformation pattern.
Predict a heart's electrical dynamics from its mechanical deformation.
Train AI ex vivo with isolated hearts.
Heart cells are electrically excitable nonlinear oscillators.
takeaway: When two physical processes connect (like electrical waves and mechanical motion), an invisible state can become inferable from a visible proxy signal.

title: Boris Kramer: Structure-Preserving Learning of High-Dimensional Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Systems
speaker: Boris Kramer
one_sentence: This lecture explains why reduced models of mechanical systems should preserve Lagrangian and Hamiltonian structure instead of only matching past data.
core_problem: High-dimensional mechanical systems are expensive to simulate, but naive learned reductions can break energy conservation, momentum conservation, symmetry, or stability. Such breaks may seem tiny over short time windows and then add up into poor predictions over long horizons.
first_principles_model: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics express how systems evolve through structured quantities like energy, momentum, and generalized coordinates (the minimal variables needed to describe the system's position). A structure-preserving learning pipeline first shrinks the dimension and then learns the motion in coordinates that keep the same mechanical form. By requiring the reduced model to follow this structure, the learner needs fewer examples and builds more stable and accurate predictions over long horizons than a model that just copies numbers without respecting the structure.
key_claims: Many scientific and engineering systems are naturally modeled by Lagrangian or Hamiltonian mechanics.
Quantities such as momentum, energy, and vorticity are not just measurements after the fact; they are woven into how the system works.
Structure-preserving reduced models can be applied to structural mechanics, soft robotics, and wave motion.
Preserving symmetry or positive definiteness (matrices that point in consistent directions) can improve accuracy over long prediction horizons.
Structured methods can need less training data than unstructured alternatives.
The goal is not just small error on past data but dynamics that stay stable and predictable far into the future.

important_terms.meaning: A way of writing how systems move based on kinetic energy (motion) minus potential energy (stored) and the idea that nature takes paths that make the total action (a sum of energies over time) stationary.
A way of writing how systems move based on total energy and how the system's state (position and velocity) evolves in a space where position and momentum are treated symmetrically.
A reduced-order model (a smaller approximation) designed to keep the physical or geometric structure of the original system intact.
Making guesses about what happens over periods where tiny structural errors add up into large failures in what actually occurs.
A property of matrices or operators (mathematical objects that transform data) that is often tied to stability, energy, and whether a problem has a well-defined solution.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together geometric mechanics (the math of shapes and symmetries), reduced models, learning operators (functions that transform whole functions), and scientific machine learning.
It complements thinking about symplectic structure (a way that preserves certain properties) and physics-informed learning by putting conservation and structure at the center.
It reinforces the seminar-wide theme that building in what you already know about the problem can reduce how much data you need to learn.
practical_caution: Structure preservation only helps if the structure you choose actually matches the system and how you split time into steps. Using the wrong mechanical form can create false confidence in predictions.
selected_evidence: Structure preserving learning of high dimensional lagrangian and hamiltonian systems.
Momentum, energy, vorticity.
Symmetry and positive definiteness is what gives us a long-term predictive accuracy.
Fewer training data than non-structured methods.
Stability, robustness, long-term predictive accuracy.
takeaway: The core lesson in mechanics is that respecting the shape of the equations matters more than fitting the next state alone.

title: Z. Zhang: DeepParticle: Learning Invariant Measure by a Deep Neural Network Minimizing Wasserstein Distance
speaker: Z. Zhang
one_sentence: This lecture shows DeepParticle, a method that learns parameterized invariant measures (long-time probability distributions) for high-dimensional particle systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs).
core_problem: High-dimensional PDEs with sharp fronts, steep gradients, or concentrated regions are hard for mesh-based methods. Particle-based methods that simulate interactions directly can handle these features better but become slow for long-time computations. The challenge: predict the behavior at expensive physical conditions without actually running the full particle simulation there.
first_principles_model: For Fisher-KPP fronts in flows without divergence, PDE theory reduces the speed calculation to finding the largest eigenvalue of an advection-diffusion operator (a number that controls how fast disturbances spread). The Feynman-Kac formula connects certain PDE quantities to paths of random particles, enabling a resampling-based particle algorithm whose distribution converges to a long-time invariant measure. DeepParticle learns a family of these invariant measures using a neural network whose inputs encode the Peclet number (the ratio of how fast particles move to how much they diffuse). The network is trained with a Wasserstein loss (how much effort to move probability mass from the network's output to the true distribution), using only moderate Peclet values where computation is cheap. This trains the network to predict the invariant measures at harder, more expensive high-Peclet regimes.
key_claims: DeepParticle combines deep learning, optimal transport, and interacting particle computation.
The method focuses on Fisher-KPP front speeds in incompressible flows.
Front-speed calculations reduce to finding the principal eigenvalue of an advection-diffusion operator.
The Feynman-Kac formula provides a stochastic interpretation that particle algorithms can use.
The learned object is a parameterized family of invariant measures.
The method extends to learning stochastic particle dynamics like Keller-Segel chemotaxis aggregation.

important_terms.meaning: A method combining neural networks, optimal transport, and interacting particles to learn invariant measures for expensive physical regimes.
A probability distribution that stays the same as a dynamical or stochastic process evolves over long times.
A mathematical relationship that expresses certain PDE quantities as expected values computed along random-particle paths.
A simulation using many particles whose dynamics affect each other or are resampled to represent a probability distribution.
An optimal-transport distance that measures the minimum total distance all particles must move to transform one probability distribution into another.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects stochastic dynamics, PDE analysis, optimal transport, and deep learning.
It differs from talks on operator learning by targeting invariant distributions instead of only learning input-output mappings of PDE solutions.
It also relates to rare-event simulation and multiscale methods because the technique targets expensive parameter regimes that would be costly to compute directly.
practical_caution: Learning invariant measures at moderate parameters does not guarantee accuracy at extreme parameters. Extrapolation to higher Peclet numbers must be checked against physics or more detailed simulations.
selected_evidence: DeepParticle.
Optimal transport (OT), and interacting particle (IP) approach.
Feynman-Kac formula.
Large time-invariant measure.
The invariant measure is parameterized by a physical parameter (the Peclet number).
takeaway: The first-principles insight is that some high-dimensional PDE questions become learnable by targeting the long-time distributional property that controls the answer.

title: Guang Lin: Towards Third Wave AI: Interpretable, Robust Trustworthy Machine Learning
speaker: Guang Lin
one_sentence: This lecture frames trustworthy scientific AI as a combination of neural operators (models that learn mappings between functions), uncertainty quantification (estimates of how sure the model should be), physics knowledge, and causal modeling (finding what causes what in data).
core_problem: Scientific and public-health decisions need real-time prediction, surveillance, and defense, but models that hide their inner workings without uncertainty or interpretability (how you can understand what the model is doing) are risky. The question is how to make machine learning reliable enough for high-stakes dynamical systems where errors have real consequences.
first_principles_model: Third Wave AI moves beyond pure data fitting toward models that combine learning, uncertainty, physics, and causal structure. Neural operator architectures learn mappings between functions while also producing uncertainty estimates. Multifidelity approaches combine data from multiple sources with different costs or accuracy levels, federated learning preserves distributed data privacy constraints, and Bayesian methods quantify how certain the model should be. Physics knowledge and causal discovery (methods that infer what causes what from data) help make the resulting models more interpretable and trustworthy.
key_claims: Trustworthy AI requires prediction plus uncertainty, reliability, and the ability to understand how the model works.
Neural operator networks can learn nonlinear operators from functions.
Bayesian neural operators provide simultaneous uncertainty estimates.
Multifidelity and federated architectures handle data from different sources and respect privacy constraints on distributed data.
Physics knowledge can be incorporated to design models you can understand better.
Applications include COVID-19 prediction with uncertainty and causal discovery for Alzheimer's disease.

important_terms.meaning: An AI approach that emphasizes systems that are contextual, interpretable (you can understand what they're doing), reliable, and trustworthy rather than models that work but hide their logic.
A neural architecture designed to learn mappings between functions or fields.
A neural operator that adds uncertainty modeling, so it can say how confident it is.
Learning that combines data of different cost, resolution, or accuracy.
Methods that infer what actually causes what from data rather than only measuring correlations (whether things move together).

stanford_connections: This talk connects neural operators, uncertainty quantification, federated learning, and trustworthy scientific machine learning.
It complements earlier safety and reliability discussions by treating uncertainty and interpretability as core model outputs.
It also links scientific ML to public-health and biomedical decision support.
practical_caution: Trustworthy AI is not achieved by adding uncertainty bars alone. The uncertainty model, causal assumptions, data quality, and feedback from real deployments all need validation.
selected_evidence: Interpretable, Robust Trustworthy Machine Learning.
Nonlinear operators from functions with simultaneous uncertainty estimates.
Multi-fidelity, federated, Bayesian neural operator network architectures.
Physics Knowledge and AI.
Data-driven causal model discovery and personalized prediction in Alzheimer's disease.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific AI becomes ready to deploy only when prediction is paired with uncertainty, interpretability (showing your reasoning), and domain structure.

title: George M. Bollas: Physics-Informed Machine Learning through Symbolic Regression
speaker: George M. Bollas
one_sentence: This lecture shows how symbolic regression—a search method that discovers mathematical expressions—can recover interpretable physics models from scarce and noisy data.
core_problem: Many engineering systems need actual equations, not just predictions that say what will happen next. This is especially true when data are scarce, noisy, or when you need to diagnose what's wrong or predict what comes next. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) can fit differential equations (rules about how things change), but they can be slow and don't directly show you the governing equation itself.
first_principles_model: Symbolic regression searches over possible mathematical expressions to find compact equations that match observed data. When combined with automatic differentiation (a method to compute derivatives exactly through the chain rule), it can estimate how quantities change over time from data and search for differential equation terms without needing to solve candidate equations repeatedly. Genetic programming (an evolutionary search that creates and mutates equations like biological evolution) can also add new symbolic equations to an existing model to show how a fault spreads over time.
key_claims: Symbolic regression is useful when you want to discover the actual model instead of just making predictions.
The method works well when you have little data.
The approach holds up even with high noise, including as much as 50 percent noise added to measurements.
Automatic differentiation removes the need to solve differential equations over and over during discovery.
Comparing symbolic regression with PINNs shows different tradeoffs—equation discovery versus fitting while respecting differential equations.
Fault detection and predicting how faults evolve both benefit from symbolic expressions that describe fault progression analytically.

important_terms.meaning: A search procedure that discovers mathematical expressions to fit data by testing many possible combinations of operations.
An evolutionary search method that creates, combines, and mutates candidate equations to find better ones, similar to how species adapt.
A computational method that computes exact derivatives (rates of change) by applying the chain rule through a program or neural network.
Finding the partial differential equations (rules describing how quantities change across space and time) from observed data.
Predicting how a system fault or damage will grow or worsen over time.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects sparse model discovery (finding the smallest set of equations needed), Physics-Informed Neural Networks, symbolic methods, and interpretable scientific machine learning.
It complements the broader physics-informed learning thread by emphasizing recovery of closed-form equations (equations you can write down and solve by hand).
It also links to industrial digital twins (virtual copies of real systems), where discovered equations can support diagnosis and prognosis.
practical_caution: Symbolic regression can find elegant-looking but false equations if the candidate library of terms, derivative estimates, or noise handling are poor. Finding an equation that looks right does not replace the need to test it against new data.
selected_evidence: Physics-informed machine learning through symbolic regression.
Successful model recovery with up to 50% noise.
Automatic differentiation.
Discovery of PDE models when data collection is expensive.
Fault detection and isolation.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that when decisions require understanding how things work, learning algorithms should try to find equations, not only predict outputs without showing the mechanism.

title: Francesco Ballarin: Regularized Reduced Order Models for Control of Navier-Stokes Equations
speaker: Francesco Ballarin
one_sentence: This lecture shows how adding smoothing terms and stabilization makes reduced-order models more reliable for steering incompressible fluid flows described by Navier-Stokes equations.
core_problem: When fluid simulations on a coarse grid miss fine detail, they produce wiggles and false oscillations. Reduced-order models (ROMs—simplified versions that run fast) make this worse because they throw away so much information. Add control to the picture: now the ROM must both simulate the flow accurately and steer it where you want it to go.
first_principles_model: Full-order simulations add dampening and filtering to stop the wiggles. A ROM compresses the flow field down to a few key patterns, but that compression can remove the natural dampening, making the reduced equations unstable. The talk compares two fixes: evolve-filter-relax, where you run one time step, filter out spurious high-frequency junk, then pull the result back toward the stable manifold (the set of states the system naturally prefers); and approximate deconvolution, where you filter and then try to guess what the missing high-frequency parts were. Both strategies then get plugged into feedback control (where you measure the flow state and use it to adjust your actuators).
key_claims: Smoothing is standard practice for full-size fluid simulations, yet few researchers study how to stabilize ROMs.
Flows where transport overwhelms diffusion, especially on marginal grids, are fragile to missing scales.
A ROM for control must stay accurate when you're feeding back the measured state, not just when you run it open-loop (no feedback).
Evolve-filter-relax smoothing can be used inside a reduced-order feedback controller.
Approximate-deconvolution smoothing offers a different way to recover the effects of filtered-out scales.
A good ROM balances speed, stability, and control accuracy.

important_terms.meaning: The laws that describe how incompressible or compressible fluids move, accounting for momentum and pressure.
A flow regime where material gets carried along faster than it spreads out, creating sharp edges and making numbers blow up on coarse grids.
A reduced model that takes one time step, removes high-frequency nonsense with a filter, then nudges the result back to a stable zone.
A technique that guesses what information was discarded by a filter, to restore accuracy lost during smoothing.
A method where you measure the current state of the system and use that measurement to decide what command to send, so the system steers toward your target.

stanford_connections: This lecture brings together ROMs, flow control, numerical smoothing, and closure methods (ways to account for unresolved scales).
It fills a gap next to talks on operator inference and projection-based methods by asking what happens when small scales destabilize a reduced controller.
It also touches digital twins: if you want a fast surrogate of a controlled flow system to run in real time, that surrogate must stay stable when you're steering it.
practical_caution: A smoothed ROM can stop wobbling but give you the wrong answer. For control, the smoothing must protect the dynamics you actually need to control, not just hide all the wiggles.
selected_evidence: Regularized reduced order models for control of navier stokes equations.
Under-resolved or marginally-resolved simulations of convection-dominated flows.
Incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.
Evolve-filter-relax regularized ROM.
Approximate deconvolution.
takeaway: Reduced-flow control needs stabilization designed for the shrunk-down equations, not just copying smoothing rules from the full simulation.

title: Yanlai Chen: GPT-PINN and TGPT-PINN
speaker: Yanlai Chen
one_sentence: This lecture presents GPT-PINN and TGPT-PINN as meta-learning approaches—methods that reuse pretrained PINNs—for fast solving of equations that depend on changing parameters.
core_problem: PINNs can solve nonlinear PDEs, but training them repeatedly for many different parameter settings is too slow for multi-query or real-time use. They can also waste neural network capacity because the same network size trains for parameter settings that need different amounts of capacity.
first_principles_model: A standard PINN learns one PDE solution by balancing data and physics residual losses. GPT-PINN changes the unit of reuse: it treats pretrained PINNs at selected parameter configurations as activation functions (outputs that feed forward into the next layer) inside a small outer meta-network. The outer network grows one hidden neuron at a time and learns how the solution changes across the parameter domain. TGPT-PINN adds a transformation layer before the pretrained PINN layer, enabling nonlinear model reduction (learning a simpler representation that still captures the physics).
key_claims: PINN training remains time-consuming in multi-query and real-time parametric PDE settings.
GPT-PINN is a network of networks in which pretrained PINNs become components of a meta-network.
The outer meta-network can be compressed to a single hidden layer with far fewer neurons.
The method builds the hidden layer one neuron at a time to find how many are actually needed.
The goal is accurate and efficient approximation across the full parameter domain.
TGPT-PINN adds a transformation layer to support nonlinear model reduction.

important_terms.meaning: A physics-informed neural network trained with losses that include differential-equation residuals.
A meta-learning architecture (a method that reuses pretrained networks) that combines pretrained PINNs to solve equations with changing parameters.
Transformed GPT-PINN, a variant with an added transformation layer for nonlinear reduction.
An equation family whose solution changes as physical, geometric, or boundary-condition parameters change.
A higher-level network that combines or controls other networks to learn how to reuse them.

stanford_connections: This talk connects PINNs, reduced-order modeling, meta-learning, and parametric surrogate modeling.
It complements neural operator lectures by learning a family of PDE solutions rather than retraining for each parameter.
It also fits the recurring DDPS theme of turning expensive repeated simulation into reusable learned structure.
