practical_caution: Pretrained PINN components are useful only if the selected parameter configurations cover the solution patterns that matter most. If coverage is poor, the meta-network can make predictions with high confidence that are actually wrong.
selected_evidence: Generative Pre-Trained PINN (GPT-PINN).
A brand-new meta-learning paradigm for parametric systems.
Its outer-/meta-network is hyper-reduced.
Grows this hidden layer one neuron at a time.
Transformed GPT-PINN, TGPT-PINN.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that parametric PDE learning becomes faster when expensive physics-trained subnetworks are reused as basis functions (learned building blocks) for a smaller meta-model.

title: Burcu Beykal: A DDPS Engineering Approach for Supply Chain Management and Enterprise-Wide Optimization
speaker: Burcu Beykal
one_sentence: This lecture applies data-driven process systems engineering to supply-chain and enterprise-wide optimization problems where planning and scheduling decisions depend on each other.
core_problem: Modern industrial enterprises coordinate many interconnected production, planning, scheduling, and supply-chain decisions. Optimizing each layer separately can produce infeasible or brittle operations because lower-level scheduling constraints feed back into higher-level planning decisions.
first_principles_model: Supply-chain management can be formulated as a hierarchical optimization problem. The planning layer acts like a leader choosing strategic or aggregate decisions, while scheduling layers act as followers imposing feasibility constraints from detailed operations. Bi-level programming (an optimization structure with a leader choosing first, then a follower reacting) captures this leader-follower structure, but large numbers of integer variables make the resulting mathematical programs difficult to solve. A data-driven process systems engineering approach combines data-driven modeling, process-systems structure, and optimization algorithms to make these interdependent decisions tractable.
key_claims: Supply-chain and enterprise systems are multi-dimensional, multi-purpose, and multi-product systems.
Reliable coordination across planning and scheduling layers is essential for efficiency, resiliency, productivity, and profitability.
Bi-level programming is well suited because scheduling problems can constrain planning decisions.
Integer-heavy scheduling subproblems create major algorithmic challenges.
A process systems engineering perspective provides structure for otherwise burdensome enterprise optimization.
Data-driven methods can support practical optimization across interconnected industrial activities.

important_terms.meaning: Optimization across multiple connected layers of an industrial enterprise rather than a single unit operation.
Coordinating material, production, inventory, logistics, and market-facing decisions.
An optimization structure with a leader problem and a follower problem whose decisions affect each other.
Optimization involving both continuous variables (that can be any real number) and integer variables (that must be whole numbers).
The field combining modeling, optimization, control, and systems thinking for chemical and industrial processes.

stanford_connections: This talk extends data-driven process systems engineering beyond PDEs into operational decision systems.
It connects data-driven modeling with constrained optimization and control.
It also parallels agentic planning: local feasible actions must be coordinated with global objectives.
practical_caution: A data-driven optimizer can recommend infeasible decisions if the lower-level constraints are simplified too aggressively. Enterprise optimization needs feasibility checks at the operational layer.
selected_evidence: Supply Chain management and Enterprise wide optimization.
Multi-dimensional, multi-purpose, and multi-product systems.
Optimal coordination of each element and their robust response to changing market conditions.
Bi-level programming is well-suited.
High numbers of integer variables are present in the scheduling problems.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that enterprise optimization is a coupled hierarchy: decisions are only good if they remain feasible across all planning and scheduling layers.

title: Yexiang Xue: Vertical Reasoning Enhanced Learning, Generation and Scientific Discovery
speaker: Yexiang Xue
one_sentence: This lecture shows how embedding explicit reasoning steps inside learning systems can improve generation quality, finding mathematical equations from data, discovering physical equations, and counting problems.
core_problem: Machine learning excels at finding patterns, while automated reasoning excels at enforcing explicit rules. Autonomous scientific agents need both skills, but combining reasoning and learning remains difficult.
first_principles_model: Vertical reasoning means placing a structured reasoning process inside or alongside a learned model instead of using it only after generation. In image generation, SPRING embeds spatial reasoning directly into a deep generator so outputs obey constraints and work on new, unseen data. In scientific discovery, reasoning shrinks the space of possible equations for symbolic regression and PDE learning to explore. In satisfiable modulo counting (a problem type combining logical rules with counting), reasoning over XOR constraints (parity rules) improves the guarantees a solver can provide.
key_claims: Automated reasoning and machine learning are complementary tools in AI.
Spatial reasoning can be woven directly into a generative network.
Reasoning steps can improve constraint satisfaction and interpretability.
Vertical reasoning can speed up finding mathematical equations from data and discovering physical equations.
Organizing XOR constraints can improve satisfiable modulo counting.
The larger goal is autonomous agents that combine learning and reasoning instead of picking one.

important_terms.meaning: A reasoning layer placed inside a learning or generation process to enforce structure and guide the search for solutions.
Spatial Reasoning INtegrated Generator; a generator with a spatial reasoning module built inside it.
Searching over mathematical expressions to discover equations that fit data.
A problem type that combines logical constraints with counting or probability reasoning.
Logical parity (odd-even) rules that can organize and speed up solver search.

stanford_connections: This talk connects directly to the first-principles reasoning and scientific discovery themes throughout the seminar.
It complements talks on finding mathematical equations from data, discovering physical equations, and generation with constraints.
It also ties to modern agent design: learned models need explicit reasoning and verification steps when constraints matter.
practical_caution: Embedding reasoning can improve reliability, but only when constraints are stated correctly. Missing or incorrect constraints can make the system confidently solve the wrong problem.
selected_evidence: Vertical reasoning enhanced learning generation and scientific discovery.
Spatial Reasoning INtegrated Generator (SPRING).
Embeds a spatial reasoning module inside a deep generative network.
Expedite symbolic regression, and to learn Partial Differential Equations.
XOR constraints enables solvers with constant approximation guarantees.
takeaway: The core lesson is that reasoning acts as an internal support structure for learning, generation, and discovery when a task has explicit structure to exploit.

title: Gianluca Iaccarino: AutoEncoders for Aerodynamic Predictions
speaker: Gianluca Iaccarino
one_sentence: This lecture uses autoencoders—neural networks that squeeze data into a compact form and then unpack it—to learn small-scale representations that predict aerodynamic flow over different wing shapes.
core_problem: Predicting aerodynamic flow over many wing shapes requires fast generation of new flow cases, but flow fields live in high dimensions and behave in nonlinear ways. Linear compression (squeezing the data along straight lines) can miss the structure of separated flow (where the flow peels away from the surface), while nonlinear compression raises questions about whether you can trust the predictions and measure their uncertainty.
first_principles_model: An autoencoder maps a high-dimensional flow field into a low-dimensional latent code (a compact summary) and then reconstructs a flow field from that code. With a carefully built dataset, the latent variables can line up with aerodynamic inputs and performance quantities that matter. The lecture compares nonlinear autoencoder compression against Gaussian process regression (a statistical method) and linear compression, while measuring uncertainty from architecture choices, hyperparameters (tuning knobs), and how much training data you have.
key_claims: Autoencoders can provide nonlinear compression for aerodynamic flow data.
The latent representation can support prediction for new wing geometries.
Building the dataset carefully can make latent variables match aerodynamic performance in ways you can understand.
The method works for both attached flow and separated flow conditions.
Uncertainty comes from architecture choices, hyperparameters, and how much training data you use.
Comparisons with Gaussian processes and linear compression show when nonlinear latent models actually help.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to squeeze data into a compact form and rebuild it from that compact form.
A learned low-dimensional coordinate that captures the most important ways the original data varies.
A flow regime where the boundary layer (the thin layer of fluid next to a surface) detaches, creating complex wake behavior.
Uncertainty caused by decisions in how you build the model or what you assume, separate from noise in the data.
Shrinking data into fewer dimensions using curved surfaces rather than straight lines.

stanford_connections: This talk connects autoencoders, reduced-order models (simplified versions that run fast), latent spaces (compact summaries), and uncertainty-aware aerodynamic prediction.
It extends talks about nonlinear reduced-order models by focusing on whether the latent coordinates actually mean something in aerodynamics.
It also applies to design workflows, where new wing shapes must be evaluated quickly.
practical_caution: A smooth latent space can appear interpretable while actually hiding problems when you predict outside the training region. Trust requires checking whether small changes to the architecture break the results, whether the training data covers the cases you care about, and how well the method performs on flow conditions it has never seen.
selected_evidence: Auto encoders for aerodynamic predictions.
Non-linear compression to construct a low-dimensional latent representation.
Generate new (unseen) cases.
Latent variables that can be interpreted in terms of aerodynamic performance.
Uncertainties due to the autoencoder architecture, the hyperparameters and the amount of the training data.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that useful aerodynamic machine learning compresses flow fields into latent variables that predict accurately, explain what is happening, and track uncertainty.

title: Fabio Giampaolo: Learning Paradigms for Neural Networks: The Locally Backpropagated Forward-Forward Algorithm
speaker: Fabio Giampaolo
one_sentence: This lecture explores an alternative training method for neural networks that combines local gradient updates with Geoffrey Hinton's forward-forward idea, which trains layers using local quality measures instead of a global backward pass.
core_problem: Backpropagation works well but can fail when models include parts that don't have smooth gradients (non-differentiable components), run on different kinds of hardware spread across a network, or contain physics simulations that don't fit into a single end-to-end calculation of gradients.
first_principles_model: Standard backpropagation optimizes one global goal by sending error signals backward through the whole network. The forward-forward algorithm instead trains each layer using local quality scores that measure how well the layer separates correct answers from incorrect ones. The locally backpropagated forward-forward strategy keeps gradient-based learning inside local sections of the network while reducing the need for a single global backward signal that travels all the way through.
key_claims: Backpropagation remains the most widely used neural-network training method.
Some real-world and physics-based settings reveal where global end-to-end backpropagation breaks down.
Parts that don't have smooth gradients can stop standard error signals from flowing backward.
Training spread across different computer types pushes us toward local training strategies that don't need a single global signal.
The locally backpropagated forward-forward algorithm merges backpropagation with forward-forward training.
The goal is to expand where deep-learning methods can work.

important_terms.meaning: The standard method for computing how to change each part of a neural network using calculus chain rule, by sending error signals backward through layers.

A training method developed by Geoffrey Hinton that uses only forward passes and local quality measures—comparing how the network responds to correct versus incorrect examples—instead of computing backward gradients.
Training where individual layers or modules use their own local goals instead of relying only on a single global error signal sent from the final output.
A part of the model where the output does not change smoothly with its input or parameters, which breaks the continuous gradient chain that backpropagation needs.
A group of different computer processors or systems with different speeds, memory, or computing styles working together.

stanford_connections: This talk connects how we design learning algorithms, how to train neural networks across many machines, and how to build machine-learning models for science and physics.
It builds on physics-informed talks where assuming smooth gradients doesn't hold, showing what to do when the math breaks those assumptions.
It also fits into wider conversations about what makes learning work beyond just transformer architecture—the actual training rules themselves determine progress.
practical_caution: Alternative training methods must be judged by how stable they are when training, how well they scale to larger networks, and actual task performance—not just by whether they sound more like how brains work or fit better on distributed computers.
selected_evidence: Backpropagation is the most widely used method for training Neural Networks.
Non-differentiable components within neural architectures.
Distributed learning on heterogeneous devices.
Locally Backpropagated Forward Forward training strategy.
Merges the effectiveness of backpropagation with the appealing attributes of the Forward-Forward algorithm.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that local training goals can make learning more separate and modular, but they still need to solve the credit-assignment problem (how each part of the network learns which of its changes help or hurt the final answer) well enough to match backpropagation.

title: Doug James: Recent Progress in Reduced-Order Modeling for Computer Graphics and Sound
speaker: Doug James
one_sentence: This lecture shows how reduced-order modeling—a way to build simpler versions of complex physical systems while keeping their essential behavior—supports art-directable physics simulation and physically based sound synthesis.
core_problem: Graphics and sound applications need physically plausible simulations that are fast, controllable, and stable for artists and interactive systems. Full simulation can be too expensive, while coarse simulation may produce different folds, wrinkles, drapes, or acoustic behavior when made finer in resolution.
first_principles_model: Reduced-order modeling can preserve essential physical behavior while lowering simulation cost. For cloth and thin shells, progressive simulation uses coarse-to-fine level-of-detail methods based on multiscale model reduction for incremental potential contact (a way to handle collisions robustly in deformable materials), allowing designers to work coarsely and then increase resolution consistently. For water sound, reduced vibration models of coupled acoustic bubbles (interacting bubble oscillators) synthesize physically grounded audio from fluid events.
key_claims: Progressive simulation enables art-directable physics for cloth and thin shells.
Coarse-to-fine level-of-detail methods can support both quasistatic and dynamic scenarios.
Multiscale model reduction helps preserve consistency when simulations are made finer in resolution.
A core goal is avoiding artifacts or unexpected changes in folds, wrinkles, and drapes.
Reduced-order vibration models can synthesize water sounds using coupled acoustic bubbles.
Graphics applications require both physical plausibility and controllable workflows.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation workflow that starts coarse and increases resolution while maintaining consistent behavior.
A representation strategy that changes simulation or rendering resolution depending on need.
A method for reliably handling contact and collision in deformable simulation.
Interacting bubble oscillators that contribute to physically based water sound.
Physical simulation designed to be controllable by artists while remaining plausible.

stanford_connections: This talk connects reduced-order models with computer graphics, sound synthesis, and human-in-the-loop design.
It complements engineering reduced-order model lectures by emphasizing perceptual and creative constraints.
It also links multiscale modeling to practical interactive simulation.
practical_caution: Graphics reduced-order models are judged by consistency and plausibility as well as physical error. A reduced model that is numerically accurate but artistically uncontrollable can still fail the application.
selected_evidence: Recent progress in reduced-order modeling for computer graphics and sound.
Progressive simulation for art-directable physics.
Coarse-to-fine, level-of-detail simulation methods.
Up-res and still get consistent, higher-fidelity results.
Reduced-order vibration models for synthesizing water sound using coupled acoustic bubbles.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that reduced-order models are not only for engineering prediction; they also make physical simulation usable in creative, interactive, and perceptual systems.

title: Francesco Romor: Intrusive Model Order Reduction Using Neural Network Approximants
speaker: Francesco Romor
one_sentence: This lecture describes an intrusive and interpretable reduced model that uses neural networks to approximate the curved surface where solutions live while keeping the physical equations active during prediction.
core_problem: Linear projection-based reduced models fail when the solution manifold (the set of all possible answers as parameters change) has slowly decaying Kolmogorov n-width, which means you need many reduced modes to get accuracy. Neural networks can approximate curved manifolds well, but most neural-network reduced models become data-only surrogates that throw away the governing equations during prediction.
first_principles_model: The method keeps the physical and numerical model running during the prediction phase while using neural networks to approximate the curved solution manifold. Autoencoders (neural networks that compress data by learning to squeeze and unsqueeze it through a narrow middle layer) compress linear approximations into fewer coordinates. Hyper-reduction techniques then lower the cost of evaluating the retained model terms, so the approach combines the power of nonlinear approximation with the interpretability of keeping the physics equations visible.
key_claims: Slow Kolmogorov n-width decay limits how well linear reduced modes can approximate curved solution manifolds.
Neural networks can accurately approximate the curved surface where solutions live.
Most existing implementations abandon the equations and become data-only surrogates.
The proposed method stays intrusive by keeping the physical and numerical model running during prediction.
Autoencoders can squeeze the dimensionality of linear approximations into lower-dimensional coordinates.
Adaptive hyper-reduction is necessary to make the retained model computationally affordable.

important_terms.meaning: Model order reduction that requires direct access to the governing equations or numerical operators.
A measure of how well a curved solution surface can be approximated by an n-dimensional flat subspace.
The collection of all solutions that emerge as parameters or input values change.
A neural network that learns to compress data by encoding it into a narrow middle layer and then decoding it back.
Techniques that reduce the computational cost of evaluating nonlinear or high-dimensional terms in a reduced model.

stanford_connections: This talk connects intrusive reduced models, autoencoders, curved solution surfaces, and scientific machine learning.
It contrasts with data-only neural surrogate talks by explaining why keeping the equations matters.
It also relates to manifold-learning discussions showing that flat subspaces are often not enough.
practical_caution: Intrusive neural reduced models need direct access to and careful handling of the governing numerical model. They offer more visibility than data-only surrogates but become harder to deploy when you have only input-output simulator data and no access to the equations themselves.
selected_evidence: Intrusive model order reduction of parametric PDEs using neural networks.
Slowly decaying Kolmogorov n-width.
Neural networks as solution manifold approximants.
Retaining the underlying physical and numerical models during the predictive/online stage.
Autoencoders to further compress the dimensionality.
takeaway: The lesson is that nonlinear neural compression can work alongside intrusive physics rather than replacing the equations entirely.

title: Alberto Padovan: Model Reduction via Optimization of Projection Operators and Reduced-Order Dynamics
speaker: Alberto Padovan
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to learn oblique projection operators and reduced-order dynamics directly from data without access to the underlying equations.
core_problem: Data-driven model reduction usually starts with orthogonal POD (Proper Orthogonal Decomposition—finding the strongest patterns in measurement data). But when a system has large sudden swings in its transient behavior, projection along the orthogonal directions can actually distort the reduced dynamics even though POD identified the right low-dimensional subspace. Systems with opaque solvers are still attractive for model reduction, yet the standard approach falls short.
first_principles_model: Projection-based reduced models need two things: a low-dimensional subspace to project onto, and a projection direction that determines how the full state maps down. Orthogonal projection (perpendicular directions) is simple but may not preserve the important behaviors you're trying to capture. Oblique projection (directions not perpendicular to the subspace) can keep input-output relationships or transient dynamics intact, but it normally requires direct access to the governing equations to compute. This method learns both the oblique projection operators and polynomial reduced equations from measurement trajectories by solving an optimization problem on special curved spaces called Grassmann and Stiefel manifolds, which respect the geometric constraints of projection operators.
key_claims: Data-driven model reduction becomes possible when the solver is opaque and you cannot access the underlying equations.
Large sudden changes in transient behavior make orthogonal projections fail even when POD finds the correct subspace.
Oblique projection operators can capture dynamics more accurately than orthogonal ones.
Standard oblique projections require direct access to the governing equations, limiting their use.
This method identifies both projection operators and reduced equations directly from measurement data.
Polynomial reduced equations and optimization on curved spaces (Grassmann and Stiefel manifolds) provide the mathematical structure for solving this problem.

important_terms.meaning: A projection onto a subspace where the projection direction is not perpendicular to that subspace.
A method that extracts the strongest repeating patterns from a collection of measurements by finding the directions along which data varies the most.
Temporary amplification of small disturbances before the system settles down, even if it is stable in the long run.
A curved mathematical space where each point represents a choice of subspace with a fixed number of dimensions.
Simplified equations where the rate of change is given as a polynomial (sum of powers and products) of the reduced variables.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together data-driven model reduction, projection geometry, transient behavior, and optimization on curved spaces.
It builds on balanced truncation and control-oriented model reduction by showing that the projection geometry itself is a design choice, not just a byproduct.
It also addresses settings where the solver is opaque and the governing equations are unavailable, making intrusive methods impossible.
practical_caution: Learning oblique projections from data can boost accuracy, but it introduces challenges: the learned projection may not be unique, and the optimization can get stuck in local minima. Always test the learned projection on new measurement trajectories outside the data used to train it.
selected_evidence: Non-intrusive optimization of projection operators.
Large-amplitude transient growth.
Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD).
Oblique projection operators.
Simultaneously identify oblique projection operators and reduced-order dynamics directly from data.
takeaway: The core lesson is that model reduction is not just about picking the right subspace—the way you project matters as much as what subspace you choose. Different projection directions can mean the difference between a reduced model that predicts well and one that fails.

title: Elizabeth Qian: Multi-Fidelity Linear Regression for Scientific Machine Learning from Scarce Data
speaker: Elizabeth Qian
one_sentence: This lecture shows how combining cheap approximate data with rare expensive data makes scientific machine learning more reliable when you don't have much high-quality information.
core_problem: Scientific surrogate models (math stand-ins that run fast instead of slow physics simulations) often need high-quality simulation data, but collecting that data costs money and time. When you train a model on a small amount of high-quality data, it memorizes the details of what you happened to measure instead of learning the underlying pattern, making predictions unreliable on new problems.
first_principles_model: Multi-fidelity learning accepts a tradeoff: expensive simulations give accurate answers but you can afford very few, while cheap approximations are easier to get but biased (consistently off in some direction). The method stacks them: use lots of cheap data to shrink the wild swings in prediction, then use the rare expensive data to fix the direction bias. For linear models (where you're fitting a straight line through your data), this gives a clear, understandable way to see how mixing data sources at different quality levels helps when you have very little good data.
key_claims: When you only have a small amount of high-quality training data, the model learns noise instead of the true pattern.
Lower-quality data can help even when it's not fully correct.
The proposed method uses multi-fidelity linear regression as a starting point for understanding the bigger picture.
Real scientific problems naturally give you data at different quality levels and different costs.
The main goal is to make predictions trustworthy when expensive high-quality data runs out.
The method recasts small-data learning as a problem of balancing prediction swings versus prediction direction, with costs factored in.

important_terms.meaning: Training from data sources that differ in how much they cost and how accurate they are.
Accurate results, usually from full physics simulation or real experiment, but expensive to collect.
Cheaper results from simplified models, coarser versions of simulations, or educated guesses.
A model that represents what you're predicting as a straight-line function of the measured input values.
A situation where you have far fewer reliable training examples than the uncertainty in your model, leaving it prone to learning noise.

stanford_connections: This talk ties together uncertainty counting (how sure am I?), smart data selection (which new test should I run?), stand-in models that run fast, and science from very little data.
It adds to neural operator and reduced model talks by showing that what data costs and how good they are both shape what you can learn.
It also speaks to how to build good training sets when running a simulation is expensive.
practical_caution: Cheap data cuts down prediction wildness but brings in its own slant. Whether multi-fidelity learning actually helps depends on whether the relationship between cheap and expensive data stays the same across the range of situations you want to predict.
selected_evidence: Multifidelity linear regression.
Scarce data.
Limited expensive High Fidelity data.
Greater volumes of Cheaper low Fidelity data.
Address the small data Challenge.
takeaway: The core lesson is that small-data learning gets stronger when the model pulls information from readily available cheaper sources without losing track of which data you can actually trust.

title: Aditi Krishnapriyan: Bridging Numerical Methods and Deep Learning with Physics-Constrained Differentiable Solvers
speaker: Aditi Krishnapriyan
one_sentence: This lecture shows how differentiable solvers (numerical methods you can compute gradients through) let neural networks learn PDE solutions while respecting physics constraints and classical numerical structure.
core_problem: Machine-learning models for spatiotemporal systems (things that change over space and time) need to make accurate predictions even with limited training data, but purely neural solvers can skip the physics rules while purely classical solvers cannot learn new behavior from data. The goal is to build models that combine the best of both: learned patterns from data and reliable physics-based computation.
first_principles_model: A differentiable solver turns a numerical method into a trainable layer so gradients can flow backward through it. Instead of solving a PDE separately from training, you embed the solve—whether spectral (expanding in basis functions), finite-difference, or optimization—as part of the neural network graph. The talk covers self-supervised learning that shifts what basis functions the network learns in, plus simulation-in-the-loop approaches where you fold PDE-constrained optimization (finding the best solution subject to the physics equations) directly into the network.
key_claims: Machine learning is becoming essential for modeling systems that change over space and time.
Learning from small datasets requires strategies that guarantee predictions stay physically valid.
Self-supervised learning can retrain spectral methods to learn in more useful basis functions.
You can build learning loops where simulation and optimization happen inside training.
Combining numerical methods and neural networks as one trainable system is possible and useful.
General learning strategies that work across many different systems and architectures are needed.

important_terms.meaning: A numerical method whose calculations can output gradients, allowing it to be trained as part of a neural network.
Learning where physical laws or conservation rules are baked into the model or training, not just added as a penalty term.
Finding the best solution to a problem where all candidates must satisfy a differential equation.
A training method that runs the simulator or solver step-by-step during training or predictions, not just at the end.
A numerical approach that represents unknown quantities as sums of basis functions (like sine waves) rather than grid values.

stanford_connections: This work bridges neural PDE solvers, physics-informed neural networks, differentiable programming, and classical numerical analysis.
It extends physics-informed learning by embedding the solver structure itself rather than only adding loss-term penalties.
It also connects to inverse design and control systems because you can compute gradients backward through the solver to optimize inputs.
practical_caution: A differentiable solver inherits all the strengths and weaknesses of the underlying numerical method: its stability properties (how errors grow), discretization errors (approximation from continuous to discrete), and modeling assumptions. Making it differentiable does not automatically make the physics correct or robust.
selected_evidence: Bridging numerical methods and deep learning with physics-constrained differential solvers.
Differentiable solvers.
PDE constraint optimization layer in the neural network.
Self-supervised learning to change the basis of learning with spectral methods.
Fluid dynamics and transport PDE problems.
takeaway: The core insight is that solver structure—not just the loss function—can become part of the neural architecture, so learning respects physical laws while still tuning predictions to fit data.

title: Jianxun Wang: Neural Differentiable Physics
speaker: Jianxun Wang
one_sentence: This lecture presents neural differentiable physics as a method for combining incomplete physical solvers with trainable neural components.
core_problem: First-principles numerical models are essential for engineering prediction, but they can be incomplete, expensive, or too slow for inverse problems, optimization, uncertainty quantification, and real-time control. Pure neural models may be fast but can lose physical reliability.
first_principles_model: Neural differentiable physics treats simulation as a differentiable program composed of known physical components and trainable neural components. The physical part supplies conservation laws, discretization structure, or partial knowledge; the neural part fills missing closures, corrections, or unknown terms. Because the whole pipeline is differentiable, data assimilation and inverse/optimization tasks can update neural and physical parameters together.
key_claims: Traditional first-principles models can fail when the underlying physics is incomplete.
High computational cost limits repeated-query applications such as inverse design and uncertainty quantification.
Neural differentiable physics creates a differentiable programming environment for computational physics.
Combining incomplete physics components with trainable neural components produces stronger predictions.
Data-augmented simulation can improve predictive modeling and control.
The approach aims to unify numerical PDEs and deep learning.

important_terms.meaning: A method that embeds physics solvers and neural components in a differentiable computation pipeline so gradients can flow through both.
Computational physics enhanced by data-trained components that correct or complete the model.
A model for missing or hidden terms needed to close a reduced or approximate physical system.
A problem where hidden parameters, inputs, or causes are inferred from observed effects.
Programming where computations are designed so derivatives can be propagated through them.

stanford_connections: This talk connects differentiable solvers, closure learning, PINNs, and hybrid physics-ML.
It complements ROM and operator-learning talks by focusing on incomplete physics rather than only fast surrogates.
It also links to scientific AI reliability because known physics remains inside the trainable loop.
practical_caution: Hybrid models can hide errors in the trainable component. Validation should check whether the neural correction is physically meaningful or merely compensating for dataset artifacts.
selected_evidence: Neural Differentiable Physics: Unifying Numerical PDEs and Deep Learning.
Incomplete understanding of the underlying physics.
High computational demands of traditional solvers.
Differentiable programming platform.
Blend of the incomplete physic component and trainable neural architecture component.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that incomplete physics should be corrected inside a differentiable simulation loop rather than replaced wholesale by a learned model with no connection to known physics.

title: Akhil Nekkanti: Data-Driven Techniques for Analysis of Turbulent Flows
speaker: Akhil Nekkanti
one_sentence: This lecture uses data-driven modal analysis, especially SPOD, to rebuild, clean up noise from, and make sense of turbulent flow data.
core_problem: Turbulent flows are high-dimensional (many variables to track), nonlinear (output is not simply proportional to input), and unstable (small changes grow fast), yet they contain organized patterns that control energy and motion. Measurements and simulations are often noisy or have gaps, so analysis tools must pull meaningful patterns out of broken data.
first_principles_model: Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition is a frequency-domain (organized by speed of oscillation) version of PCA (principal component analysis, a method that finds the main directions of variation in data) tailored to flow data. It breaks turbulent fields into organized structures sorted by energy and frequency. Extending SPOD to low-rank rebuilding, noise cleaning, and frequency-time analysis allows missing regions to be estimated from patterns in space and time, and brief-lived structures to be tracked.
key_claims: Turbulent flows are hard because they have many variables to track, they are unstable, and they are nonlinear.
Data-driven techniques reduce complexity by extracting major flow patterns.
SPOD is a frequency-domain modal tool well-suited for turbulent-flow analysis.
Low-rank rebuilding can recover data with gaps or damage.
Frequency-time analysis helps study when organized structures appear and fade.
Organized structures matter for energy and motion even though turbulence looks chaotic.

important_terms.meaning: Chaotic, multi-scale fluid motion where instability and nonlinear effects create disorder.
Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition: a method to break flow data into pieces organized by oscillation frequency.
An organized region of flow that carries meaningful energy or motion within the turbulence.
Filling in missing or damaged parts of data using the patterns from the parts you can see.
Approximating data using just a handful of the strongest patterns instead of all the pieces.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together modal analysis, reduced-order models (simplified versions that capture main behavior), turbulent-flow diagnosis, and data repair.
It builds on POD/DMD/Koopman lectures by focusing on frequency-domain and brief-lived structure.
It also touches sensor placement and experiment design because missing data can be filled in using patterns discovered in the full data.
practical_caution: Low-rank turbulent-flow rebuilds can remove noise but may also erase rare yet important dynamics. Rebuild quality should be checked against real physical events, not just average error across all values.
selected_evidence: Data-driven techniques for analysis of turbulent flows.
Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD).
Low-rank reconstruction, denoising, and frequency-time analysis.
Gappy-data reconstruction.
Coherent structures are dynamically and energetically important.
takeaway: The foundational lesson is that turbulence analysis becomes doable by pulling out organized low-rank structure while keeping track of brief-lived anomalies.

title: Ching-Yao Lai: Machine-Precision Neural Networks for Multiscale Dynamics
speaker: Ching-Yao Lai
one_sentence: This lecture shows how multi-stage neural networks fit prediction errors one layer at a time to push scientific ML accuracy to the limits of what computers can store in numbers.
core_problem: Neural networks can theoretically fit any function, but in practice their predictions stop getting better at some error level above the precision needed for scientific computing. Multiscale dynamics (processes that matter at many different sizes and speeds) make this worse because tiny remaining errors compound across many scales and long time steps.
first_principles_model: A multi-stage neural network views learning as step-by-step error correction. The first network captures the main signal; the second network captures what the first one missed (the residual, or leftover error); later networks repeat this. By breaking the total error into pieces handled by separate networks, the method drives prediction mistakes close to the smallest possible error for double-floating-point numbers (the precision standard computers use) in a finite number of steps.
key_claims: Scientific problems often need much higher accuracy than standard neural networks normally provide.
Simply making networks bigger or training longer does not always break through the error plateau.
Multi-stage training teaches each new network to fix the mistakes of the previous one.
The method works for both pure curve-fitting and physics-informed neural networks.
Prediction errors can get close to the smallest floating-point accuracy a computer can represent.
This addresses a long-standing problem: neural networks have struggled to reach the precision scientists need for multiscale phenomena.

important_terms.meaning: The smallest difference a computer can distinguish in its internal number storage; for double-precision floating-point, about 15-16 decimal places.
Training a new model to predict the error (the leftover difference) that a previous model did not capture.
A sequence of separate neural networks, where each one is trained to correct the mistakes made by all the previous ones combined.
Physical systems where important changes happen across vastly different spatial or time scales that all interact with each other.
A standard computer number format that stores floating-point values with about 15-16 significant decimal digits.

stanford_connections: This talk combines ideas from numerical accuracy, physics-informed neural networks, error correction, and high-precision scientific computing with machine learning.
It complements talks on machine learning for differential equations by asking not just whether networks can approximate, but how accurately they can do it.
It also connects to long-time prediction problems, where even small errors from each step add up to large mistakes over many time steps.
practical_caution: Achieving machine precision on simple test functions does not mean the method will reliably predict in situations it never saw before. Precision (how exact the numbers are) should be kept separate from generalization (how well it works on new data) and whether the answers are physically correct.
selected_evidence: Machine Precision neural networks for multiscale Dynamics.
Prediction errors below a certain threshold.
Multi-stage neural networks.
Each stage utilizing a new network optimized to fit the residue from the previous stage.
Nearly reach the machine precision of double-floating point.
takeaway: The core insight is that neural approximation error can be attacked step by step: fit the function, then fit the remaining error, then repeat.

title: Marius Zeinhofer: Infinite Dimensional Optimization for Scientific Machine Learning
speaker: Marius Zeinhofer
one_sentence: This lecture shows how to design scientific ML optimizers by first choosing a method for the function-space problem, then converting that method into updates for neural-network parameters.
core_problem: Scientific ML typically treats neural networks as lists of numbers to optimize, but the real problem lives in the world of functions (curves you can draw on a graph). Working directly with numbers can hide what the problem actually looks like geometrically and make it harder to build algorithms that scale or make sense.
first_principles_model: The proposal is: optimize first in function space, then discretize. You pick an algorithm suited to the function-space problem, then convert it into a concrete update rule for your neural-network numbers using the tangent space (local direction) of your chosen neural architecture. This approach can re-derive existing scientific ML algorithms and adapt natural-gradient ideas, including Kronecker-factored approximations, for use on large problems.
key_claims: You can understand scientific ML optimization problems by thinking about them as infinite-dimensional (working with whole functions instead of just lists of numbers).
The talk shows that you should optimize in function space first, then convert to network parameters.
Algorithms should be built at the function-space level before you represent them using neural networks.
The conversion from functions to network numbers happens in the tangent space (the set of small, allowable changes) of your chosen neural architecture.
Well-known scientific ML algorithms can be re-derived using this function-space way of thinking.
You can transfer natural-gradient approximations that use Kronecker products to scientific ML optimization.

important_terms.meaning: Optimization over complete functions or fields, not just finite lists of numbers.
A numerical-analysis approach where you design the continuous (smooth, infinite-precision) optimization problem before converting it into concrete computer steps.
A collection of all possible functions (or curves) you could pick from; a mathematical playground where the elements are functions, not numbers.
A gradient method that changes your steps to respect the true shape and distances in your parameter or function space, not just moving in the steepest direction.
A way to approximate the curvature (how sharply the landscape bends) using a special product structure that keeps computation fast for large problems.

stanford_connections: This talk bridges optimization theory, neural-network ansatz spaces, PINNs (physics-informed neural networks), and how to train scientific ML models.
It complements talks about embedding differential solvers by instead focusing on the geometry of the optimizer itself rather than how the solver fits inside the neural network.
It also links to first-principles ML theory by treating neural-network training as a discretized version of functional optimization.
practical_caution: Thinking in function space can make algorithms clearer, but actually running them still depends on which neural ansatz you pick and how you convert the math into code. A sloppy conversion can lose all the advantages you got from thinking in function space.
selected_evidence: Infinite dimensional optimization for scientific machine learning.
First optimize, then discretize.
Function Space level.
Tangent space of the neural network ansatz.
Kronecker-factored approximation for natural gradient descent.
takeaway: The core insight is that scientific ML optimization should think about the problem in function space first, before deciding on a particular neural network size and shape.

title: Yasaman Bahri: A First-Principles Approach to Understanding Deep Learning
speaker: Yasaman Bahri
one_sentence: This lecture uses statistical physics (how large groups of interacting parts create patterns), exactly solvable models, mean-field theory (averaging effects across many units), and nonlinear dynamics to explain how deep learning works from the ground up.
core_problem: Deep networks work well in science and AI, yet treating them as unexplainable black boxes stops us from predicting what they'll do, controlling them, and trusting them. The field needs basic principles that answer: why do certain network designs, training methods, and learning behavior actually work?
first_principles_model: The lecture uses a physics method: find simple regions where the model can be solved exactly, solve them completely, then apply those solutions to understand real networks. When neural networks grow very wide, they connect to Gaussian processes (a way to think about probability distributions over functions) and kernels (similarity measures that let you do learning in hidden spaces). Mean-field and statistical-physics tools describe what happens as networks train and build their internal representations. Nonlinear dynamics provides the language for how the path an optimizer takes unfolds over time.
key_claims: Understanding deep learning is a major unsolved problem for AI and science.
Physics gives you tools to derive true principles, not just measure how well something works.
When neural networks are very wide, they relate to Gaussian processes and kernel methods.
Models simple enough to solve exactly help isolate what actually causes behavior.
Mean-field theories can describe the combined behavior of millions of neurons.
Nonlinear dynamics helps track how training and internal representations evolve.

important_terms.meaning: How macroscopic patterns arise from many tiny interacting components—like how heat emerges from jiggling molecules.
A way to assign probabilities to functions (rather than just numbers), connected to neural networks when they become infinitely wide.
A function that measures similarity between two things, allowing linear learning to happen in a hidden space of features.
A method that studies the average combined effects in systems where many units interact, instead of tracking every individual.
The study of systems where what happens next depends on current conditions in a way that isn't just multiplication by a constant.

stanford_connections: This talk directly addresses the study system's focus on first-principles understanding of AI.
It builds on discussions of how algorithms improve and how data quality matters by asking what deep learning mechanisms are actually understood.
It also connects scientific machine learning to broader learning theory through Gaussian processes, kernels, and training dynamics.
practical_caution: Exactly solvable limits reveal mechanisms but may leave out finite width (networks that aren't infinitely wide), finite data (real training sets), specific optimizers (like Adam), and design choices that often dominate what happens in practice.
selected_evidence: A first-principles approach to understanding deep learning.
Statistical physics, exactly solvable models and mean-field theories, and nonlinear dynamics.
Large-width deep neural networks.
Gaussian processes, and kernels.
Foundations of deep learning from a physics perspective.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that deep learning theory moves forward by finding simple regions where mechanisms can be solved exactly, not just watched and measured.

title: David Bortz: The Weak Form Is Stronger Than You Think
speaker: David Bortz
one_sentence: This lecture shows how weak-form methods make finding equations and estimating parameters work better when data contains noise.
core_problem: Early data-driven methods for discovering equations often minimized errors by computing derivatives directly from data at each point. Noise in the data makes those derivatives unreliable, which causes the discovered equations and estimated parameters to be wrong.
first_principles_model: A weak form multiplies the equation by test functions (auxiliary functions you choose) and integrates over a region, moving the need to compute derivatives from noisy data onto smoother test functions through integration by parts. This cuts down sensitivity to noise and errors from discretization choices. WSINDy (Weak-form Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) uses this idea to find equations, while WENDy applies similar reasoning to estimate parameters and quantify uncertainty.
key_claims: Finding governing equations is valuable because it produces scientific machine learning models that humans can understand and explain.
Methods that minimize pointwise equation errors perform poorly when data is noisy.
Weak-form methods address difficulties in building models, handling discretization choices, estimating parameters, and refining equations.
WSINDy enables weak-form equation discovery.
WENDy enables weak-form parameter estimation.
This approach can deliver big improvements in reliability, accuracy, and speed.

important_terms.meaning: An integral version of a differential equation, written using test functions you multiply by and integrate instead of taking derivatives at individual points.
A differential equation written by taking derivatives directly at each point without integration.
Weak-form Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics, a method to discover equations from noisy data.
A weak-form method for finding the parameters (numbers that define a system) in dynamical equations.
Finding the governing equations (the rules that describe how a system behaves) by observing data from that system.

stanford_connections: This talk connects symbolic regression (turning data into human-readable equations), sparse model discovery (finding which terms matter most), inverse problems (working backward from measurements to find what caused them), and noise-tolerant scientific machine learning.

It complements lectures on PINNs (Physics-Informed Neural Networks) and differentiable solvers by focusing on variational and integral formulations (different mathematical angles on the same equations).
It also bridges to real experimental data, where noise is always present.
practical_caution: Weak forms reduce noise effects but require you to pick test functions, set the size of integration regions, and choose a library of possible terms. These choices change which equations get discovered.
selected_evidence: The weak form is stronger than you think.
Weak form based scientific machine learning and inverse problems.
Noise-corrupted data.
Equation learning (WSINDy).
Parameter estimation (WENDy).
takeaway: The main insight is that integrating equations against test functions can turn a problem of noisy derivative calculation into one that is more stable and reliable.

title: Annalisa Quaini: Reducing the Cost of Ocean Modeling with a Data-Driven ROM and LES
speaker: Annalisa Quaini
one_sentence: This lecture combines POD (extracting the main patterns in data), LSTM (a neural network for sequences), and LES (simulating large features while approximating small ones) to speed up two-layer quasi-geostrophic ocean simulation.
core_problem: Ocean models such as the two-layer quasi-geostrophic equations need large areas and fine detail to capture turbulent motion. Running the full equations is slow, but simpler models must still keep the right potential-vorticity (a number that nearly stays constant in rotating fluids) and stream-function (the flow pattern) behavior.
first_principles_model: The approach has two parts. First, large eddy simulation uses nonlinear spatial filters to create cheap training data that still shows how unresolved small-scale turbulence affects the larger flow. Second, a data-driven reduced model applies POD to pull out the main patterns in each field and trains LSTM networks to update the reduced numbers forward in time. Together, the filter makes training data fast to create while the reduced model makes predictions fast to run.
key_claims: Two-layer quasi-geostrophic equations describe stratified wind-driven ocean flow.
High-resolution ocean simulation costs a lot because of large domains and the wide range of turbulent scales.
The proposed method joins a data-driven reduced model with data from large eddy simulation.
Nonlinear spatial filters are used in the large eddy simulation step.
POD pulls out the main modes for each field variable.
LSTM recurrent neural networks track how the reduced numbers evolve over time.

important_terms.meaning: A simplified ocean model that describes stratified rotating flow using potential vorticity (a conserved number in the flow) and stream function (the flow pattern).
A way to simulate turbulence by resolving the large swirls exactly and approximating the small swirls.
Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, a method that extracts the dominant patterns from simulation or measurement data.
Long Short-Term Memory, a type of recurrent neural network (a network that processes sequences) built to remember and update information over time.
A quantity in rotating stratified fluids that stays roughly constant and drives the dynamics.

stanford_connections: This talk connects reduced models, turbulent geophysical flows, large eddy simulation, and recurrent neural networks.
It complements climate and ocean surrogate modeling by pairing physics-based filtering with learned updates.
It also links to multiscale modeling because large eddy simulation and reduced models each cut cost at different stages.
practical_caution: The reduced model depends on how well the large eddy simulation captures the small-scale effects. If the filter misses important physics at the small scales, the LSTM may learn a distorted version of the dynamics.
selected_evidence: Reducing the cost of ocean modeling with a data driven ROM and LES.
Two-layer quasi-geostrophic equations.
Potential vorticity and stream function.
Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD).
Long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks.
takeaway: The core lesson is that ocean-model cost drops when you mix physics-based coarse simulation to generate data with a learned reduced model to make fast predictions.

title: Max Welling: Machine Learning for Molecules and Materials
speaker: Max Welling
one_sentence: This lecture surveys how machine learning is changing molecular and materials science through learned energy models, density-functional calculations, and math-based scientific applications.
core_problem: Natural-science problems like molecular simulation and materials discovery need accurate models of how atoms and molecules interact across different scales. Traditional physics equations are expensive to solve, while generic machine learning often ignores symmetries (patterns that repeat), conservation laws (quantities that never change), and the physical structure that should guide how the model works.
first_principles_model: Machine learning for molecules and materials builds in physical constraints—symmetries and conservation laws—to learn energy landscapes, atomic forces, how electrons behave, and continuum models that predict what happens at large scales. Learned force fields quickly approximate what expensive quantum or atomic-scale calculations would give. Density-functional theory (a physics method using electron density instead of full wave equations) and partial-differential-equation models are places where machine learning components can speed up scientific prediction while keeping the mathematical structure intact.
key_claims: Machine learning has become a major application area in the natural sciences, not just text and images.
Machine learning has made significant contributions to molecular and materials modeling.
Learned force fields are a central example of how machine learning can copy scientific models.
Density-functional theory and partial-differential-equation modeling are important areas where machine learning helps science.
Mathematics, physics, and neuroscience continue to inspire better machine learning algorithms.
Machine learning applied to science may help address large challenges like climate change.

important_terms.meaning: A learned model that predicts how much energy a molecule has and what forces push atoms around, enabling fast simulation without expensive quantum calculations.
A physics method for modeling systems with many particles by tracking electron density instead of solving full wave equations.
Computer calculation of how molecules move and interact with each other.
Finding new materials with desired properties by combining computation, experiments, and machine learning.
A choice in how the model is built, derived from physical principles like symmetry or conservation, that steers the model toward physically sensible answers.

stanford_connections: This talk connects foundation models for science, geometric deep learning (machine learning that respects shapes and symmetries), physics-aware architectures, and materials discovery.
It complements lectures on molecules, partial-differential equations, and neural operators by placing them as part of a broader shift where machine learning enters science.
It also links to the data-progress theme because high-quality scientific data and simulation results shape how well the model works.
practical_caution: Scientific machine learning models for molecules and materials must respect symmetries and physical constraints. High accuracy on benchmark tests is not enough if the model breaks on chemistries or material conditions it hasn't seen during training.
selected_evidence: Machine learning for molecules and materials.
Natural sciences.
ML Force Fields.
Classical DFT and PDE modeling.
Mathematics, physics and neuroscience continue to deliver inspiration for improving ML algorithms.
takeaway: The core lesson is that science machine learning works best when learned approximations are guided by the geometry and laws of the physical system.

title: Kyongmin Yeo: Reducing Data Resolution for Better Reconstruction: Super-Resolution of Navier-Stokes Flows
speaker: Kyongmin Yeo
one_sentence: This talk shows why deliberately coarsening data can improve reconstruction of fluid flows from noisy measurements.
core_problem: When we want to recover a high-resolution fluid state from low-resolution measurements, noisy data creates a painful choice: keeping every fine-grained observation preserves the nominal resolution but also keeps all the noise. The specific challenge is recovering the true state of a 2D fluid governed by the Navier-Stokes equations from measurements corrupted by random error.
first_principles_model: The method starts by averaging measurements on a coarse grid, intentionally sacrificing resolution to filter out noise. It then uses a dynamic observer — a system that watches measurements and evolves them forward in time using the physics model — to reconstruct the fine-scale flow. The core insight is that reconstruction quality is not monotone in measurement resolution when observations are noisy; a coarser but cleaner signal can actually be better input to a physics-aware observer than a fine but noisy signal.
key_claims: Super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution fluid states from low-resolution data.
For physical systems, empirical results need theoretical understanding.
This work studies noisy measurements of 2D Navier-Stokes flows.
Averaging over a coarse grid reduces noise at the cost of losing fine resolution.
A dynamic observer then reconstructs the full flow state.
The key tradeoff is resolution against noise reduction.

important_terms.meaning: Recovering high-resolution information from lower-resolution measurements.
A system that combines measurements with a physics model to estimate the true hidden state over time.
Fluid motion governed by the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids move under forces and viscosity.
Averaging measurements over larger spatial regions to reduce noise and resolution together.
A measurement corrupted by random or systematic error.

stanford_connections: This talk connects data assimilation (combining measurements with models), observer design (inferring hidden state), super-resolution, and fluid reconstruction.
It complements sensor-placement and state-estimation work by showing that how you preprocess measurements — before inference — can improve the final result.
It also relates to weak-form methods and denoising approaches because handling noise is central to scientific machine learning.
practical_caution: Averaging only helps if the lost fine details can be recovered by the physics dynamics and the observer. Averaging too aggressively can erase features that the model cannot rebuild from the coarse information.
selected_evidence: Super-resolution (SR) refers to the problem of reconstructing high-resolution information from low-resolution data.
Reconstruct the ground-truth state of 2-D Navier-Stokes (NS) flows from noisy observations.
Observation data is averaged over a coarse grid to reduce the noise.
At the expense of losing resolution.
A dynamic observer is employed.
takeaway: Better reconstruction can come from cleaner measurements, not simply from measuring at higher resolution.

title: Youngjoon Hong: Operator Networks Based on Numerical Analysis
speaker: Youngjoon Hong
one_sentence: This lecture proposes operator networks for PDEs with varying parameters, built on the same ideas that make finite-element and spectral-element methods (classical numerical techniques for solving PDEs on meshes) work well.
core_problem: Solvers need to find PDE solutions quickly and accurately, even when the PDE's coefficients or forcing functions change. Most learning-based operator networks need many input-output pairs from expensive PDE solutions to train. Classical numerical methods already capture the right structure for this problem—why build a solver from scratch when we could take what works and add neural learning on top?
first_principles_model: The approach merges deep learning for operators with numerical analysis ideas from finite element and spectral element methods. Instead of treating PDE solving as generic function approximation (fitting any curve), it anchors the neural network to how numerical methods discretize the PDE—breaking the domain into small pieces and solving locally. This design handles difficult PDEs like convection-diffusion (flow with smoothing) and Navier-Stokes (fluid motion) without needing paired example solutions.
key_claims: Operator networks can solve PDEs with changing parameters by learning how to map input properties (like coefficients) to solution functions.
Using the structure of numerical analysis methods improves how well operator networks learn.
Finite element and spectral element methods provide natural ways to split up the problem that neural networks can build on.
The method handles difficult PDE families across different parameter ranges.
You don't need thousands of paired PDE solutions to train the network.
Tests show the method stays accurate, generalizes well to unseen parameters, and runs efficiently.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network that learns the relationship between inputs (like a PDE's coefficients) and outputs (the solution function), rather than solving point-by-point.
A way to solve PDEs by dividing the domain into many small elements and approximating the solution inside each piece.
A higher-accuracy version of finite elements that uses special polynomials (spectral polynomials) to get very precise solutions without needing finer mesh divisions.
A PDE whose solution changes when certain numbers (the parameters—like speed, viscosity, or source strength) are changed.
A PDE where something (heat, pollutant, etc.) both moves with a flow and spreads out over time.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together neural operators and classical numerical methods, showing how to use the old tools inside the new learning approach.
It builds on work about learnable differential equations by going deeper: making the numerical analysis method itself central to how the network is designed.
It also relates to learning PDEs with less data, since building numerical structure into the network reduces how many example solutions you need to collect.
practical_caution: How you split up the domain and how fine you make the mesh still matters. The method works well in research papers, but testing across more types of PDEs and real applications is needed before assuming it will work everywhere.
selected_evidence: Operator networks based on the numerical analysis.
Solving parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) using an operator network.
Finite element or spectral element methods.
Without requiring paired input-output training data.
Accuracy, generalization, and computational efficiency.
takeaway: When you learn to solve a PDE with a neural network, the neural network should be built on top of the same ideas that already made numerical solvers work, not from blank canvas.

title: Kunihiko Taira: Extreme Aerodynamics: Flow Analysis and Control for Highly Gusty Conditions
speaker: Kunihiko Taira
one_sentence: This lecture studies how to model and control aircraft in extreme unsteady aerodynamic conditions such as gusts, wakes, and urban-canyon flows.
core_problem: Small and medium air vehicles can encounter atmospheric disturbances whose sudden forces are far larger than those assumed in traditional aerodynamics. When disturbances are this large, flight control can become difficult or impossible unless the flow is analyzed, modeled, and controlled in real time.
first_principles_model: Extreme aerodynamics treats unsteadiness as a dominant effect rather than a small variation. Large gusts, wakes, and instabilities interact with the vehicle on time scales comparable to when the flow becomes unstable. The high-dimensional flow must be reduced into control-relevant structures so that computational and data-driven methods can predict sudden forces and design control actions.
key_claims: Adverse weather and urban or mountainous wakes create strong large-scale disturbances.
Extreme aerodynamic conditions produce enormous sudden forces.
Traditional aerodynamic assumptions are insufficient when unsteadiness is very large.
The study focuses on analysis, modeling, and control of extreme aerodynamic flows.
High dimensionality and unsteadiness make data-driven and reduced-order approaches valuable.
Operations of fixed and rotating wing aircraft can be limited by these flow phenomena.

important_terms.meaning: Aerodynamic regimes with large unsteady disturbances and sudden forces.
A sudden change in incoming wind velocity or direction.
Actively or passively modifying a flow to achieve a desired aerodynamic outcome.
A force that changes rapidly over time rather than settling into steady behavior.
Aerodynamics where time-dependent effects are central to the flow and forces.

stanford_connections: This talk connects fluid dynamics, control, reduced-order models (simplified versions of complex flows), and data-driven analysis.
It complements turbulent-flow and aerodynamic-autoencoder lectures by focusing on control under severe sudden changes.
It also links to robust decision-making because the system must react under conditions outside the expected design range.
practical_caution: A controller trained or designed for moderate unsteadiness may fail under extreme gusts. Validation must include the rare high-amplitude events that drive risk.
selected_evidence: Extreme aerodynamics flow analysis and control.
Highly gusty conditions.
Strong large-scale atmospheric disturbances.
Enormous transient forces.
Analysis, modeling, and control of extreme aerodynamic flows.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that when disturbances are large, aerodynamics becomes a fast state-estimation and control problem, not just a steady-flow prediction problem.

title: Cecilia Pagliantini: Dynamical Approximation and Sensor Placement for the State Estimation of Transport Problems
speaker: Cecilia Pagliantini
one_sentence: This lecture studies how to reconstruct transport-dominated states from limited measurements using time-varying approximations and strategic sensor placement.
core_problem: State estimation asks for an unknown function from finitely many measurements. For parametric transport problems, the solution set may shift or deform in ways that fixed linear subspaces cannot capture well, making standard projection-based model reduction break down.
first_principles_model: The unknown state lives in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space (a mathematical space for functions with well-defined inner products), but its possible values lie on a solution manifold (the surface of all solutions as parameters change) generated by a parametric differential equation. A common strategy approximates that manifold by a finite-dimensional linear subspace and estimates the state there. Transport dynamics break this strategy because shifts and moving fronts need many linear modes to represent accurately. Dynamical approximation (changing the representation over time) and sensor placement (choosing where to measure) address both the representation itself and where measurements should be taken.
key_claims: The problem is reconstructing an unknown function from finite measurements.
The function is assumed to be generated by a parametric differential equation with unknown inputs.
The geometry of the solution set is not known in advance.
Linear model-reduction subspaces can fail for transport problems.
Sensor placement is central because measurements determine what state information is recoverable.
The talk combines approximation strategy with state-estimation design.

important_terms.meaning: Inferring the current state (everything you need to know to predict what happens next) of a system from limited observations.
Choosing where to measure a system to get the most information for reconstruction or control.
A system where features move through space, often making fixed linear subspaces inefficient for representing the solution.
The set of all possible solutions as parameters or inputs vary; a lower-dimensional surface within a higher-dimensional space.
An infinite-dimensional vector space with an inner product (a way to measure angles and distances), commonly used to represent functions.

stanford_connections: This talk connects inverse problems (inferring hidden quantities from observations), sensor placement, model reduction, and transport-dominated dynamics.
It complements oblique-projection and nonlinear-manifold ROM talks by showing where linear subspaces fail.
It also links to experimental design because better sensors can compensate for having fewer measurements.
practical_caution: A sensor layout optimized for one transport regime may fail when fronts or coherent structures move differently. Sensor design must reflect the expected dynamics, not only average variability.
selected_evidence: Dynamical approximation and sensor placement.
State estimation of transport problems.
Reconstructing an unknown function from a finite set of measurements.
Infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Ineffective for approximating the dynamics of transport problems.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that reconstruction quality depends on both how you represent the state and where you choose to measure.

title: Sung Ha Kang: Identifying Differential Equations from Single Observation with Numerical Methods
speaker: Sung Ha Kang
one_sentence: This lecture shows numerical methods for discovering the equations that govern a system from a single noisy measurement taken over time.
core_problem: Finding equations usually works better with many separate measurement runs or clean derivative data. But often you have only one noisy sequence of measurements, which makes taking derivatives, picking the right terms, and solving for the equation coefficients all unstable and unreliable.
first_principles_model: The governing equation is built as a sum of candidate terms—basic pieces like powers of the variable or combinations of derivatives. This turns discovery into solving a linear system where the columns are the candidate terms tested against the data and the unknown values are how much each term contributes. The talk covers methods including IDENT, step-by-step denoised differentiation, subspace pursuit (a method for picking the most important terms), weak-form recovery (using integrals instead of point-by-point values), and group subspace pursuit to handle noise and limited measurements better.
key_claims: The problem is finding differential equations from a single noisy measurement recorded over time.
A library of candidate terms—built from the data—forms the feature matrix used for recovery.
The unknown coefficients (telling you how much each term matters) are found using sparse methods or structured linear algebra.
Applying noise reduction before taking derivatives helps make the derivative estimates more stable.
Integral-based methods handle high noise and derivatives of higher order better than point-by-point approaches.
Group subspace pursuit extends sparse recovery to select related terms as groups rather than individually.

important_terms.meaning: Finding the differential equation that describes a system by working backward from observed data.
A table whose columns hold each candidate term calculated on the observed data.
An algorithm that finds a small set of candidate terms that best explain the data.
A version of the equation written using integrals, which avoids needing to calculate derivatives at each point (making it more stable when data is noisy).
Computing derivatives by first reducing noise in the measurement, then calculating the rate of change.

stanford_connections: This talk builds on symbolic regression (finding equations as formulas), weak-form discovery (using integrals for stability), sparse recovery (picking the right small set of terms), and numerical differentiation (computing rates of change from data).
It extends the WSINDy and WENDy lecture by tackling the hardest case: when you have only one measurement sequence.
It ties to model discovery where making equations interpretable and working with scarce data are both critical.
practical_caution: Identifying an equation from one measurement is highly sensitive to which candidate terms you include in the library and how you model the noise. Finding a sparse (few-term) equation does not mean you've found the true equation without testing it separately on new data.
selected_evidence: Identifying differential equations from single observations with the numerical methods.
Single set of noisy time dependent data.
Linear combination of linear and nonlinear differential term.
Feature matrix multiplied by a coefficient vector.
Weak form shows robustness against higher level of noise and higher order derivative.
takeaway: The lesson is that finding an equation from a single trajectory only becomes practical by imposing strong structure: sparse candidate libraries, noise reduction, and integral-based (weak-form) methods.

title: Johannes Brandstetter: The Next Wave of Scientific Breakthroughs Is in the Latent Space
speaker: Johannes Brandstetter
one_sentence: This lecture argues that scientific models trained on broad datasets will unlock new progress by learning useful latent spaces—simplified, learned representations—for complex physical systems.
core_problem: Scaling and language model methods have transformed how we handle text, but scientific and engineering domains need models that respect physical structure, multiple types of fields, geometry, and long-range dynamics. The question is where the next useful way of representing information for scientific machine learning will come from.
