first_principles_model: A latent space is a learned, compressed representation where complicated states become easier to model, compare, generate, or improve. The talk connects recent progress in weather and climate modeling, computer vision, physics-informed learning, neural operators (neural networks that learn mappings between functions), multi-physics modeling (systems where multiple physical processes interact), molecular dynamics, computational fluid dynamics (CFD: simulating how fluids flow and behave), and nuclear fusion. The claim is that scientific breakthroughs will come from latent spaces that encode the right physical variables and interactions.
key_claims: Scientific machine learning must adapt the techniques that work at large scale in language to engineering and physical domains.
Weather and climate modeling show recent successes in machine learning for science.
Scientific latent spaces connect ideas from computer vision, physics-informed learning, and neural operators.
The next challenges involve multi-physics systems, molecular dynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and nuclear fusion.
Latent spaces can support building models, generating new possibilities, and scientific discovery.
The value of a latent space depends on whether it actually captures the important physical structure.

important_terms.meaning: A learned, simpler lower-dimensional representation of data or physical states.
A model trained on broad scientific data to handle multiple tasks or domains.
Modeling systems where multiple physical processes interact and affect each other.
A neural network that learns mappings between functions or types of data.
Numerical simulation and analysis of how fluids flow and behave.

stanford_connections: This talk connects the DDPS technical arc to broader themes about models trained on large datasets.
It complements autoencoder, neural-operator, and materials-foundation-model lectures by making learned representation the central object.
It also links to earlier discussions on how AI capabilities grow with scale: what a model learns depends heavily on the representations and data distributions it encounters.
practical_caution: A latent space can compress data without preserving why things happen (causal relationships) or the underlying physical laws. Scientific value requires checking whether it actually predicts well on unseen problems, whether you can control the system using it, and whether it helps discover new scientific insights.
selected_evidence: The next wave of scientific breakthroughs is in the latent space.
Weather and climate modeling.
Physics-informed learning and neural operators.
Multi-physics modeling, molecular dynamics, computational fluid dynamics, nuclear fusion.
Scientific or engineering domains.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific machine learning progress often depends on finding the representation where the physics becomes simpler.

title: Mandela Quashie: Smarter Particles for Smarter Plasma Simulations: A Moment-Enhanced PIC Framework
speaker: Mandela Quashie
one_sentence: This talk shows how particle-in-cell simulations of plasma can work better if each simulated particle carries extra information about the local particle distribution around it.
core_problem: Plasma behavior (how charged particles move under electromagnetic forces) is described by equations that involve both position and velocity—a massive search space that's costly to simulate. Standard particle-in-cell methods work by following many individual particles, but they need huge numbers of them to get good results, and they often produce noisy, spotty answers when particles are sparse in some regions of the position-velocity space.
first_principles_model: In a normal particle-in-cell method, each particle represents a tiny sample of the full distribution of particles. The moment-enhanced approach gives each simulated particle not just a location but also local summary numbers—density, momentum, and higher-order statistics—that describe what the particle distribution looks like nearby. These extra numbers let you capture the distribution's shape with far fewer particles while staying true to the physics.
key_claims: The Vlasov-Poisson equations describe how charged particles move under mutual electromagnetic forces in a collisionless plasma.
This pair of equations is infinite-dimensional and computationally expensive to solve exactly.
Standard particle-in-cell methods are noisy and lack fine detail in sparse regions.
You can add moment information to each particle—local measurements of density, momentum, and higher-order statistics.
These local statistics let you represent the full particle distribution more accurately.
Fewer particles plus richer information per particle gives you better accuracy and speed.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation method that tracks individual particles while calculating forces on a regular grid.
Equations that describe how a distribution of charged particles evolves in space and time under the electric fields those particles create.
The combined space of positions and velocities that describes where particles are and how fast they're moving.
A summary number calculated from a distribution, like total density (first moment) or average momentum (second moment).
A mathematical function that tells you the density of particles at each point in position-velocity space.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together kinetic plasma theory, particle-tracking methods, moment averaging, and efficient ways to store information.
Later talks in this series cover related ideas: keeping structure intact in particle methods and handling collisions in plasma.
It sits within the wider theme of using localized statistics to make low-cost simulations physically meaningful.
practical_caution: Including these extra moment numbers makes each particle carry richer information, but those moments must change over time in a way that's consistent with the kinetic equations. If they drift out of sync, the method can look like it's conserving the right quantities while actually steering the physics in the wrong direction.
selected_evidence: Moment-enhanced PIC method.
Enriches each simulation particle with local moment data.
Density, momentum, and higher-order derivatives.
More accurate representation of the distribution function with fewer particles.
Noise and poor resolution in sparsely sampled regions of phase space.
takeaway: The core insight is that you can make particles do double duty: instead of just being point samples, they can carry local structure information about the distribution, letting you build accurate simulations with fewer particles.

title: Gabor Csanyi: Foundational Models for Materials Chemistry
speaker: Gabor Csanyi
one_sentence: This lecture surveys machine-learned force fields for materials chemistry based on fitting potential energy surfaces (the energy landscape that determines how atoms move).
core_problem: Materials chemistry needs accurate simulations of large material systems over long times, but quantum calculations are too slow for this. The challenge is to build force fields that handle reactions, involve interactions among many atoms at once, stay accurate, and work across different material structures and compositions.
first_principles_model: The core computation is fitting the Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface (the energy of the system as a function of where atoms sit) by learning from quantum calculations. Learned force fields predict energies and atomic forces much faster than quantum methods. Modern approaches use geometry descriptors that respect atomic symmetries (like rotations and reflections) and graph neural networks that pass information between atoms, often trained with active learning to reach accuracies of a few millielectronvolts per atom for the systems they target.
key_claims: A new task has become mature: simulating energy and forces for large materials systems.
The task centers on fitting potential energy surfaces from quantum calculations.
The resulting force fields handle reactions and depend on how multiple atoms interact together.
Modern force fields run fast enough to simulate real molecules and materials systems.
Training on selected data points can reach accuracies of a few millielectronvolts per atom.
Successful designs use symmetry-respecting geometry descriptors and neural networks that pass information between atoms.

important_terms.meaning: The energy landscape describing what a system of atoms is worth in energy at each possible configuration, after accounting for electrons settling into their lowest-energy arrangement.
A trained model that predicts the energy and forces on atoms for any atomic arrangement.
A neural network technique where atoms exchange information through edges in a graph while respecting physical symmetries like rotations and translations.
A training strategy where you run simulations, find configurations where the model is most uncertain or wrong, add those to your training data, and retrain.
How the energy depends on arrangements of three or more atoms together, not just pairs.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the materials and molecules focus from Max Welling's earlier presentation.
It brings together foundation models, geometric deep learning, active learning, and atomic-scale simulation.
It shows why physical symmetries matter for building machine-learning models that work on real science.
practical_caution: A force field can be accurate on the data it was trained on and fail dangerously outside that regime. Materials force fields need testing across reactions, defects, different crystal phases, and rare or unexpected atomic arrangements.
selected_evidence: Foundation models for materials, chemistry.
Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface.
Force fields.
Reactive, many-body.
Equivariant message passing networks.
takeaway: The key lesson is that materials force fields are learned simulations of atomic physics, and their reliability depends on capturing symmetry rules, conserving energy, and covering enough of the possible atomic configurations to generalize well.

title: Alessandro Alla: Data-Driven Algorithms for Online Identification and Control of Partial Differential Equations
speaker: Alessandro Alla
one_sentence: This lecture shows algorithms that learn unknown PDE parameters at the same time they control the system.
core_problem: PDE control usually assumes you know all the parameters and have complete information, but real systems have unknown coefficients, unknown starting conditions, sparse measurements at the boundary, or limited observations. The controller must make decisions while simultaneously learning what the system actually is.
first_principles_model: In the first case, assume the PDE produces measurements from a control input and starting condition. The controller begins with an initial guess for the parameters and computes control actions using the State-Dependent Riccati Equation (a method that adapts control design to systems where behavior depends on the current state). After each step, the observed trajectory updates the parameter estimates using Bayesian linear regression (a statistical method that treats parameters as quantities with uncertainty and updates them as new data arrive) until a stopping rule is met. In the second case, the method uses physics-informed neural networks (neural networks trained to respect physics equations) to handle incomplete information such as unknown starting conditions, sparse boundary measurements, and unknown PDE coefficients.
key_claims: The goal is to identify and control PDEs with unknown parameters in real time.
One scenario assumes you can observe the PDE state given a control input and starting condition.
The State-Dependent Riccati Equation produces a control rule from the current parameter estimate.
Observed trajectories are used to repeatedly refine the parameter estimate.
Bayesian linear regression gives a data-driven way to update parameters with uncertainty.
Physics-informed neural networks are used when the available information is incomplete.

important_terms.meaning: Estimating model parameters while the system is running and data are arriving.
Choosing inputs to guide systems whose behavior is described by partial differential equations.
A method to design control that adapts the solution at each state, generalizing classical Riccati methods to systems where the equations depend on the current state.
Linear regression where parameters are treated as uncertain quantities that shift as you gather more data.
A neural network trained by enforcing physics equations as constraints alongside data fitting.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together control theory, online learning, Bayesian updating, and physics-informed neural networks.
It extends flow-control and reduced-order-model control lectures by treating model uncertainty as something the controller must handle actively.
It also connects to adaptive digital twins because the model evolves as the system runs.
practical_caution: Online identification can make control unstable if parameter updates are noisy or delayed. The system that learns and controls must include safeguards, stopping rules, and control decisions that account for uncertainty in the current parameter estimate.
selected_evidence: Data-driven algorithms for online identification and control of partial differential equations.
PDEs with unknown parameters.
State-Dependent Riccati Equation (SDRE).
Bayesian Linear Regression.
Unknown initial conditions, sparse boundary data and coefficient in the PDE.
takeaway: The central lesson is that controlling a PDE with unknown parameters requires learning and control to run together as a single closed loop.

title: Raphael Pestourie: Input-Space Scientific Machine Learning for PDE-Constrained Optimization of Geometries
speaker: Raphael Pestourie
one_sentence: This lecture proposes input-space scientific ML, where learned models speed up PDE-driven design by learning solver inputs rather than relearning the PDE solution.
core_problem: Most SciML methods learn the PDE solution directly, forcing the model to relearn physical laws already built into the numerical solver. For geometry optimization, this wastes effort because the design variable is the input geometry and the solver already understands the governing PDE (the equations describing the physics).
first_principles_model: Input-space SciML keeps the physics inside the numerical solver and learns transformations or surrogate structure in the solver input space. Physics-Enhanced Deep Surrogates (PEDS) speed up simulation of PDE-driven properties, while HiLAB supports efficient search through high-dimensional geometry design spaces for PDE-constrained optimization (finding the best shape when the quality is measured by running a PDE solver). The method is tested on benchmark PDEs and nanophotonic metasurface design.
key_claims: Scientific ML can improve both simulation and optimization of PDE-governed properties.
Learning the PDE solution wastes effort by relearning laws already built into solvers.
Input-space SciML learns in the input space of a PDE solver.
The numerical solver stays responsible for the physics.
Physics-Enhanced Deep Surrogates speed up simulation of PDE-driven properties.
HiLAB enables efficient optimization across high-dimensional geometry spaces.

important_terms.meaning: Scientific ML that learns transformations of solver inputs while leaving the actual PDE solving to a numerical physics solver.
Finding the best design when each candidate design must be evaluated by running a PDE (partial differential equation) solver.
A learned speedup model that replaces expensive simulation while keeping a real physics solver in the loop to stay accurate.
Design optimization where you change the shape or physical form to improve some goal.
An engineered surface made of tiny repeated structures (smaller than the wavelength of light) that control how light behaves.

stanford_connections: This talk connects PDE-constrained design, differentiable solvers, inverse design, and scientific ML.
It complements neural PDE surrogate talks by arguing that the solver can stay as the physics engine.
It also links to materials and nanophotonics design where the geometry is the main input you can change.
practical_caution: Input-space ML can be efficient, but the solver determines what physics gets simulated. If the solver model is incomplete, input-space learning will optimize against incomplete physics.
selected_evidence: Input-space scientific machine learning (SciML).
Model the input space of a PDE solver, leaving the physics to the numerical solver.
Physics-Enhanced Deep Surrogates (PEDS).
PDE-constrained optimization of geometries.
Nanophotonic metasurface design.
takeaway: The key lesson is that for design problems, learning the input-to-solver interface can be more effective than learning the whole PDE solution.

title: Jingwei Hu: Structure-Preserving Particle Method for Collisional Plasmas
speaker: Jingwei Hu
one_sentence: This lecture shows a particle method for collisional plasmas that keeps conservation laws and entropy dissipation intact.
core_problem: The Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation (a model that tracks how particles distribute in space and speed, their electromagnetic fields, and how Coulomb collisions between charged particles reshape that distribution) describes plasma transport and collisions, but particle simulation methods must preserve physical invariants—quantities that should stay constant or change only in certain ways. A method that breaks mass, momentum, energy, or entropy behavior produces plasma dynamics that violate the physics.
first_principles_model: The method starts from a variational formulation (a way to write the collision equations as an optimization principle) of the Landau collision operator and regularizes it (smooths out mathematical singularities) to get a particle discretization. Collisional effects become a deterministic effective force that works alongside classical PIC (particle-in-cell, a standard plasma simulation where particles evolve while sending charge/current to a grid that computes fields). The discretization conserves mass, momentum, and energy while dissipating entropy—the disorder in the system monotonically increases, just as real collisions do.
key_claims: The Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation is a first-principles model of plasma.
The new particle method models transport, electromagnetic fields, and Coulomb collisions together.
The method comes from regularizing the variational formulation of the Landau collision operator.
The discretization conserves mass, momentum, and energy.
It dissipates entropy, keeping the thermodynamic direction of collisions intact.
The deterministic effective collision force works naturally alongside standard PIC.

important_terms.meaning: A kinetic model that couples the distribution of particle velocities, electromagnetic fields, and the collisional rearrangement from Coulomb interactions.
An equation that models how charged particles redistribute velocities when they collide with each other.
A numerical method designed to keep the invariants or physical laws of the continuous system.
The one-way increase of disorder in the system, consistent with how irreversible collisions always spread energy into randomness.
A plasma simulation method where individual particles are tracked, and the charge/current they carry is interpolated onto a grid that computes electromagnetic fields.

stanford_connections: This talk connects structure-preserving numerics, kinetic theory, and plasma particle simulation.
It complements moment-enhanced PIC by focusing on collisional invariants and entropy.
It reinforces a core DDPS theme: numerical schemes should respect the physics that define the model.
practical_caution: Preserving invariants is necessary but not enough. The method must also be tested for accuracy and speed on different plasma regimes: damping (how disturbances die away), instability (waves or structures that grow), and shock-like behavior (sharp transitions in density or temperature).
selected_evidence: Structure preserving particle method for collisional plasma.
Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau equation.
Particle transport, electromagnetic field effects, and Coulomb collisions.
Conserves mass, momentum, and energy.
Dissipates the entropy.
takeaway: Plasma particle methods should preserve the conservation and dissipation laws of the kinetic equation they are built to solve.

title: Siddhartha Mishra: AI for Data-Driven Simulations in Physics
speaker: Siddhartha Mishra
one_sentence: This lecture covers neural PDE surrogates and neural operators that speed up simulations used across physics and engineering.
core_problem: PDEs (partial differential equations—rules that describe how things change in space and time) are essential to physics and engineering, but solving them precisely with traditional numerical methods is very expensive. Fast AI-based replacements offer a cheaper option, but they must learn to predict solutions accurately even when the starting conditions, physical constants, or geometry change.
first_principles_model: Neural operators learn the PDE solution operator from data—they map from inputs like initial conditions, coefficients, sources, or geometry to the resulting solution fields. The talk reviews neural operators built with convolution (sliding filters across data) and attention (learning which parts matter most), graph structures for irregular meshes, transformers for arbitrary domains, and conditional diffusion models (methods that build solutions by removing noise step by step based on input conditions).
key_claims: PDEs describe how a huge range of physical and engineering systems behave.
Traditional numerical methods for solving PDEs are often too slow for practical use.
AI-based neural PDE surrogates aim to give both speed and accuracy.
Neural operators are a major machine learning method for PDEs.
Convolution and attention designs produce leading neural operators today.
Graph, transformer, and diffusion-based models extend PDE learning to irregular domains and generative settings where we sample new solutions.

important_terms.meaning: A model that learns mappings between function spaces—often from PDE inputs (starting conditions, coefficients) to solutions.
A trained approximation that predicts PDE solutions much faster than running a numerical solver.
A neural operator that uses graph connections to handle irregular domains or irregular meshes.
An attention-based neural design used here to learn PDE solutions and handle interactions across arbitrary geometries.
A generative model that builds outputs step by step by removing noise, guided by input conditions.

stanford_connections: This talk pulls together many DDPS threads: PDE surrogates, neural operators, attention, graphs, and data-driven physics.
It connects to talks on operator networks, differentiable solvers, and latent-space methods.
It also links to broader interests in AI scaling because neural operators are a domain-specific foundation-model direction for physics.
practical_caution: Neural PDE surrogates must be tested to ensure they conserve key quantities, stay stable, capture uncertainty, and work on situations the model never saw during training. Speed means nothing if the model misses rare or extreme physics.
selected_evidence: AI for data-driven simulations in Physics.
Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) model a large variety of phenomena.
Machine Learning/AI based neural PDE surrogates.
Neural Operators.
Graph and transformer based architectures for PDEs on arbitrary domains and conditional Diffusion models.
takeaway: The core idea is that neural operators try to learn the simulator itself—the map that takes in a PDE problem's starting state and parameters and produces the solution.

title: Youngsoo Choi: Defining Foundation Models for Computational Science: Toward Clarity and Rigor
speaker: Youngsoo Choi
one_sentence: This lecture asks what should rigorously count as a foundation model for computational science and proposes DD-FEM as one concrete path.
core_problem: Foundation models work well in language and vision, but in computational science the term risks becoming a marketing word. Without a shared definition, models for fluids, materials, climate, design, and uncertainty quantification may be labeled foundation models without meeting domain-specific standards for generalization, reuse, scalability, and scientific rigor.
first_principles_model: A computational-science foundation model should be reusable across tasks, scalable across problem families, and grounded in the actual structure of scientific computation. The lecture frames necessary and desirable properties and introduces the Data-Driven Finite Element Method as a concrete route: keep the modularity and mathematical discipline of finite-element numerical methods while adding data-driven machine-learning components that adapt automatically.
key_claims: The foundation-model idea is spreading from language and vision into computational science.
The domain needs a shared definition to stop the term from becoming empty.
Generalization, reusability, and scalability are central criteria.
Scientific foundation models must be judged against computational-science needs, not only machine-learning benchmarks.
DD-FEM combines classical numerical-method structure with modern data-driven adaptability.
The goal is clarity and rigor rather than picking one single fixed architecture.

important_terms.meaning: A broadly reusable model trained or designed to handle many different downstream tasks.
Scientific investigation using mathematical models, simulation, and numerical computation to solve real-world problems.
A method that combines finite-element structure (which divides space into small regions and solves equations locally) with machine-learning models that adapt to data.
The ability of a model or component to handle multiple tasks or systems without needing complete retraining from scratch.
The ability to handle larger problems, richer domains, or more demanding calculations without breaking down.

stanford_connections: This lecture ties together the playlist's reduced-order models, neural operators, materials science, and scientific-foundation-model threads.
It connects to the user's broader foundation-model discussions by insisting on definitions specific to each domain.
It also complements numerical-analysis-based operator networks by treating scientific computation structure as foundational, not optional.
practical_caution: A large model is not automatically a foundation model for computational science. The label should demand evidence of reusable scientific structure and proven generalization across real problems.
selected_evidence: Defining foundation models for computational science toward clarity and rigor.
Necessary and desirable characteristics.
Generalization, reusability, and scalability.
Data-Driven Finite Element Method (DD-FEM).
Modular structure and mathematical rigor of classical numerical methods with the adaptability of modern machine learning.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a scientific foundation model must be defined by reusable scientific capability, not by analogy to large language models alone.

title: Ulisses M. Braga-Neto: Scientific Machine Learning: From Physics-Informed to Data-Driven
speaker: Ulisses M. Braga-Neto
one_sentence: This lecture reviews scientific machine learning as a range from physics-informed collocation methods (enforcing known equations at selected points) to data-driven operator learning (finding the mathematical map from input to solution without writing equations).
core_problem: SciML combines scientific computation and machine learning, but different methods use physics and data in very different ways. Practitioners need to understand the tradeoff between enforcing known differential equations and learning directly from solution data when equations are unknown, incomplete, or expensive to solve.
first_principles_model: Physics-informed methods such as PINNs and physics-informed Gaussian processes enforce differential equations at collocation points (chosen spots in the domain where you check the equations hold). Data-driven operator learning instead learns the map associated with a parametric differential equation—the mathematical transformation that takes input data to solution—often without explicit knowledge of the equation itself. The idea is that the physics may be embedded in the data rather than written in the loss function. The lecture compares these regimes and discusses applications including plasma turbulence.
key_claims: SciML joins scientific computation and machine learning by applying neural methods to simulation, discovery, and inverse problems.
PINNs and PIGPs became widely used by making physics-informed collocation straightforward.
Operator learning is a newer data-driven approach to SciML.
Operator learning often does not require explicit knowledge of the underlying differential equations.
The physics-informed and data-driven approaches have different strengths and weaknesses.
The Hasegawa-Wakatani model of plasma turbulence is one application setting.

important_terms.meaning: Machine learning methods applied to scientific computation, simulation, discovery, and inverse problems (finding what caused observed measurements).
A physics-informed neural network that enforces differential equation constraints (the equation residuals must be near zero) during training.
A Gaussian process model incorporating differential equation constraints.
Learning maps between functions, such as transformations that take PDE input conditions to their solution.
Enforcing an equation or constraint at selected points in the domain.

stanford_connections: This lecture synthesizes many earlier talks: PINNs, neural operators, data-driven PDEs, and scientific surrogates.
It connects to the first-principles theme by clarifying where physics enters the model.
It also links to data-progress discussions because data-driven SciML moves physical structure into the dataset.
practical_caution: The idea that 'physics is in the data' is only true if the data cover the relevant conditions and actually preserve the physics. Otherwise data-driven operator learning can make poor predictions when the situation falls outside the data.
selected_evidence: Scientific Machine Learning: From Physics-Informed to Data-Driven.
Physics-informed neural networks (PINN).
Physics-informed Gaussian processes (PIGP).
Operator learning has emerged as a powerful SciML paradigm.
The physics is in the data.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that SciML methods differ mainly in where they put physics: in the equations, in the architecture, or in the data.

title: Nan Chen: Bridging Models and Data: Assimilation, Model Hierarchies, Causal Inference and Digital Twins
speaker: Nan Chen
one_sentence: This lecture uses data assimilation (updating model predictions with real observations) to connect model hierarchies, causal inference, and digital twins.
core_problem: Scientific systems have three sources of knowledge that usually stay separate: real data, simplified models that capture basic physics, and detailed models that handle real-world complexity. A working digital twin (a live copy of a physical system inside a computer) needs to combine all three, deal with scattered observations, and answer questions about what caused what and whether predictions will hold—not just forecast one step ahead.
first_principles_model: Data assimilation updates what a model thinks the system's state is (and the model's own settings) by comparing predictions to real measurements. The lecture extends this in three directions. Latent data assimilation—a technique where models of different complexity map into a shared compressed space—lets simple and detailed models trade information without rewriting either one. Assimilative causal inference uses Bayesian updates (a method for updating beliefs with new evidence) to trace backward from what you see to what caused it. Digital twins combine these assimilation and causal tools to test "what if this happened?" scenarios and predict rare extreme events.
key_claims: Data assimilation connects models and observations in a mathematically sound way.
Model hierarchies let you combine simple idealized models with detailed operational ones.
Latent data assimilation cuts cost and connects models that would otherwise be incompatible.
You can trace causes backward from observed effects using Bayesian data assimilation.
Answering "what caused what?" and "will this hold?" matters for climate tipping points and rare extreme events.
These tools are essential for building working digital twins.

important_terms.meaning: A method that updates a model's view of the system (its state and settings) by comparing model predictions to real measurements.
A set of models arranged by how detailed they are, from simple physics-based models to complex real-world versions.
Assimilation done inside a compressed representation learned from data, so models of different detail levels can interact.
Using Bayesian updates (mathematical methods for changing beliefs based on new evidence) to figure out what causes produced the effects you see.
A constantly updated computer model of a real physical system that predicts its future and supports decisions about it.

stanford_connections: This talk brings together data assimilation, latent spaces, digital twins, model hierarchies, and causal reasoning.
It builds on earlier lectures about oceans, underground reservoirs, weather, and uncertainty by showing assimilation as a common workflow across all of them.
It also connects to agentic reasoning because a digital twin lets you test out counterfactual scenarios ("what if we changed this?") before acting.
practical_caution: A digital twin can appear reliable while passing along bias from the choice of model hierarchy and the gaps in where you collected observations. Assimilation must track uncertainty and admit when models don't match reality.
selected_evidence: Data assimilation as a crucial bridge between models and data.
Model hierarchies.
Shared latent space.
Assimilative causal inference (ACI).
Digital twins.
takeaway: The core lesson: assimilation is not just filtering out noise. It is a bridge for combining models, observations, causality, and real-world decision-making.

title: Michael Shields: The Nexus of Machine Learning, Physics-Based Modeling, and Uncertainty Quantification
speaker: Michael Shields
one_sentence: This lecture explains how to measure and account for uncertainty in machine-learning models that simulate physics and make scientific predictions.
core_problem: Physics-based models have uncertainties in inputs, parameters, and how we model the world itself. When we add machine learning, we introduce more uncertainty from data, training choices, and whether the learned model works on new problems. Scientific predictions that matter need both machine learning and uncertainty measurement—not treating uncertainty as a last-minute afterthought.
first_principles_model: Uncertainty falls into two types: epistemic (what we could know if we had more information) and aleatory (randomness built into nature itself). In scientific machine learning, there are two directions. First: UQ for ML asks how sure we can be about a machine-learning model's predictions. Second: ML for UQ means using machine learning to speed up or improve how we calculate uncertainty through a system, build simpler models that replace expensive ones, figure out which inputs matter most, and solve inverse problems (working backward from measurements to find unknown causes). The lecture frames these roles as increasingly vital for broad scientific models that other researchers can trust.
key_claims: Uncertainty measurement and machine learning are increasingly needed in physics-based models that run on computers.
Physics-based models are filled with epistemic and aleatory uncertainties.
Adding machine learning to a physics model creates additional uncertainties beyond what the original physics had.
Uncertainty measurement has become central to physics-based modeling.
The talk separates uncertainty measurement of ML models from using ML to improve uncertainty measurement itself.
Scientific models that can be widely applied require methods that measure and account for uncertainty.

important_terms.meaning: Measuring and calculating uncertainty in model inputs, parameters, model structure, and what the model predicts.
Uncertainty from not knowing something that could be learned with more data or better measurements.
Uncertainty that comes from randomness or natural variation in the world.
Measuring how uncertain a machine-learning model is in its predictions.
Using machine learning to speed up or improve the process of measuring uncertainty in physical systems.

stanford_connections: This talk connects ideas about trustworthy AI, Bayesian methods for neural models, multi-fidelity learning (combining simulations with different levels of detail), and scientific foundation models.
It strengthens all other DDPS lectures by making uncertainty a main output alongside predictions.
It also ties to evaluation discussions: reliability means knowing when a model might be wrong and by how much.
practical_caution: Uncertainty measurements can give false confidence. They should be tested against known cases, checked on data the model hasn't seen before, and examined for how sensitive they are to assumptions about the model's form.
selected_evidence: The Nexus of Machine Learning, Physics-based Modeling, and Uncertainty Quantification.
Epistemic and aleatory.
Parameters, inputs/excitations, and sometimes in the form of the models themselves.
UQ for ML.
ML for UQ.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific machine learning is incomplete unless it measures how uncertain its predictions are and explains why.

title: Balint Kaszas: Invariant Manifold-Based Nonlinear Model Reduction for Fluid Dynamics
speaker: Balint Kaszas
one_sentence: This lecture uses spectral submanifolds (curved surfaces that organize the long-term behavior of high-dimensional dynamical systems) to build nonlinear reduced-order models for fluid dynamics.
core_problem: Fluid flows live in very high dimensions and behave nonlinearly, and linear approximations often miss sudden transitions, multiple steady states that coexist, or chaotic motion. A better model should capture the low-dimensional curved geometry that attracts and governs the motion.
first_principles_model: Dynamical-systems theory identifies invariant manifolds (geometric sets where solutions that start on them stay on them). Spectral submanifolds are nonlinear curved versions of the flat subspaces you get from linearizing the system near fixed states. When high-dimensional fluid flow quickly approaches or evolves along such a curved surface, you can restrict the full equations to just that surface, producing a small nonlinear model that still captures sudden transitions, coexisting steady states, and chaos.
key_claims: Model reduction for nonlinear systems can be grounded in invariant manifolds.
Spectral submanifolds are nonlinear curved extensions of flat spectral subspaces.
These curved surfaces can act as low-dimensional attractors that solutions approach.
Invariant manifold models capture the essential behavior of fluid dynamics.
The approach can represent sudden transitions between coexisting steady states and chaotic motion.
Examples span wall-bounded shear flows and fluid-structure coupling observed in measurements.

important_terms.meaning: A curved geometric surface such that any solution starting on it stays on it as time evolves.
A curved invariant surface that extends a flat subspace obtained by linearizing the system near a fixed state.
Shrinking the dimension of a system by mapping its solutions onto a low-dimensional curved surface rather than a flat linear subspace.
A set of states that solutions move toward and gather near as time increases.
A fluid flow confined between walls where velocity changes with position (shear), commonly used to study turbulence.

stanford_connections: This talk completes the model-reduction arc by connecting nonlinear curved geometry, dynamical systems, and fluid dynamics.
It extends autoencoder, charting, and oblique-projection lectures by offering a dynamical-systems grounding for what the reduced curved surface represents.
It also ties to Koopman and modal-decomposition talks through spectral structure and eigenvalue relationships.
practical_caution: Invariant-manifold models depend on whether the identified curved surface actually attracts the real dynamics across your operating range. If solutions suddenly jump away from the surface for part of the motion, predictions may fail.
selected_evidence: Invariant Manifold-Based Nonlinear Model Reduction for Fluid Dynamics.
Restrict high-dimensional dynamics to very low-dimensional invariant manifolds.
Spectral submanifolds (SSMs).
Low-dimensional attractors.
Transitions between coexisting steady states to chaotic dynamics.
takeaway: The core lesson is that nonlinear reduced models should project dynamics onto the curved geometric objects that organize motion.

title: Su Jiang: Generative Models for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow
speaker: Su Jiang
one_sentence: This lecture shows how generative models (systems trained to create realistic samples from learned patterns) can describe and sample high-dimensional subsurface states for data assimilation.
core_problem: Subsurface-flow data assimilation must infer hidden properties and forecast reservoir behavior in high-dimensional nonlinear inverse problems. Ensemble simulations are expensive to run, and geological structures such as fracture networks or faulted reservoirs are hard to describe efficiently.
first_principles_model: Generative models learn a low-dimensional or structured distribution over possible subsurface fields and responses. A latent diffusion model (a diffusion generative model operating in a compressed representation) parameterizes discrete fracture networks and is coupled with ensemble data assimilation to tune networks and improve flow and thermal predictions. Generative data-space inversion parameterizes spatiotemporal system responses, enabling posterior prediction of flow and geomechanical quantities for carbon storage in faulted reservoirs.
key_claims: Data assimilation is critical for inferring subsurface properties and forecasting reservoir performance.
The inverse problem is high-dimensional and nonlinear.
Ensemble simulations require significant computational effort.
Deep generative models provide efficient description and conditional sampling.
Latent diffusion can model discrete fracture networks inside an ensemble assimilation workflow.
Generative data-space inversion supports direct posterior prediction for flow and geomechanical quantities.

important_terms.meaning: A model trained to create samples from a distribution of plausible data or states.
Combining model predictions and observations to infer states or parameters.
Flow through underground porous media, reservoirs, aquifers, or fractured rock.
A diffusion generative model operating in a compressed latent representation.
An inverse workflow that describes and updates predicted observations or responses rather than only physical parameters.

stanford_connections: This talk connects generative models, latent spaces, data assimilation, and subsurface digital twins.
It complements Nan Chen's assimilation lecture by focusing on generative description for inverse problems.
It also links to uncertainty and foundation-model themes because posterior sampling is central to trustworthy prediction.
practical_caution: A generative prior can make assimilation efficient but can also limit posterior possibilities to what the generator learned during training. Geological plausibility and whether the posterior distribution covers all realistic outcomes must be checked.
selected_evidence: Generative Models for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow.
Inferring subsurface properties and forecasting reservoir performance.
High-dimensional, nonlinear nature of the inverse problem.
Latent diffusion model for discrete fracture network parameterization.
Generative-model-based data-space inversion.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that generative models help data assimilation by turning impossible high-dimensional inverse problems into structured conditional sampling problems.
